case_report: A 38-year-old premenopausal woman presented with a mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, measuring 19 × 28 mm. The mass was mobile and not attached to the chest wall. No palpable lymph nodes were found in the left axilla, and no mass was detected in the right breast. Mammography identified a 22-mm, well-defined, oval, isodense mass with partially indistinct borders (BI-RADS category 4). Ultrasonography showed a 20 × 15 × 8.8-mm, well-defined, hypoechoic lesion with slightly irregular margins in the outer part of the left breast. Bilateral breast dynamic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a well-circumscribed mass with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. On contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, the mass exhibited strong enhancement with a microlobulated margin. Dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging showed rapid enhancement of the mass, with signal intensity peaking within 90 seconds after the administration of gadolinium contrast medium.
test_results: Histologically, the tumor was identified as fibroadenoma with focal mastopathic change. Microscopically, Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed benign ductal and lobular units, adipose tissue, fibrous stroma and bundles of elongated spindle cells in a disorganized pattern. Immunohistochemically, the smooth muscle tissue stained diffusely positive for smooth-muscle actin (SMA), vimentin, desmin, and HHF35. In contrast, both cytokeratin and S-100 protein expressions in the stroma were negative.

case_report: A 62-year-old male reported experiencing tingling and numbness in the right upper and lower limbs for one month. Additionally, he described a burning pain in both upper and lower limbs for the past 10 days, which worsened when exposed to cold water. Initially, the symptoms began with tingling and numbness on the right side of the face and upper limb, eventually spreading to most of the right side of the body. Despite being evaluated and managed conservatively, there was no improvement. The patient follows a vegetarian diet. There was no history of neurological disorders such as confusion or seizures, nor other symptoms like vomiting, weakness, or fever. He also had no significant medical history, including hypertension, diabetes, or ischemic heart disease. The patient does not smoke or consume alcohol and has a moderately built physique with a body mass index of 22. On physical examination, his pulse rate was 88 beats per minute, and his blood pressure was 140/90 mmHg. Examination of the central nervous system showed an absent ankle reflex and impaired pinprick and temperature sensations, indicating peripheral neuropathy. Other neurological assessments were normal.
test_results: Peripheral smear was suggestive of macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils. A nerve conduction study revealed neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with magnetic resonance angiography and magnetic resonance venography was suggestive of acute evolving infarct in the left side of the body of the septum pellucidum and left thalamus. Magnetic resonance angiography was suggestive of normal course and calibre in the bilateral internal carotid arteries, vertebral artery, circle of Willis, and its branches. No obvious filling defects and dilatation were noted. Magnetic resonance venography revealed normal internal jugular veins and sigmoid, transverse, and superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant, born by cesarean section at full term to nonconsanguineous Bulgarian parents, had a normal Apgar score. The amniotic fluid was green, but there were no other signs of perinatal asphyxia. His birth weight, length, and head circumference were within normal ranges. At 3 months, he experienced feeding difficulties, including inconsolable crying after feeds and regurgitations. Movement issues such as dystonic postures and spontaneous Moro reflex were observed. Neurodevelopmental delay was noted: visual tracking of objects and faces was inconsistent; he began smiling at 3 months but then stopped and was not cooing. His 4-year-old sister had been diagnosed with dyskinetic CP, characterized by microcephaly, severe psychomotor delay, dyskinesias, and epilepsy. Physical examination at 3 months was normal except for a low growth rate in head circumference (−1.9 SD). Neurologic examination showed decreased neck muscle tone with absent head control, spasticity in the extremities, tendon hyperreflexia, and persistence of grasp reflex and automatic crawling. General movements were jerky and/or stiff, and dystonic postures were frequent. There was moderate psychomotor delay with a developmental quotient (DQ) of 35. Laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, biochemistry, arterial blood gases, urine organic acids, plasma acylcarnitine, and amino acid profiles, were within reference ranges. Serology tests for congenital infections (Cytomegalovirus, Rubella, Toxoplasma gondii) and Epstein-Barr virus were negative. Sleep EEGs (lasting about 30 minutes with no seizure-like events) showed occasional primary generalized single spike-and-slow-wave complexes. Transfontanelle sonography revealed slightly dilated lateral ventricles and a large cyst-like cisterna magna, suggesting cerebellar hypoplasia.
test_results: A homozygous missence mutation c.919G > T (p.Ala307Ser) was found.

case_report: A 9-year-old boy was referred to the pediatric respiratory clinic with a persistent dry cough since birth, tachypnea at rest, and failure to gain weight. He was born at 37 weeks and 1 day, weighing 1.6 kg, and experienced respiratory distress at birth, requiring 21 days of hospitalization and 10 days of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). There was no history of aspiration, oily stools, ear or nasal symptoms, or exposure to allergens. Family history indicated that the paternal grandfather had died from an undiagnosed lung condition at 35 years. A chest CT at 1 year old during an exacerbation showed patchy bilateral consolidation but otherwise normal lung parenchyma. Extensive evaluations during infancy, including an Immunoglobulin profile, sweat chloride analysis, and clinical exome sequencing, were normal. The child was treated with pulse steroids with minimal improvement. Over the years, he continued to have a persistent dry cough, exercise intolerance, and failure to gain weight, leading to multiple hospitalizations and treatments with antibiotics, nebulized bronchodilators, and steroids. Upon presentation, the child was significantly malnourished (height 115 cm and weight 18 kg, both below the 3rd percentile), had grade 3 clubbing, tachypnea (rate 35/min) with suprasternal and subcostal retractions, hypoxemia (saturations 91% in room air), and hypercarbia (Pc02 46 mmHg) at rest. Systemic examination revealed diffuse bilateral coarse crackles predominantly in the bases, with other systems being normal. A chest X-ray showed significant bilateral hyperinflation. Pulmonary function tests indicated a combined restrictive and obstructive pattern (FVC 46%, FEV1/FVC 63% with 21% improvement post-bronchodilator). A second opinion on the chest CT from age 1 suggested early bronchiectasis.
test_results: A high-resolution CT of the chest with both inspiratory and expiratory hold showed central and peripheral bronchiectasis involving the right middle lobe, lingula, and bilateral lower lobes. There was significant ballooning of 3rd generation bronchi with an inspiratory hold (Inspiratory diameter–6.2 mm) with subsequent collapsibility of the bronchiectactic segments on expiratory hold (Expiratory diameter–3 mm). Bronchoscopy showed, normal upper airways with significant collapsibility of 3rd and 4th generation bronchioles on gentle negative pressure suctioning with suction pressure of 20–30 mm Hg.

case_report: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and no significant past medical or surgical history presented with joint stiffness, a burning sensation, and generalized weakness. She received symptomatic treatment with ibuprofen and omeprazole. Basic investigations were conducted, including an electrocardiogram (ECG), chest X-ray, and ultrasound sonography (USG) of the abdomen and pelvis, all of which returned normal results. Laboratory findings were as follows: Hemoglobin: 11.5 g/dL; RBC count: 3.83 million/mm3; WBC count: 7900/mm3; platelet count: 2.48/mcL. Serum creatinine: 0.61 mg/dL; serum potassium: 3.13 mEq/L; serum sodium: 144 mmol/L; serum urea: 18.45 mg/dL. Albumin: 3.45 g/dL; alkaline phosphatase: 70.56 U/L; alanine transaminase (ALT): 15.64 U/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 28.07 U/L; bilirubin (total): 0.42 mg/dL; HDL cholesterol: 34.34 mg/dL; total cholesterol: 157.46 mg/dL; LDL cholesterol: 98 mg/dL; triglycerides: 122.94 mg/dL; C-reactive protein (CRP): 0.3 mg/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 18 mm/hr.

case_report: The patient is a 56-year-old male who had an appendectomy at 15 years old due to severe abdominal pain. Post-surgery, he experienced acute abdominal pain intermittently, approximately once a week, leading to repeated hospital admissions for several days. Between the ages of 33 and 34, he underwent five different surgical procedures and was hospitalized for a total of 9 months due to persistent abdominal pain. At 35 years old, he had a jejunectomy for intestinal obstruction, followed by adhesiotomies at 36 and 48 years old, and a jejunum-colic bypass at 50 years old. From the age of 46, opioids were administered to manage severe abdominal pain, and he regularly visited the hospital for treatment. Additionally, he experienced upper respiratory tract edema four times at the ages of 48, 49, and 53, and priapism twice, once in his 30s and again at 53 years old. Over the past decade, he required hospitalization on average 19 times a year due to severe abdominal pain.
test_results: Low levels of serum C4 (3–16 mg/dl) and CH50 (29 U/ml) with normal serum C3 levels (79–102 mg/dl). Characteristic computed tomography (CT) scan findings of submucosal edema of the intestinal tracts and colectasia during an acute attack. Extremely low function level of C1-INH (25.2%).
diagnosis: Hereditary Angioedema due to C1-inhibitor deficiency

case_report: A 5-year-old girl was brought to our institute with significant delays in mental and motor development. She is the younger of two children born to a nonconsanguineous Indian Hindu couple. She was delivered at term through normal vaginal delivery, cried at birth, and had an uneventful neonatal period. Severe developmental delays were observed from early infancy. There was no history of exposure to infections, drugs, or radiation during pregnancy. Her elder sibling, a 7-year-old girl, is apparently healthy. There is no family history of brain malformations, developmental delays, facial abnormalities, or chromosomal abnormalities. On physical examination, the child exhibited partial neck control, reached for objects with an immature grasp, recognized only family members, and vocalized meaningless vowel sounds. She weighed 13.5 kg (<3rd percentile) and had a head circumference of 48 cm (5–15th percentile). Dysmorphic facial features included metopic prominence, bushy eyebrows with synophrys, broad nasal root, flat nasal bridge, telecanthus, and a shallow philtrum. Neurological examination showed normal cranial nerves, bilaterally symmetrical muscle bulk with increased tone in all limbs, and generalized hyperreflexia. The rest of the systemic examination was normal.
test_results: On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), deficient interhemispheric fissure was observed in posterior frontal and parietal regions with failure of separation of posterior frontal and parietal lobes. The anterior and posterior parts of the interhemispheric fissure were normally formed. Sylvian fissures showed abnormal vertical orientation and were fused across midline over the vertex of brain. Genu and splenium of corpus callosum were normally formed, and the body was absent in the region of interhemispheric connection. Septum pellucidum was absent. Basal forebrain structures were normally cleaved. Brainstem and posterior fossa structures were normal.

case_report: A 4-year-old boy, firstborn to third-degree consanguineous parents of north Indian origin, exhibited progressive spasticity in the lower limbs and regression of motor milestones starting at 1 year of age. The antenatal and perinatal periods were uncomplicated, and there were no affected family members. He achieved motor, adaptive, social, and language milestones appropriately until 1 year of age. Prior to the onset of symptoms, he could walk with one handheld, had a mature pincer grasp, waved bye-bye, and spoke two meaningful words. Initially, he experienced gait instability, toe walking, and frequent falls without diurnal fluctuation. By 2 years of age, he ceased walking and had significant difficulty standing independently, with a crouch at the knee. He also developed tightness in the bilateral lower limbs at the knee and ankle. Despite slower progress compared to peers, he continued to gain social and language milestones. At 4 years old, he had a vocabulary of 10–20 words and could indicate bowel and bladder needs but required assistance. He had difficulty with fine motor tasks in the upper limbs and slurred speech. Examination revealed Ashworth grade III spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, and dynamic flexion contractures at the ankles in the lower limbs. In the upper limbs, there was grade I spasticity, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and spastic dysarthria. Anthropometry and physical examination were otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine showed no abnormalities. A clinical trial of levodopa/carbidopa combination over 4 weeks, with doses ranging from 1–5 mg/kg/day, showed no favorable clinical response. Nerve conduction studies were normal.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing detected a novel homozygous two base pair deletion in exon 2 of the CYP2U1 gene (c.1080_8081delTT [p.Leu361AlafsTer19]) that results in a frameshift and premature truncation of the protein 19 amino-acid downstream to codon 361.

case_report: A 19-year-old man visited our outpatient clinic in 2011. Since the age of 2 years, he had been seen by multiple dermatologists in other clinics. He experienced pruritic sub-erythroderma with extensive skin peeling and scaling since birth, with symptoms worsening in winter. He also had complaints of atopic dermatitis and hay fever. His hair, teeth, and nails appeared normal. Routine laboratory tests were normal, except for elevated IgE levels (2222 kU/L; normal, <100). Hair shaft analysis did not show trichorrhexis invaginata. Over the years, the patient was treated with topical moisturizing agents, local corticosteroids, and a prolonged course of low-dose isotretinoin; only the latter provided slight improvement according to the patient. His non-consanguineous parents of Lithuanian and Russian Jewish descent did not exhibit any skin symptoms. Initially, the patient reported that his parents had no history of obvious hair loss.
test_results: No pathogenic mutations were detected.
diagnosis: Mutations in the CDSN gene causing peeling skin disease and hypotrichosis simplex of the scalp

case_report: A 6-month-old Chinese male child was admitted with recurring episodes of low blood sugar for 6 months. His parents were healthy, not related by blood, and his family history was unremarkable. The child was first admitted to the hospital at 2 days old due to repeated cyanosis and poor reaction. His blood glucose level was 0.3 mmol/L, and he recovered after receiving glucose and glucocorticoid infusion. At 22 days old, after fasting for 4 hours for an MRI examination, he appeared pale, had a poor reaction, and reduced muscle strength. His blood glucose was 2.06 mmol/L, and he recovered after glucose infusion. Subsequently, the child showed increased muscle tension and delayed movement. At 4 months old, he experienced repeated vomiting and diarrhea for one day, and low blood sugar reappeared (blood glucose, 4 mmol/L). He also had a convulsion lasting 2–3 minutes. After intravenous glucose infusion, his blood glucose returned to normal. At 6 months old, he was admitted for a systematic examination. Physical examination showed a body weight of 6600 g (3rd percentile); body length, 76.0 cm (97th percentile); head circumference, 41.0 cm (3rd percentile); chest circumference, 43.0 cm (50th percentile). He was conscious with good mental reaction, nutrition levels, and skin elasticity. He had strabismus in both eyes, more prominent in the left eye. He was unable to use his elbows to get up from a reclining position, and when standing upright, his head tilted to one side. He could not turn over or bear his weight, leaned forward fully in the sitting position, and flexed his legs in the standing position. He was not actively conscious of grasping objects but could hold objects without changing them between hands. He could pronounce vowels but was insensitive to locating sources of sound or light. He had normal muscular strength in both upper limbs, but greater muscular strength in both lower limbs, mainly in the adductor muscles. The testes were not completely lowered into the scrotum, and the transillumination test was negative. Laboratory tests, including blood routine (platelet count, 435 × 10^9/L; hemoglobin, 107 g/L), thyroid function, biochemical tests, stool and urine routine, and blood lactic acid, were normal. A fasting test was conducted for 4 hours, and the results showed that both insulin and cortisol were within the normal range. Brain CT indicated scattered low-density shadows in the brain parenchyma and plump bilateral ventricles. Brain MRI indicated extensive abnormal signals in both cerebral hemispheres, suggestive of atrophic cystic changes caused by encephalomalacia. EEG showed multiple spikes/sharp-slow waves in the left and right occipital regions during both waking and sleep, with a 2–3 Hz increase in δ activity in the occipital region, and the dominant rhythm of the occipital region was not significant in the waking state. Echocardiography indicated patent ductus arteriosus. The Gesell Developmental Schedules showed that the gross motor skills of the patient at 4 weeks and 3 months were equivalent to those of neonates at 0 months, and the fine motor skills were equivalent to those of neonates at 0–1 month. The Gesell Intelligence Scale showed that the ability to respond to people and the environment was equivalent to that of infants at 6 weeks (Developmental Quotient [DQ] = 35 points), while the ability to respond to physical objects was equivalent to that of infants at 3 weeks (DQ = 18 points). Additionally, the patient’s gross motor skills were equivalent to that of infants at 0 weeks (DQ = 0 points); his fine motor skills were equivalent to that of infants at 2 weeks (DQ = 12 points), and the ability to communicate was equivalent to that of infants at 6 weeks (DQ = 35 points).
test_results: The results revealed the heterozygous intron mutation c.1070 + 3A > G (splicing) in the coding region of the COG1 gene that was inherited from the mother, and the heterozygous mutation c.2492 g > A (p. Arg831Gln) in exon 10 of the COG1 gene that was inherited from the father.
diagnosis: Component of oligomeric Golgi complex 1  deficiency leading to Congenital Disorder of Glycosylation type IIg

case_report: A 68-year-old male was directed to the Veterans Affairs Emergency Department by his primary care physician due to a white blood cell (WBC) count of 28 x 10^3 per microliter (µL). His medical history includes a bronchogenic cyst resection six years ago, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and past episodes of rheumatic fever and malaria over forty years ago. Over the past month, he experienced a productive cough, decreased appetite, and a weight loss of approximately 10 pounds. He reported no fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or changes in bowel or urinary habits. His medications included amlodipine and atorvastatin. He had no family history of malignancy or blood disorders. He had a 42 pack-year smoking history and a history of heavy alcohol use but had been abstinent for several years, with no illicit drug use. On examination, his temperature was 98.6˚F, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and blood pressure 150/92 mmHg. He appeared in no acute distress and had a body mass index (BMI) of 33 kg/m2. Physical examination revealed bilateral lung wheezes and splenomegaly, with no cervical, axillary, or inguinal adenopathy. Laboratory results showed a WBC count of 28.65 x 10^3 per µL, an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 4.53 x 10^3 per µL, hemoglobin level (Hgb) of 12.9 grams per deciliter (g/dL), and a platelet count of 95 x 10^3 per µL. Electrolytes, liver function tests, and renal function were within normal limits. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest with contrast revealed a small left-sided effusion and left lower lobe atelectasis versus consolidation. The abdomen showed splenomegaly and enlarged gastro-hepatic ligament nodes. A follow-up CT of the abdomen confirmed marked splenomegaly with a spleen span of 21 cm. The patient was admitted and started on treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. Further evaluation was conducted due to weight loss, leukocytosis, splenomegaly, and adenopathy. A peripheral smear revealed lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes featuring thin cytoplasmic projections. The patient showed clinical improvement and was discharged a day after admission with plans for outpatient follow-up.
test_results: A bone marrow biopsy was performed six days after discharge. Complete blood count (CBC) done on the day of the bone marrow biopsy showed a WBC count of 39.26 x 103 per µL, ANC of 3.36 x 103 per µL, Hgb of 12.0 g/dL, and a platelet count of 113 x 103 per µL. The aspirate showed normoblastic myeloid and erythroid maturation without significant dyspoeitic features. There was no increase in blasts. Atypical lymphocytes morphologically similar to those seen on the peripheral smear were seen. The core biopsy and clot sections showed cellularity of 20-40%. A reticulin stain showed mild, focal increase in reticulin fibers (grade 1). Immunophenotyping showed B-lymphocytes that were positive for CD19, CD20, had a moderate expression of CD200, and had a bright CD11c and CD103. They were negative for expression of surface kappa and lambda light chain, CD5, CD10, CD38, CD23, and CD25. Fluorescence in situ hybridization was negative for BCR/ABL translocation. Cytogenetics detected two separate complex karyotypes involving multiple deletions, monosomy 5, and an apparent derivative of chromosome 16. Molecular studies were negative for BRAFV600E mutation.

case_report: A 46-year-old male with a history of asymptomatic hyperuricemia and small psoriatic plaques on the lower limbs (resolved without treatment 10 years ago) began hypouricemic therapy due to persistently high uric acid levels over three years (8.4 mg%, 8.7 mg%, and 9.4 mg%). The patient had no known muscle, renal, or hepatic diseases and consumed fewer than 5 units of alcohol per week. He reported progressive muscle weakness and myalgia in the lower limbs over three weeks, starting six weeks after initiating hypouricemic treatment and prophylactic gout flare prevention. The treatment regimen included allopurinol, starting at 100 mg/day and increasing by 100 mg/day every two weeks to a maximum of 300 mg/day, along with 0.5 mg/day of colchicine. Mild diarrhea occurred three days after starting the medication but resolved spontaneously. By the third week, the patient experienced progressive myalgia, and by the fifth week, progressive weakness, difficulty climbing stairs, and general malaise prompted him to discontinue the medication and seek medical evaluation. He also reported tenderness and contractures in the thighs and calves, as well as dark urine by the third week, although urine analysis was not performed. Physical examination showed proximal muscle weakness in the limbs (4/5 on the Research Medical Council grading system) and tenderness in the thighs and calves, with intact sensory system, coordination, and reflexes. Biochemical evaluation revealed a five-fold increase in creatinine kinase (CK) to 1101 U/L (normal: 30-200 U/L). Hepatic enzymes were within normal limits, with alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at 33 U/L (normal: 0-55 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) slightly elevated at 37 U/L (normal: 5-34 U/L). Uric acid levels decreased to 5.5 mg/dL (previously 9.4 mg/dL before treatment). Creatinine was normal at 0.99 mg/dL, and no other biochemical or hematological abnormalities were noted.
test_results: On ENG testing, sensitive and motor nerve conduction studies, late F-responses and H-reflex were normal. After EMG evaluation of unilateral right biceps brachii and bilateral quadriceps, bilateral medial gastrocnemius and bilateral biceps femoris, increased insertional activity and spontaneous activity such as fibrillations, positive sharp waves, high-frequency myotonic discharges, and myopathic motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) of small amplitude and duration and increased polyphasic index were observed. On biceps brachii and quadriceps muscles, at maximal effort, an interferential pattern with reduced amplitudes was observed. Motor unit action potentials showed a decrease in mean duration (36% and 39% decreased for both quadriceps and 17% decreased for biceps brachii), and their polyphasic index was also increased. Some MUAPs showed satellite potentials.

case_report: A 77-year-old male was referred for further evaluation of unilateral iris rubeosis in the right eye (RE) discovered during a routine examination prior to cataract surgery. The patient was asymptomatic and had no previous ocular issues except for divergent strabismus since childhood, resulting in left eye amblyopia. His medical history included arterial hypertension with renal effects, metabolic syndrome, atrial fibrillation, prostatic syndrome, and moderate chronic obstructive pulmonary emphysema. During the examination, his visual acuity (VA) on the decimal scale was 0.5 in the RE and 0.15 in the left eye (LE), along with divergent strabismus. Slit lamp examination revealed radial iridian vascular engorgement at the 5 to 7 o'clock position in the RE, with vessels appearing to originate from the iris stroma and extending circumferentially. Gonioscopic examination showed a grade IV open angle with a vascular racemose network spanning 360 degrees in the iridocorneal angle. No sentinel vessels were observed at the episcleral level, and no masses were detected in other parts of the iris. Intraocular pressure was 10 mmHg in the RE and 12 mmHg in the LE. The LE examination was normal. Ocular fundus examination of the RE revealed an oblique papilla and myopic chorioretinitis, without exudates, hemorrhages, or neovascularization. There were no clinical signs of conditions that could cause retinal ischemia, such as diabetic retinopathy, central or branch vein occlusion, or central artery obstruction. Peripheral tumor masses, including choroidal melanoma, retinoblastoma, metastasis, or ciliary body lesions, were ruled out through fundus examination with indentation and maximum mydriasis. Supra-aortic trunk examination using ecoDoppler showed no other causes of ocular ischemia, and no carotid stenosis with hemodynamic significance was observed. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography was performed, revealing poorly defined intrastromal hyporeflective spaces corresponding to the lumen of the vessels.
test_results: Normal contrast uptake was demonstrated without extravasation at the level of the iridian, iridocorneal angle, and retinal vessels. An early filling of the iridian vessels was observed without contrast diffusion, ruling out retinal ischemia and neovessels.

case_report: A 3-year-old male child came to the pediatric surgery outpatient department with complaints of generalized weakness and malaise. The child had experienced 2–3 episodes of constipation over the past year, which were managed with laxatives. The patient had a history of multiple blood transfusions over the past 3 years. There was no history of melena or hematochezia. On physical examination, the child was vitally stable but showed marked pallor. His body mass index was 12.96. The abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no palpable mass or organomegaly. Rectal examination and proctoscopy were normal. Routine blood tests indicated microcytic hypochromic anemia with a hemoglobin level of 6.2 g/dl. An ultrasound of the whole abdomen revealed a complex cystic lesion (59 mm × 28 mm × 34 mm) with irregular dense septations and both hypo- and hyperechoic cystic areas involving pelvic bowel loops and extending into the adjacent mesentery. Doppler imaging showed high internal vascularity within the lesion. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen showed a well-defined lesion with progressive enhancement on subsequent postcontrast studies (measuring 49 mm × 22 mm × 38 mm) in relation to the pelvic ileal loops and mesentery. The lesion was abutting the dome of the urinary bladder inferiorly, the rectum, and the sigmoid colon posteriorly, with indistinct fat planes laterally. The lesion was also seen in relation to the pelvic iliac vessels.
test_results: The submucosa showed lymphoid follicles and blood-filled vascular spaces. Muscularis propria showed muscle hypertrophy. Serosa showed numerous proliferating, dilated, and congested blood vessels.

case_report: A 9-year-old Chinese girl presented with pain in the posterior part of the left mandibular region and a nodule with pus discharge, noted one month prior to her visit. The patient exhibited normal growth without any height or developmental abnormalities. Physical examination identified a nodule with pus discharge and swelling under the left side of the chin. Applying gentle pressure to the surrounding tissue resulted in thick purulent drainage from the central punctum. Intraoral examination showed red and swollen alveolar mucosa in the region of the primary left mandibular second molar (#75), which was only partially erupted. All teeth in the mixed dentition displayed abnormal shapes, except for the bilateral permanent incisors in both the maxillary and mandibular regions, which were misaligned. The crowns of the primary canines and the primary maxillary first molars (#54 and 64) were enlarged, bulbous, and malformed with 2 or 3 cusps, resembling either fusion or germination. Tooth #64 exhibited level III mobility without any positive signs on percussion or palpation. The primary maxillary second molars (#55 and 65) and the primary right mandibular first molar (#84) were similarly enlarged with developmental grooves dividing the crowns into various lobules. Additionally, small tooth-like structures were observed around tooth #84. The first permanent molars lacked clearly defined cusps, resembling the tied end of a sausage. Teeth #75 and 85 were only partially erupted. According to her guardians, the patient's incisors began to erupt at age 4 and had never been replaced, indicating congenital absence of the primary incisors. Her parents also noted that the eruption of her primary dentition was delayed compared to normal children.
test_results: The panoramic radiograph revealed tooth-like radiopaque masses surrounded by a large radiolucent zone with a well-defined margin in the molar area of left mandibular. Radiopaque masses in the bilateral primary mandibular molar region appeared to be 4 odontoma and the germs of bilateral permanent mandibular premolars were absent. Radiologic and clinical findings were mostly consistent with a diagnosis of pericoronitis causing cutaneous sinus tracts in the left mandibular premolar region. Radiographic analysis of the abnormal molars showed taurodontism changes with larger pulp chambers, some of which were duplicated, and the root length was short compared with crown height; some were taurodont in configuration. The spiral CT images of both jaws were reconstructed and the craniofacial skeletons were normal. According to the otolaryngologic examination, the patient had distinct bilateral sensorineural hearing loss of acuity to frequencies above 1000 Hz. Her threshold was normal at low frequencies but obviously drop up to 75 dB at higher frequencies. The otolaryngologic examination confirmed her auditory structures, temporal bone, and ethmoid air cells were normal.

case_report: The patient is a 3-year-old male child, the youngest of three siblings, born to non-consanguineous parents with no family history of neuropsychiatric disorders or congenital malformations. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and he was delivered vaginally at term with a birth weight of 3,200 grams. At birth, he exhibited cyanosis and delayed crying. The parents first noticed abnormalities in his eyes, and clinical examination confirmed bilateral coloboma involving the iris and retina. An echocardiography was performed and found to be normal. At 5 days old, he was hospitalized due to involuntary movements in the face and upper limbs accompanied by hypotonia and was treated for hypoglycemia attributed to poor feeding. At 27 days old, he developed tonic-clonic seizures and was hospitalized again, presenting with poor feeding, vomiting, floppiness, and cold limbs. He received intravenous antibiotics and seizure control was achieved with phenobarbitone 20 mg, sodium valproate 200 mg syrups, and intravenous benzodiazepines at maximum dosages for his weight. Physical examination revealed dysmorphic facial features including flat occiput, low set ears, arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, bilateral coloboma, hypertelorism with downslanting palpebral fissures, bulbous nasal tip, wide mouth with downturned corners, smooth philtrum, tented thin upper lip, and thin upper vermilion. Additional findings included muscular hypotonia, clinodactyly of the little fingers, a well-defined hypopigmented plaque on the umbilicus, and lichenified skin on the soles of both feet. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasonography showed bilateral cryptorchidism but was otherwise normal. Electroencephalogram indicated a hypsarrhythmic pattern, suggestive of generalized epilepsy. Brain MRI revealed mild cerebral atrophy, mild thinning of the corpus callosum, and mild bilateral retinal coloboma. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was inconclusive. Based on MRI and CSF analysis results, antibiotics were discontinued, and treatment focused on brain atrophy with epilepsy. After one week of hospitalization, he was discharged on the same antiepileptic syrups. At 6 months old, his parents observed back arching dystonia, chewing, twitching movements, uncontrolled laughing, giggling, and grimacing. By 1 year old, his seizures were controlled with levetiracetam syrup 100 mg twice daily, though his family remained concerned about his prognosis.
test_results: The whole exome sequence analysis revealed a heterozygous c.607C > T (p. Arg203Trp) mutation in PACS1 gene (NM_018026.3).

case_report: A 48-year-old female arrived at the emergency department after experiencing a fainting episode. Her medical history includes mild mental retardation, previous tobacco use, and a past hernia repair. She was not taking any medications at home. The patient reported feeling lightheaded while cooking, leading to a brief loss of consciousness and a fall. Upon regaining consciousness, she noticed a decrease in her exercise tolerance, experiencing shortness of breath after climbing one flight of stairs. She also mentioned having heavy menstrual bleeding for the past two weeks. She did not report chest pain, palpitations, sweating, swelling in the lower extremities, difficulty breathing while lying down, or sudden nighttime shortness of breath. On examination, her heart rate was 88 beats per minute, blood pressure was 113/48 mmHg, oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, and her temperature was 98.4°F. A cardiac examination revealed a 3/6 decrescendo diastolic murmur best heard at the right sternal border with radiation to the carotids. The physical exam also noted poor dental health with multiple decayed teeth and pallor in the mucous membranes, palms, and soles. Laboratory tests indicated severe iron deficiency anemia with hemoglobin at 2.9 g/dl, hematocrit at 10.7%, mean corpuscular volume at 54 fl, ferritin at 15 ng/ml, iron at 261 µg/dl, and transferrin at 218 mg/dl. In the emergency department, she received three units of packed red blood cells. A chest X-ray showed an enlarged heart, a head CT scan ruled out hemorrhage, and an abdominal/pelvic CT scan revealed multiple myomas, which were considered the likely source of bleeding.
test_results: A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was obtained, demonstrating a thickened aortic valve with severe aortic insufficiency. Left ventricular chamber size was normal with an ejection fraction of 65%. A transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was performed revealing an irregularly shaped mobile echodensity (1.7 cm×1.0 cm) on the aortic valve consistent with a vegetation. Also, a root abscess was present with fistula formation between the right sinus of Valsalva and the right atrium.

case_report: A 3-month-old male infant presented with a 20-day history of bilious and projectile vomiting after each feed, accompanied by significant weight loss and lethargy. He was born full-term with a birth weight of 3 kg (50th percentile weight for age) to healthy consanguineous parents, had an uneventful prenatal history with a normal antenatal ultrasound, and is developmentally age-appropriate. The patient had been admitted twice to different hospitals for fluid therapy. During his last admission, almost 5 days prior to the current presentation, an abdominal ultrasound was performed. On examination, the infant appeared cachectic, lethargic, and severely dehydrated, with multiple cautery marks on his abdomen from a traditional healer. His weight upon admission was 2.9 kg (below the 3rd percentile weight for age). He had a scaphoid abdomen and visible peristalsis transversely across the epigastrium from left to right. Test feeding demonstrated a palpable firm, nontender mass in the right upper quadrant, measuring 1 to 2 cm in diameter. Bilateral reducible inguinal hernias were also noted. The rest of the examination was normal. Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count (CBC) and serum chemistry values, including potassium (K+ 4.3 mmol) and chloride (Cl− 96 mmol/L). Venous blood gas (VBG) analysis revealed uncompensated metabolic alkalosis with a pH of 7.54, pCO2 of 35.7 mmHg, cHCO3 of 31.1 mmol/L, and cBase of 7.4 mmol/L. An abdominal ultrasound showed a markedly distended stomach and the first part of the duodenum with no signs of pyloric stenosis.

case_report: A 60-year-old Caucasian male presented to the dermatology clinic with a painful rash. Four weeks earlier, he noticed a lesion on his left wrist. Within 24 hours, a red and purple rash appeared on his left forearm, elbow, and left dorsal hand, accompanied by tingling and swelling of the affected skin. He initially sought care at an urgent care clinic and was prescribed cephalexin, but his condition did not improve. He then visited his primary care physician, who started him on a prednisone taper (40mg PO daily for four days, then 20mg PO daily for four days, then 10mg PO daily for four days) and referred him to the dermatology clinic. By the time he presented to the dermatology clinic, he had completed six days of the prednisone taper, resulting in mild symptom improvement. The patient reported no factors that alleviated or worsened his condition, no previous skin diseases, and no contact with sick individuals. He had a history of varicella infection during childhood and had not received the shingles vaccine. A review of systems showed no systemic symptoms such as malaise, fever, muscle pain, or joint pain. His medications included tamsulosin for benign prostatic hypertrophy and intermittent use of Vicodin and ibuprofen for chronic low back pain. He reported no known immunodeficiencies, occasional alcohol consumption, and a history of cigarette smoking and marijuana use. Physical examination revealed normal mood and affect, and orientation to place, person, and time. A full-body skin exam showed pink, ill-defined, irregular papules of varying sizes on the left distal forearm, and well-defined, round, violaceous papules on the dorsal and palmar aspects of the left digits two through five. No intact vesicles were observed.
test_results: Findings included small vessels with marginating neutrophils, fibrin thrombi, fibrinoid necrosis of blood vessel walls, karyorrhectic debris, and numerous extravasated red cells. Pathology also reported a vesicle with numerous necrotic keratinocytes with marked acantholysis and large red intranuclear inclusions, and a superficial and deep neutrophilic infiltrate with the destruction of vessels. The tissue samples at both sites also stained positive for VZV antigen and stained negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV) antigen.

case_report: A 74-year-old man presented with severe aortic valve insufficiency and left ventricle dilatation. His medical history included hypercholesterolemia and a recent episode of atrial flutter treated with electrical cardioversion. Current medications were atorvastatin, nebivolol, and dabigatran. He quit smoking 40 years ago and consumes 14 units of alcohol per week. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination showed normal pulmonary, abdominal, and neurological functions. Cardiovascular examination noted a diastolic murmur at the right lower sternal border, with otherwise normal heart sounds. Coronary angiography did not reveal significant coronary artery disease. Transthoracic echocardiography indicated severe aortic valve insufficiency and somewhat impaired left ventricular function. Cardiac MRI confirmed severe aortic valve insufficiency, a dilated aortic root (46 mm), and a severely dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 50%.
test_results: Microscopic examination of cross-sections of the aortic valve leaflets showed areas of calcification with focal ceroid. In between the calcification areas, a few reactive small thin-walled blood vessels were found. Next to calcification, fibrosis and mucoid degeneration was also observed. In the periphery of the valve, an agglomerate of thin walled, often dilated, blood vessels was observed. These vessels stained positive for CD31 and were negative for D2-40. The vessels were predominantly negative for SMA.

case_report: A 34-year-old woman reported incomplete closure of the left eyelid and restricted eye movement for 8 years, with no relevant family history. She also experienced mild limitations in physical activity but did not seek immediate medical attention. Her parents are healthy and not related by blood. In 2017, she visited an ophthalmology hospital where fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography showed no abnormalities. She was prescribed oral pyridostigmine (60 mg tid) and prednisone (30 mg qd), but her symptoms did not significantly improve. The prednisone dosage was gradually reduced to 15 mg qd. In 2018, she experienced fatigue and weakness 6 months postpartum. In September 2019, she stopped taking pyridostigmine and prednisone due to a lack of noticeable improvement in her symptoms. case_report: A 12-year-old male presented with intellectual disability, limited speech, axial hypotonia, and distinct facial features. He reported a one-month history of bloody urethral discharge without associated flank or urethral pain. He is the second child in his family, with an older sister who is healthy. He was born at 37 weeks of gestation via vaginal delivery, weighing 3.8 kg, measuring 51 cm in length, and with a head circumference of 34 cm. At birth, he experienced mild asphyxia, which resolved with oxygen administration. He had no feeding difficulties, persistent drooling, or poor suckling, and his initial neurological examination was normal. Developmental milestones included head control at 3 months, sitting unsupported at 8 months, creeping at 15 months, and walking at 3 years. By 6 months, he exhibited axial hypotonia, developmental delay, and mild dysmorphic features. He began cooing at 5 months and babbling at 8 months, but by 1 year, he could only say 'baba' and 'mama.' He lost the ability to speak by 18 months. At 4 years, he showed poor eye contact and aversion to strangers, and by 6 years, occasional hand wringing and automatism were noted. He had no history of hospitalization, recurrent respiratory infections, constipation, or seizures. No magnetic resonance imaging was performed, and he was not on any chronic medication. Family history revealed that his mother and sister had a confirmed genetic condition, and his maternal uncles had developmental delays and died at 8 years old. His mother and grandmother had no psychiatric symptoms. The grandmother's first husband died of gastric cancer, and she remarried, having two daughters with her second husband. One of these daughters has two children, one of whom has a similar developmental delay. Additionally, the boy's grandaunt had three children, two girls and a boy, with cognitive and developmental delays, with the boy dying at 5 years old. On admission, the patient required assistance for standing, moving, and feeding. Observed craniofacial features included a broad face, deep-set eyes, protruding ears, midface retrusion, a depressed nasal bridge, and an everted lower lip vermilion. Mild hypoplasia of the scrotal sac and rugae were noted, with both testes descended bilaterally. An intelligence assessment using the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test indicated severe mental retardation, as he could recognize only a few pictures and words.
test_results: The aCGH performed on the patient’s genomic DNA showed Xq28 duplication with breakpoints located between positions 153273980 and 153375749 bp with a size of 563.70 kb, and duplication of chromosome 17 (17p11.2p11.1) with a size of 237.67 kb. Size variations were also observed. In addition, analysis of the proband’s clinically normal sister revealed a duplication of the same region (153273980–153375749 bp), albeit with a different size, 574.40 kb. The mother showed Xq28 duplication at the same breakpoint, with a size of 543.49 kb, whereas the father’s DNA showed no duplication. No microduplication of genes, such as IRAK1, L1CAM, FLNA, or RAB39B, was observed in the Xq28 region.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman presented with upper abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and vomiting for 2 months, along with hot flushes over the past 3 months. Her past medical history, family history, and physical examination were unremarkable. Laboratory results showed mild to moderate anemia (Hb = 10.8 g/dL, HCT = 35.4%, MCV = 81.5 fL, MCH = 24.9 pg) and elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels (378 IU/L, normal <280 IU/L). Abdominal ultrasonography did not reveal significant findings, prompting the use of magnetic resonance enterography (MRE). MRE indicated circumferential thickening in the wall of the proximal jejunum, bowel loop distention, shouldering appearance of the lumen’s margins, and mucosal destruction. An enlarged lymph node was also noted on the posterior aspect of the greater curvature of the stomach. Due to symptoms indicative of small bowel obstruction, the patient underwent jejunal resection and anastomosis with margins of 6.5 cm from the duodenal site and 15 cm from the jejunal site. Intraoperative assessment confirmed anastomotic integrity, and a feeding jejunostomy was placed 36 hours post-operation. The patient began a diet six days after admission and was discharged in good condition.
test_results: Histologic investigation of the resected tumor demonstrated discohesive sheets of medium-sized immature cells with round to oval, lobulated, or indented nuclei. These cells mostly had clear to eosinophilic cytoplasm. Giemsa staining showed a metachromatic tone in the tumor cells’ cytoplasm. On immunohistochemistry assay, LCA, and C-kit (CD117) were positive in tumor cells while CD1a, CD20, CD3, MPO, Cytokeratin (AE1/AE3, CK7, CK19, and CK20), and Vimentin tests showed negative results. The Ki-67 marker of proliferation was measured, and the results showed levels as high as 30%. No bone marrow cytogenetic abnormality or involvement was found. KIT mutation analysis showed gain-of-function mutations in the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase, an aspartic acid to valine substitution (D816V).

case_report: A 10-year-old girl was admitted with a history of convulsion followed by unconsciousness since day one. She had been hospitalized six months prior for a similar episode, during which a lumbar puncture was performed. Although the cerebrospinal fluid analysis did not confirm tuberculous meningitis, antitubercular chemotherapy was initiated and continued, which the patient adhered to until the current admission. The patient was referred to dermatologists for evaluation of her unusual skin and hair color. On examination, the patient was deeply comatose with generalized hypotonia; there was no focal neurological deficit. Cutaneous examination revealed a diffuse bronze-tan of her photo-exposed body parts like face, neck, and extremities along with scattered freckles. Hair showed a silvery shine. Her parents were consanguineously married. According to them, the patient’s intelligence was normal and she was a fourth standard student. She and her six-year-old younger sister had this type of skin and hair color since early childhood, which was progressive and had not been observed in any other family member. The younger sibling did not suffer from any neurological abnormality till that age.
test_results: CT scan of the brain revealed diffuse cerebral edema. Few hairs were plucked from patient′s scalp and examined under microscope, which revealed irregular clumps of melanin along the hair shaft. A skin biopsy was done from the forearm; H and E stained histopathological section showed irregular-sized melanin granules dispersed along the basal layer of epidermis.

case_report: A 33-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented with a two-day history of dystonic posturing affecting his left hand and arm. The episodes involved bending of the elbow and specific finger posturing, without any oculo-bulbar or sensory symptoms. These episodes occurred randomly throughout the day and were later found to be triggered by caffeine consumption. The duration of the episodes varied from several minutes to one instance lasting nine hours. The episodes were painful, with the patient unable to voluntarily relax the affected arm and hand. Mental clarity was maintained throughout and after the episodes, which ceased during sleep. Initially, the symptoms were confined to the left arm but later spread to the right arm, occurring independently in both arms at random intervals. The patient reported no family history of movement disorders and did not smoke, consume alcohol, or take any medications. On examination, his blood pressure was 129/79 mmHg, heart rate was 77 beats per minute, weight was 195 pounds (88.5 kilograms), height was six feet (182.9 centimeters), and body-mass index was 26.4. His speech was normal, and his gait was unremarkable. Cranial nerve examination was normal, with intact ocular motion and no nystagmus. Facial strength was symmetric and full, with no oro-buccolingual dyskinesias. Cervical musculature examination showed no cervical dystonia, and oropharyngeal examination revealed a brisk gag reflex without palatal myoclonus. Muscle strength in both upper and lower extremities was graded 5/5, and deep tendon reflexes were 2+ and symmetric. There was no spasticity, and Hoffman and finger flexor reflexes were absent bilaterally. No cogwheeling was detected at the wrist. The Babinski sign was absent with bilateral plantar strokes. Finger sequencing, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin maneuvers were accurate and symmetric bilaterally. During the clinic visit, an episode was observed, starting with a 90-degree flexion of the left elbow and extending to the hand. The posture involved flexion of the first, third, and fourth fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints with extension of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, while the second and fifth fingers remained extended, resembling a bovine longhorn.
test_results: An electroencephalogram (EEG) did not reveal any focal epileptiform discharge. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of the brain with and without contrast enhancement was normal. A T1-weighted image did not reveal any metal deposition in the basal ganglia. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences did not reveal any white matter disease. Gradient-echo and susceptibility-weighted images did not reveal any hemosiderin deposits in the basal ganglia. Serum chemistries, including free and total calcium and a thyroid screen, were normal. A comprehensive paraneoplastic panel and an antiphospholipid antibody screen were also negative.

case_report: A 77-year-old male presented with a complaint of a droopy left eyelid. His medical history includes hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and hyperlipidemia, managed at a local clinic. Three days after receiving the first dose of ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (AstraZeneca, AZ) vaccine, he noticed gradual ptosis of the left eyelid. Eleven days post-vaccination, he experienced weakness in the left facial muscles. Physical examination showed impaired blink reflex on the left side, ptosis, and weakness in the left facial muscles, including the orbicularis oris. Extraocular movements and light reflexes were normal in both eyes. No vesicles or blisters were observed on his face. Laboratory tests, including thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, glucose, cell count, electrolytes, renal function, and liver function, were within normal limits. He was treated with prednisolone (40 mg QD) for 14 days, but the ptosis showed minimal improvement. He then sought further evaluation for the persistent droopy eyelid. His corrected visual acuity was 6/7.5 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg in both eyes. Slit-lamp examination was notable for puffy eyelids on the left side with intermittent myokymic motion of the left upper and lower lids. Marginal reflex distance 1 (MRD1) was 1 mm on the left eye compared to 3 mm on the right. The left eye closed tightly when he was asked to open his mouth or smile, although his smile was symmetric during the examination.
test_results: Fundus imaging and optical coherence tomography of his macula and disc were unremarkable, and no obvious inflammatory lesions, including on the oculomotor and facial nerve region, were observed on the brain MRI.

case_report: The patient, a 4-year-old male, experienced intermittent high fevers and a mild cough for six weeks. Physical examination showed tachypnea without other respiratory symptoms, and the central nervous system examination was normal. Laboratory tests indicated hypogammaglobulinemia, elevated C-reactive protein levels, and mild pancytopenia. Sputum and blood cultures were negative for bacteria, fungi, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Additional tests, including serum fungal G test, galactomannan test, toxoplasma antibodies, cryptococcal antigens, anti-nuclear antibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and extractable nuclear antigens, were all negative. Bone marrow morphology was normal. Chest X-ray and CT scans showed diffuse lung infiltrates. The patient was treated with ganciclovir and a γ-globulin (400 mg/kg) infusion. Despite treatment, high fevers and coughing persisted, and the patient developed lethargy, slurred speech, and convulsions. A head CT scan revealed multiple low-density areas in the left frontal lobe, right temporal lobe, parietal lobe, left parietal-occipital lobe, bilateral basal ganglia, and trigone of the left lateral ventricle, with bleeding in the right temporal lobe. The patient succumbed to a pulmonary hemorrhage two weeks after admission. The patient had a history of recurrent respiratory tract infections and had been exposed to a cat since birth. Plasma DNA screening for HHV 1-8 virus infections using multiplex PCR was negative. Reverse transcription-quantitative PCR revealed an LCMV load of 7.8×105 copies/ml at admission and 2.3×106 copies/ml on the eleventh day of admission when the patient developed lethargy, slurred speech, and convulsions.
test_results: PCR amplification and sequencing results demonstrated that the proband carried both hemizygous SH2D1A c.7G>T/p.A3S and c.228T>A/p.Y76X mutations.
Orpha_name: X-linked lymphoproliferative disease due to SH2D1A deficiency

case_report: A 58-year-old male patient presented with abnormal serum creatine kinase (sCK) levels in August 2020. The patient first noticed abnormal sCK levels on January 29, 2019, and has since observed irregular fluctuations in these levels. His medical history includes an acute cerebral stem infarction in January 2019, resulting in mild aphasia, dysphagia, and right-sided numbness and weakness. He also has a history of acute pancreatitis, a left acetabular fracture from a car accident 18 years ago leading to left leg weakness post-surgery, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes. From January 29, 2019, to November 6, 2020, the patient received daily standard treatment with metformin (500 mg/d), amlodipine besylate (2.5 mg/d), atorvastatin (20 mg/d), and aspirin (100 mg/d). Between November 12, 2019, and December 2, 2019, atorvastatin was temporarily replaced with ezetimibe (10 mg/d) due to concerns about its impact on sCK levels, but was resumed after no significant changes were observed. Additionally, the patient underwent traditional Chinese medicine treatments, including acupuncture 3-5 times a week over 18 months and three courses of herbal medicine. Acupuncture points used included Neiguan (PC6), Shuigou (DU26), Sanyinjiao (SP6), Baihui (DU20), Yifeng (SJ17), Jianyu (LI15), and Taichong (LR3). Herbal medicines included Pinellia ternata, Magnolia officinalis, Poria cohoe, Perilla leaf, and cassia twig. Physical examinations over the past two years showed normal electrocardiogram, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and creatine kinase MB (CK-MB) isoenzyme tests, with no morphological changes in echocardiography. Neurological examination revealed normal tendon reflexes, grade 5 limb muscle strength, normal muscle tension and volume, and no edema or color changes. The patient's limb dysfunction symptoms improved significantly after acupuncture treatment. The patient declined further tests such as electromyogram (EMG) or muscle biopsy.
test_results: No myogenic lesion was found in both lower extremities, however, neurogenic lesion could not be excluded.
Orpha_name: Isolated asymptomatic elevation of creatine phosphokinase

case_report: A 19-month-old boy was referred to the pediatric endocrinology unit for low calcium levels and short stature. He is the third child of healthy consanguineous Turkish parents, who have two healthy boys and experienced two abortions. The family history showed no affected members. The prenatal period was normal. The child was born at term via Cesarean section with a birth weight of 3,200 g (+0.02 SDS). He experienced a convulsion due to low calcium levels on day 4 and received intravenous calcium and vitamin D supplementation. He was discharged on day 14 with phenobarbital therapy. From the age of 4 months, he was hospitalized three times for lower respiratory tract infections. At 19 months, physical examination showed his height, weight, and head circumference were at −3.1, −2.7, and +0.2 SDSs, respectively. Notable features included midface hypoplasia, swollen eyelids, down-slanting palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, long philtrum, high arched palate, low set ears, and a small jaw. Additional findings were a prominent forehead, an open anterior fontanelle (4 × 4 cm), pectus carinatum, a café-au-lait spot (4 × 3 cm) on the anterior thorax, and bowing of the femora and ulnae. Eye examination showed optic atrophy and horizontal nystagmus. There was a moderate delay in developmental milestones. Biochemical evaluation revealed serum calcium at 7.4 mg/dl (N: 9.0–11), phosphorus at 4.4 mg/dl (N: 4–6.5), ALP at 84 U/L (N: 116–450), albumin at 4.1 g/L (N: 3.5-5.5), PTH at 102.3 ng/L (N: 15–88), and 25-OH vitamin D at 27 μg/L (N: 30–100). Liver and kidney function tests, thyroid function tests, and ion levels were normal.
test_results: Skeletal survey showed diffuse osteosclerosis of the craniofacial, axial and appendicular skeletons, especially in diaphyseal areas of the long tubular bones. In the evaluation of the vertebral structures, end plate irregularities, mildly reduced height (platyspondyly) and thoracic and lumbar scoliosis were observed. Pelvic bones showed sclerosis, especially in the iliac bodies.

case_report: A 3-year-old Iranian girl presented with progressive weakness, lassitude, and pallor over the past 6 months. She was born at 38 weeks’ gestation to second-degree consanguineous parents, with a birth weight of 2900 grams (10th-25th percentile) and a head circumference of 35 cm (50th percentile). Chronic anemia was noted at 1 year of age, unresponsive to oral iron and other hematinics. There was no history of bleeding or bone pain. Her intellectual and motor development were normal, and she was fully immunized according to the national vaccination schedule without complications. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, a weight of 12.5 kg (10th-25th percentile), and a height of 83 cm (<3rd percentile). There was no icterus, lymphadenopathy, or purpuric spots. The spleen was palpable 6-7 cm below the costal margin, but the liver span was normal. No deformities of the radial bones or thumbs were observed. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Initial blood work showed a hemoglobin concentration of 5.7 g/dL, hematocrit of 16.5%, platelet count of 48,000/µL, and leukocyte count of 4,900 cells/µL (with a differential of 47% neutrophils, 1% bands, 45% lymphocytes, and 6% monocytes). The reticulocyte count was 2%, and the MCV was 76.8 fl. Liver function tests, uric acid, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear indicated normochromic, normocytic anemia with moderate thrombocytopenia. Iron studies and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal. Direct Coombs test, G6PD, and osmotic fragility tests showed no abnormalities. Serology tests for CMV, EBV, and leishmaniasis were negative. Bone marrow needle aspiration performed twice revealed normocellularity with normoblastic erythropoiesis and no atypical cells. Bone marrow biopsy showed unremarkable bone trabeculae with severely hypocellular marrow.
test_results: Radiographic examination showed widening of diaphysis with symmetrical endosteal thickening of the long bones of extremities. Erlenmeyer deformity of distal femoral metadiaphysis was seen.

case_report: A 14-year-old male, weighing 45 kg, was transferred to our clinic for further evaluation after being found to have pericardial effusion at a provincial hospital. Initial symptoms included fever and left shoulder pain. Physical examination revealed a reduction in the intensity of cardiac sounds and an elevated heart rate. Notably, the patient did not exhibit arthralgia or abdominal pain at any point during the clinical course. Three weeks before this event, the patient had an upper respiratory tract infection, which was treated with ibuprofen.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed a moderate pericardial effusion and a mild bilateral pleural effusion. Biological investigations showed the white blood cell count was 19,670/µL, the neutrophils count was 16.8/µL, the lymphocytes count was 810/µL, and there were high levels of inflammatory markers in the plasma tests: the C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 131 mg/L, the erythrocytes sedimentation rate (ESR) was 72 mm/h, the rheumatoid factor was positive (20UI/mL, normal value, NV < 14 UI/mL), and the ferritin level was high at 380.3 ng/mL (NV = 14–152 ng/mL). The complement fractions (C3, C4) were normal; autoantibodies were not detected; and the Quantiferon TB Gold, tuberculin skin test, and antibody work-up for common viral infections were all negative. An immunogram showed hypoIgG (652 mg/dL, NV 720–1700 mg/dL). Echocardiography revealed a circumferential pericardial effusion of 9–15 mm. Furthermore, a left pleural effusion was associated. The ECG showed PR segment depression and ST elevation in the inferior leads. In addition to a negative antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) profile, a Sanger sequencing for the MEFV gene was performed without any mutations identified. Biological investigations showed an elevated interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) level in the patient’s blood, with a 10 pg/mL recorded value (normal values < 5 pg/mL). Next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed by the Invitae Corporation, San Francisco, USA, revealed a previously unreported de novo missense mutation in the NLRP12 gene (c.1264G > A).
diagnosis: Autoinflammatory Recurrent Pericarditis Associated with a New NLRP12 Mutation

case_report: A 35-year-old woman visited the neurology outpatient department with an 11-month history of unusual tongue movements and protrusion, which worsened during speech. She also reported difficulty swallowing. Her medical history showed no significant comorbidities, psychiatric conditions, or endocrine, metabolic, and neurological diseases. There was no family history of neurological disorders. The patient had previously seen multiple doctors without a definitive diagnosis and had been prescribed Fluoxetine (40mg daily) and Alprazolam (0.5mg nightly) by a psychiatrist for three months, which exacerbated her symptoms and were discontinued two months prior to her visit. No abnormal postures or movements were observed in her face, neck, or other muscle groups. She experienced difficulties with eating, drinking, whistling, and singing. A speech therapist noted impaired tongue movement, and the patient struggled with simple tongue tasks. During speech evaluation, she was asked to repeat words and sentences, read texts, engage in conversation, sing, and perform vowel and fricative phoneme prolongation. The tongue movement disorder was present in all speech tasks and phonemes except for vowel and sound prolongations. Tongue protrusion was more frequent with alveodental and alveolar phonemes and less frequent with palatal and velar phonemes. Slower speech and lower voice intensity reduced tongue protrusion. General physical and detailed neurological examinations showed normal motor, sensory, and cerebellar functions. Fundoscopic and cranial nerve examinations were normal. Various tests were conducted to exclude secondary causes. A thorough medical history ruled out post-traumatic, drug-induced, or post-infectious causes. Baseline laboratory work, including complete blood count, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, creatine phosphate kinase, and thyroid profile, were normal. A peripheral smear ruled out neuroacanthocytosis, and normal serum ceruloplasmin excluded Wilson’s disease. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable, and an electroencephalogram showed a normal rhythm.
test_results: An MRI brain with contrast was done on 1.5 tesla, which showed no apparent abnormality.

case_report: A one-and-a-half-year-old boy of Indian origin presented with a 1-year history of intermittent fever and progressive abdominal distension over 10 months. The fever ranged from mild to moderate. The child had been prescribed multiple antibiotics, including anti-tubercular therapy, over the past year. He received one aliquot of packed red blood cells at 6 months of age and multiple random donor platelets in the last 2 months. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination revealed pallor and multiple petechial spots on both lower limbs. Abdominal examination showed the spleen palpable 7 cm below the left costal margin and the liver palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory results included hemoglobin of 3.4 mmol/L (5.5 g/dl), WBC count of 17×10^9/L, and platelet count of 3×10^9/L. Peripheral smear indicated spherocytes and numerous nucleated RBCs. Serum LDH level was 441 mg/dL, and the direct Coomb’s test was significantly positive (4+). Peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed 4.8% double negative αβ+ T cells out of total CD3+ cells. The autoimmune panel was positive for antinuclear antibody (>1:40) and high anti-dsDNA antibody (ELISA) (200 IU/ml). 2D echocardiography revealed mild pericardial effusion without valvular defects. The patient was started on steroids. After one week of steroid therapy, there was inadequate response, so IVIG (2 g/kg) was administered over 2 days. Gradual improvement in hemoglobin and platelet count was observed, and the patient became transfusion independent. During the fever workup, blood culture grew Escherichia coli, which was treated with sensitive antibiotics.
test_results: Clinical exome sequencing detected a pathogenic variant of KRAS (Gly13Cys) at exon 2.
diagnosis: Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome  with Monogenic Lupus due to KRAS mutation

case_report: A 49-year-old woman reported experiencing a bilateral temporal headache for over a month. Her medical history includes treatment for tuberculous lymphadenitis 20 years ago and a diagnosis of metabolic syndrome four years ago. She began menstruating at age 12, had regular cycles, and entered menopause at age 42. The headache was primarily retro-orbital and was somewhat relieved by analgesics. It was accompanied by inflammatory joint pain and occasional pain and redness in the right eye. The patient denied any history of trauma or seizures and mentioned recent visual blurriness. Physical examination revealed an alert and conscious patient. Pulmonary auscultation and skin examination were normal. A comprehensive neurological examination, including assessments of sensorium, cranial nerves, motor and sensory functions, cerebellar function, and reflexes, was normal. Ophthalmological examination identified right panuveitis with multiple choroidal granulomas.
test_results: Brain MRI showed a pituitary adenoma of 16x16x12 mm diameter with parasellar extension and without compression of the optic chiasm. The mass was hypointense on T1- and hyper-intense on T2-weighted images and homogeneously enhanced after the administration of Gadolinium. A hormonal assay of the pituitary gland at 8 AM showed central hypothyroidism and an elevated level of prolactin. Other pituitary hormones, including morning cortisol, were within normal levels. Histological examination revealed a granulomatous hypophysitis (epithelioid and giant cells without caseous necrosis). Laboratory parameters showed an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and hypercalciuria. A chest and abdominal CT scan revealed hepatomegaly but no lymphadenopathies. Polymerase chain reaction, for the specific detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, was negative on the pituitary tissue.
Orpha_name: Pituitary hormone deficiency of meningeal origin

case_report: The patient is a 49-year-old male who began experiencing difficulty standing up from a sitting position at the age of 38. Over time, he noticed progressive weakness in both upper and lower limbs, which affected daily activities such as carrying a child and walking without stumbling. By the age of 49, he had significant difficulty walking unaided, climbing stairs, and standing up from both sitting and lying positions. A neurological examination at age 46 showed symmetric atrophy and weakness in the proximal muscles of the limbs. Shoulder abduction and adduction were graded 4/5 on both sides, elbow flexion and extension were also 4/5 bilaterally, while wrist and finger movements were normal. Hip flexion was graded 3/5 and hip extension 4/5 bilaterally. Knee flexion and extension were 3/5 bilaterally, and ankle plantar flexion and dorsiflexion were both 4/5 on both sides. There was notable weakness in the axial muscles, particularly the paraspinal and abdominal muscles. The patient exhibited a wide-based gait with a lordotic posture, a positive Gowers’ sign, and mild calf enlargement. Tendon reflexes, sensory examination, and cranial nerve examination were normal. Cognitive testing showed no abnormalities. Over a four-year follow-up period, muscle weakness progressed slowly, with more noticeable deterioration in the distal parts of the upper limbs and slight asymmetry, with the right side being more affected. The patient could walk a few meters unaided but primarily used walking sticks. No cognitive decline was observed. A nerve conduction study at age 46 showed no abnormalities, while needle electromyography indicated myopathic changes, more prominent in the proximal limb muscles, without spontaneous activity. His creatine kinase (CK) level was 1,237 U/L at age 46 and increased to 1,309 U/L a year later. Whole-body bone scintigraphy showed no abnormalities characteristic of Paget’s disease. Whole-body MRI revealed fatty replacement, predominantly in the right vastus intermedius and medialis, gastrocnemius and soleus in the calf, abdominal wall, and lumbar muscles. Family history indicated similar symptoms in the patient’s father and paternal uncle. The uncle experienced muscle weakness and difficulty walking from age 40 and passed away at 59. The patient’s father, now 73, began having trouble climbing stairs and frequent falls at age 60, and by age 68, he had difficulty walking and started using crutches. He also struggled to stand up from sitting and lying positions. ENMG examination of the father showed partial axonal degeneration of motor nerves in the lower limbs and myopathic patterns in all lower limb muscles, especially the quadriceps femoris, and proximal upper limb muscles. His CK level was 119 U/L.
test_results: Next-generation sequencing analysis of the proband revealed a previously reported pathogenic heterozygous variant NM_007126.5:c.277C > T (NP_009057.1:p.(Arg93Cys)) in exon 3 of the VCP gene. Segregation analysis showed that the detected variant is inherited from the affected father.
diagnosis: Hereditary Inclusion Body Myopathy with VCP Gene Variant
Orpha_name: Adult-onset distal myopathy due to VCP mutation

case_report: The patient is a 19-year-old woman who was born full-term to a non-consanguineous couple. At birth, she exhibited low muscle tone, and her breathing and crying were weak. During her first month of life, she experienced respiratory failure and required a tracheotomy and mechanical ventilation. Throughout infancy, her muscle weakness persisted; however, she achieved all motor developmental milestones on time. She also experienced intermittent cyanosis due to a patent ductus arteriosus and underwent corrective heart surgery at the age of 2.
test_results: Repetitive stimulation of the left axillary nerve at 2 Hz resulted in a 36% decrement of the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) area. No repetitive CMAPs were observed after single nerve stimulation. Serum antibodies against AChR and MuSK were negative.
diagnosis: Congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by mutations in MUSK

case_report: A 20-year-old Asian male patient, with no family history of tumors or genetic diseases, presented with a painful anterior mediastinal mass in March 2010. Laboratory tests showed elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) at 327.6 ng/mL (normal range, 0–10.0 ng/mL) and human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) at 116.1 mIU/mL (normal range, 0–5.0 mIU/mL). He underwent complete surgical removal of the tumor, and histopathology revealed a malignant mixed germ cell tumor with seminoma and immature teratoma components. Post-surgery, AFP levels decreased to 85.4 ng/mL and β-HCG normalized to 1.2 mIU/mL. The patient then received 4 cycles of cisplatin-based chemotherapy along with three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy, with a total absorbed dose of 3060 centigrays (cGy) in 17 fractions of 180Gy each, targeting the primary mediastinal lesion, middle and superior mediastinum, and double supraclavicular area. At the end of 2014, a metastatic lesion was found in the posterior basal segment of the lower lobe of the left lung. He underwent pneumoresection, and pathology confirmed a single immature teratoma. He then received 6 cycles of chemotherapy with vindesine, ifosfamide, and cisplatin. The patient remained in stable remission. In early 2020, he was admitted to the hospital with persistent chest pain and severe fatigue lasting one day. Clinical examination revealed low-grade fever, flushed skin, and splenomegaly. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin: 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (15.66*10^9/L), and thrombocytopenia (38*10^9/L). Coagulation tests indicated an elevated D-dimer value (2340 µg/L) and a slightly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (37.4 s). Chemical analysis showed high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels (878 U/L) in the peripheral blood. Imaging studies, including computed tomography scan and transabdominal ultrasound, revealed hepatosplenomegaly and seroperitoneum. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed a diffuse increase in systemic bone metabolism and hepatosplenomegaly with slightly increased FDG metabolism, consistent with blood system diseases. There was no evidence of a second recurrence of the germ cell tumor.
test_results: BM aspiration showed substantial infiltration (67% of all nucleated cells) from morphologically heterogeneous atypical circles to oblong cells containing abundant cytoplasm with metachromatic coarse granules. Chemical staining results showed that atypical cells were negative for nonspecific esterase (NSE), peroxidase (POX), and naphthol AS-D chloroacetate esterase staining (NAS-DCE), except for toluidine blue staining. An analysis of the BM aspirate via multiparameter flow cytometry revealed that abnormal cells were positive for CD45, CD117, CD13, CD33, and CD9 but weakly positive for CD2 and CD22, and negative for CD16, CD7, κ, λ, CD19, CD38, HLA-DR, CD35, CD65, CD15, CD11b, CD123, CD79a, CD10, CD25, CD34, and MPO. The chromosomal G banding analysis showed a normal karyotype (46, XY). 16 myeloid leukemia-associated fusion genes, including MLL-AF6, CBFB-MYH11, AML1-ETO, PML-RARα, and BCR-ABL, were negative through reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). In addition, fluorescence in situ hybridization detected that RARα rearrangement was negative. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the BM aspirate identified stable mutations in TP53 P301Qfs*44, FLT3 R973X, SETBP1 N272D, and JAK3 I688F, whereas KIT mutations were not detected. The bone marrow biopsy revealed atypical cells that were mainly oval and short spindle cells distributed in clusters and eosinophilic by hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining, accounting for 80% of the nucleated cells. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed positivity for CD117 and negativity for MPO, CD25, and CD34.
