case_report: A 9-year-old boy, born to nonconsanguineous parents, was brought to the pediatric emergency department with worsening abdominal pain and fever over the past 24 hours. His medical history included recurrent episodes of fever, pharyngitis, and diarrhea since age 4, occurring in a cyclical pattern every 21 days and lasting about a week. On initial physical examination, he had a fever of 39.6°C, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, and a heart rate of 100 beats per minute. Abdominal tenderness and guarding were noted, particularly in the right lower quadrant. No superficial lymph nodes or hepatosplenomegaly were detected. Pulmonary and heart examinations were normal, and the rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests on admission showed a total white blood cell count of 3000/mm3, an absolute neutrophil count of 340/mm3 (normal range: 1500–8000/mm3), hemoglobin level of 13 g/dl, and platelet count of 174000/L. Bleeding time and coagulation time were within normal limits. C-reactive protein was elevated at 268 mg/L (<3 mg/L), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 420 UI/L (normal range: 200–400). A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen indicated increased bowel wall thickness of the small intestines and ascending colon at 8 mm (normal: 4 mm). Bacterial and fungal cultures showed no growth, and stool polymerase chain reaction assay was negative. Additional laboratory tests were conducted, with serology for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus, and cytomegalovirus returning negative. Epstein–Barr virus serologic test results were consistent with previous exposure. Serologic tests for antinuclear and antinative DNA antibodies were negative.
test_results: Bone marrow aspiration examination demonstrated a maturation arrest of granulocytic cells.

case_report: A 7-month-old female was admitted with respiratory distress, rapid breathing, low oxygen levels, and severe growth failure not explained by confirmed gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). She is related to another patient from the paternal side. Born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, her birth weight was 3.2 kg. At 5 hours old, she developed respiratory distress with rapid breathing and cyanosis, requiring oxygen therapy through a nasal cannula. At 10 days old, she was hospitalized for 50 days and diagnosed with severe GERD through an upper gastrointestinal contrast study. Anti-reflux therapy was initiated but did not lead to significant improvement. Extensive investigations, including bronchoscopy and bronchoalveolar lavage, were conducted. Her condition worsened, complicated by respiratory syncytial virus-positive bronchiolitis, necessitating mechanical ventilation for 10 days. A CT scan of the chest revealed ground-glass opacities in both lungs and airspace disease features in the bilateral lower lobes, with no pleural effusion or significant interstitial abnormalities.
test_results: The genetic result was homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 29 of the ABCA3 gene. This mutation is defined as C.4545delC.

case_report: A 39-year-old female presented with pain, swelling, and heaviness in the left lower limb, accompanied by recurrent skin ulceration that began 4 years prior. Over time, similar symptoms developed in the right lower limb, including heaviness, pain, and swelling. The patient had a history of left lower extremity deep venous thrombosis 10 years earlier, treated with a 6-month course of anticoagulation therapy. She experienced a gradual onset of progressive left lower limb swelling, pain, and heaviness, which worsened with walking and led to skin ulceration. Despite multiple healthcare visits, effective management was not achieved. Physical examination revealed a body mass index of 27.2, significant swelling in the left leg with coldness on palpation, minimal pitting edema, and circumferential erythematous skin changes. Multiple skin ulcerations were present, primarily on the anterior and medial sides of the leg, with the largest ulcer located on the distal anterior third of the leg, measuring approximately 10 × 6 cm. The ulcer bases were granulating, with the largest ulcer extending deeply into subcutaneous fat and exhibiting minimal discharge. Circumferential measurements of the affected limb below the knee at 5-cm increments were 47, 47, 42.5, and 38 cm, with a calculated volume of 1.857 L. In comparison, the contralateral limb measurements were 41.5, 41.5, 37.5, and 34 cm, with a calculated volume of 1.452 L.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment showed diffuse circumferential fatty hypertrophy and thickened hyperintense dermis with extensive reticular edema in the left lower limb. Lymphoscintigraphic evaluation of both lower extremities showed intact lymphatic system which ruled out lymphedema as a potential diagnosis. Perfusion assessment of the involved limb was done through indocyanine green (ICG) imaging and showed impaired foot tissue perfusion with low fluorescence signal intensity.

case_report: A 15-month-old female child from Dire-Dawa, Ethiopia, presented with a regression of developmental milestones and truncal ataxia starting at 11 months of age, following a febrile illness one month prior. Initially, she was diagnosed with pneumonia during the febrile illness and showed improvement after treatment. One month later, she developed upper extremity weakness, truncal ataxia, and increasing difficulty reaching for objects. Up to 10 months of age, her growth and development were normal, but she then progressively regressed in her developmental milestones. There is no history of seizures, loss of consciousness, or prior neurological illness. She was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, had a normal neonatal period, and is immunized according to the EPI schedule. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and anthropometric measurements, including a head circumference of 48 cm. No dysmorphic features were noted. Neurologic examination showed that she was conscious, with midsized, reactive pupils bilaterally. Optic disc and retina assessments were normal bilaterally, and she could move her eyes in all directions. Limb power was observed to be 3/5 in all extremities, with bilateral hyperreflexia, truncal ataxia, and dysmetria. No sensory loss was detected. Laboratory blood work results were within normal ranges.
test_results: MRI of her brain revealed diffuse white matter abnormality.

case_report: A 33-year-old female with a history of autoimmune hepatitis post orthotopic liver transplantation in 1999, Crohn's disease post colectomy in 2019, and asthma presented to the hospital with worsening shortness of breath over the past day, not relieved by nebulized albuterol. Five days before hospital admission, she experienced a sore throat, dry cough, and nausea. She was treated with amoxicillin for otitis media at an urgent care facility four days before hospital admission, but her symptoms persisted. She reported fevers, chills, and rhinorrhea starting two days before hospital admission. She denied any contact with sick individuals. On the way to the hospital, she received 15 liters of supplemental oxygen via a non-rebreather mask due to increased breathing effort and suspected low oxygen levels. Her home medications included oral tacrolimus 2mg twice daily and oral budesonide 3mg twice daily. Initial vital signs were blood pressure 152/88 mmHg, pulse rate 121, respiratory rate 49, temperature 99.1 °F, and oxygen saturation 98% on high flow nasal cannula with settings of 60L flow rate and 100% fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2). Physical examination revealed an ill-appearing female in acute distress, with rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, use of accessory muscles, and increased work of breathing. A chest radiograph showed bilateral opacifications in the lower lung fields. Initial laboratory tests showed bandemia without an increase in white blood cells, normocytic anemia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent respiratory alkalosis on the given oxygen settings, elevated lactate, elevated serum creatinine, and a normal urinalysis.
test_results: A nasopharyngeal swab sample demonstrated a positive result for human rhinovirus. A computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the chest demonstrated bilateral lower lobe consolidations with air bronchograms and no evidence of pulmonary embolism.
diagnosis: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome  secondary to rhinovirus infection

case_report: A male infant was delivered at 34 weeks gestation via caesarean section to a 24-year-old mother, her second pregnancy, from a non-consanguineous marriage. The pregnancy was without complications, and there was no exposure to known teratogens. An antenatal ultrasound at 28 weeks indicated oligohydramnios. The infant did not experience perinatal asphyxia. At birth, the infant weighed 1.5 kg and had a head circumference of 34 cm. Limb deformities were observed, with joint contractures affecting both flexion and extension. Joint mobility, both active and passive, was restricted, particularly in the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints. The shoulders exhibited bilateral internal rotation, and the elbows were flexed. The infant had arachnodactyly with a wide gap between the index and middle fingers on both hands. In the lower limbs, the hips were fixed in flexion, the knees were extended, and the ankles were dorsiflexed. The left foot had a congenital talipes equinovarus deformity. Facial abnormalities included an asymmetric face, low-set ears, a high-arched palate, a short neck, and micrognathia. The muscles in both the upper and lower limbs were significantly underdeveloped. Additionally, the infant had hypospadias and bilateral inguinal hernia.
test_results: MRI head revealed dilatation of the ventricles with hypoplastic brainstem and hypoplasia of the inferior vermis and cerebellar hemispheres. Echocardiography revealed small-size ostium secundum atrial septal defect without pulmonary hypertension.

case_report: A 22-year-old Caucasian woman presented for evaluation of infertility and had experienced secondary amenorrhea since the age of 18. She had been on hormonal replacement therapy for the past two years, which induced cyclical bleeding, but ovulation did not occur. There was no family history of premature menopause. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed an anteflexed uterus with normal profile, echostructure, and dimensions. The endometrium appeared normal on ultrasound. Both ovaries were normal in size and shape, with no liquid effusion. A hysterosalpingogram confirmed normal uterine and tubal anatomy. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary gland with paramagnetic contrast showed a sellar cavity with regular morphology and dimensions, and no structural alterations. The adenohypophysis appeared normal, and the hypophyseal peduncle was correctly oriented. Serum tests showed the absence of anti-ovarian and anti-adrenal antibodies. The patient had elevated levels of gonadotropins (LH: 41.17 IU/L and FSH: 79.90 IU/L). Thyroid-stimulating hormone, free tri-iodothyronine, and free thyroxin levels were within normal ranges, while anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were significantly elevated.
test_results: An examination of her karyotype revealed the presence of a mutual translocation, apparently balanced, that involved the X chromosome long arm (q13) and the 14 chromosome short arm (p12), with consequent karyotype 46,X,t(X;14)(q13;p12). Breakpoints were confirmed with fluorescent in situ hybridization. The assay demonstrated that the active X chromosome was translocated (X-autosome: X; 14).
diagnosis: Premature ovarian failure due to a chromosomal anomaly

case_report: A 16-year-old male exhibited significant weakness in the proximal muscles of all four limbs, which began at age 11 with difficulties in walking and tip-toe gait. By age 16, he demonstrated a waddling gait with tip-toe walking and genu recurvatum, covering less than 50 meters. Clinical examination revealed severe proximal muscle weakness and muscle wasting, more pronounced in the lower limbs. Muscle strength was assessed using the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale: 4+/5 for arm abduction and elbow flexion, and 2/5 for hip flexion, hip abduction, and knee extension. Achilles tendon contractures were present. Bilateral symmetrical scapular winging and axial muscle weakness were noted. Sensory examination was normal, and deep tendon reflexes were intact except for absent patellar reflexes. No abnormalities were observed in the head and neck region. Cognitive development was normal, and no cardiac abnormalities were detected. Respiratory function tests showed a vital capacity of 69%, with no dyspnea. Serum creatine kinase levels were elevated at 1385 IU/L (normal <200 IU/L). Electromyography indicated abundant spontaneous activity (fibrillations and complex repetitive, myotonic discharges at rest) and clear myogenic changes during effort. Ultrasonography revealed homogeneous muscle hyperechogenicity, especially in the quadriceps. MRI of the pelvis, upper thighs, and legs showed bilateral symmetric muscle fatty replacement without muscle edema or contrast enhancement. At age 22, upper limb weakness had progressed (deltoids, biceps MRC scale 3/5; grip strength approximately 40% of normal, around 20 kg), and walking was limited to about 50 meters with a knee orthosis for genu recurvatum, though he primarily used an electric wheelchair. A muscle biopsy of the left deltoid at age 16 showed non-grouping, atrophic, round fibers with multiple internalized nuclei. Numerous cytoplasmic autophagic vacuoles were observed, strongly positive for PAS and phosphatasic acid. Immunohistochemistry staining for p62 and TDP 43 was positive in the cytoplasmic autophagic vacuoles. Vacuolated fibers expressed MHC class I and complement C5b-9 without inflammatory infiltrates. Maltase acid activity and sequencing of the exon regions and junctions (+/-25 nt) of the LAMP2 and GAA genes were normal.
test_results: Sanger sequencing of the VMA21 gene detected hemizygous, unreported, intronic, single-nucleotide substitution c.164-20T>A (NM_001017980.4) in the last intron. This variant has never been described to our knowledge (absent from gnomAD and HGMD). Its in silico analysis predicted a loss of strength of the acceptor site located 20 bp downstream. Alamut Visual Plus (v1.6.1 from Sophia Genetics) predicted a negative impact based on four algorithm predictions (GeneSplicer: −25%; MaxEntScan: −18%; SpliceSiteFinder-like: 0%; NNSPLICE: 0%). Additionally, Splice AI predicted an acceptor loss with a score of 0.42 in a scale from 0 to 1.
diagnosis: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy due to a novel intronic mutation in the VMA21 gene

case_report: A 15-year-old male was admitted due to stumbling and weakness. At age 3, he developed a cough and diarrhea, followed by an abnormal and unsteady gait without an apparent cause. Partial remission was achieved after symptomatic treatment. Since then, he experienced recurrent episodes of ataxia and limb weakness following each incidence of diarrhea. His self-care, learning, and communication abilities gradually declined, accompanied by abdominal flatulence, gastrointestinal disturbance, and polyuria. Initially, these episodes occurred once or twice a year but increased in frequency, becoming constant approximately three years after onset. He received treatments with immunoglobulin and glucocorticoid on several occasions without success. At admission, he was emaciated, measuring 150 cm in height and weighing 40 kg. He was unable to walk independently or sit upright. Physical examination revealed decreased advanced mental function, dysarthria, right ptosis, nystagmus, hypomyotonia, hypesthesia, and pallhypesthesia in the limbs. The bilateral finger-nose test and heel-knee-tibia test results were unstable. He exhibited obvious scoliosis and a mild foot drop deformity. The patient was not born prematurely and had normal development prior to the onset of symptoms. His parents were not consanguineous. All basic metabolic, cerebrospinal fluid, and microbial pathogen tests were normal.
test_results: Brain MRI showed marked cerebellar atrophy in addition to signal changes in cerebral white matter. The electromyography showed a fibrillation potential and a positive sharp wave in the left biceps and tibialis anterior muscle. The voltage increased slightly but the polyphase wave increased by more than 40%. The amplitude and conduction velocity of the motor nerve was notably decreased, and the amplitude of the sensory nerve could not lead out. Reflexes of the bilateral tibial nerves were not elicited. These findings revealed neurogenic and myogenic lesions. The neurogenic lesions in question had appeared when the patient was 3 years old. The electroencephalogram showed frequent irregular slow waves with a high amplitude of 1.5–2 Hz in the whole cephalic region. An auditory brainstem response test showed a mild left sensorineural hearing loss. The ECG showed sinus arrhythmia, incomplete right bundle branch block, and electric axis right anteroclock transposition. Hematoxylin and eosin staining showed different sizes of muscle fibers. The reduced form of nicotinamide-adenine dinucleotid (NADH) and ATPase-staining showed a pathological aggregation in myofibrillary groups. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on this patient, and Sanger sequencing was applied to verify his parents. A compound heterozygous mutation of ADPRHL2 was recognized in the proband [NM_017825: c.62C>A, p.[S21*]; c.535C>T, and p.[Q179*]]. The mutations c.62C>A and c.535C>T were inherited from his father and mother, respectively.
diagnosis: Stress-Induced Childhood-Onset Neurodegeneration With Ataxia-Seizures Syndrome
Orpha_name: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia-epilepsy-intellectual disability syndrome due to RUBCN deficiency

case_report: A 19-month-old girl presented with haemolytic anaemia and developmental delay. She was the first child of third-cousin parents, born at 38 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy. She was hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care unit for 38 days due to neonatal jaundice and early sepsis, requiring five blood transfusions immediately after birth and an exchange transfusion on the second day of life due to maternal-foetal ABO incompatibility. Another blood transfusion was required at 30 days old for non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. At 9 months, she experienced multiple haemolytic crises triggered by infections and exhibited mild psychomotor developmental delay, unable to sit independently. At 11 months, she was diagnosed with hereditary spherocytosis through a pathologic osmotic fragility test. At 19 months, she was referred with symptoms of an inability to walk and sit without support. Physical examination revealed a weight of 7.3 kg (<3 percentile; z-score −3), height of 78 cm (9th percentile; z-score −1.3), and head circumference of 44.5 cm (5th percentile; z-score −1.6). She exhibited severe malnutrition, paleness, axial hypotonia with muscle bulk loss, and muscle weakness. Decreased deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy, and hyperelasticity of the joints were noted in the extremities. Laboratory findings showed severe macrocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, haematocrit 13.1%, mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration 31 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 104 fL, normal white blood cell count 8.868 × 10^9/L, platelet count 95,000/mm3, elevated total bilirubin 24.63 mg/dL, and direct bilirubin 18.58 mg/dL. Plasma amino acids, very long-chain fatty acids, serum transferrin isoelectric focusing, and urine organic acids with GCMS were unremarkable. The acylcarnitine profile by MSMS showed normal C0 (62.8 µmol/L, normal range: 10–90 µmol/L) and elevated C3 (7.1 µmol/L, normal range: 0–4.9 µmol/L), with negative methylmalonic acid in the urine by GCMS. Plasma vitamin B12, folic acid, and homocysteine levels were normal. Bone marrow aspiration was normocellular. Ophthalmologic fundus examination, brain stem electric response audiometry (BERA), electromyography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging were all normal. No epileptic activity was observed in the electroencephalography. Muscle biopsy indicated myopathy. During follow-up, the patient required multiple hospitalizations due to haemolytic crises, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, and gastroenteritis. At 3 years old, she was admitted to the intensive care unit for pneumonia, required a tracheostomy, and lost most of her acquired developmental milestones.
test_results: Molecular analysis using next-generation sequencing disclosed a p.E105D (c.315G>C) homozygous mutation in the TPI1 gene.

case_report: A 1-year-old girl was admitted to the hospital due to significant growth retardation. She was born to a nonconsanguineous couple, with the mother experiencing gestational diabetes in the third trimester. At 24+3 weeks of gestation, a color Doppler ultrasound revealed that one femur was shorter than expected for the gestational age, with a femur length to plantar length ratio of 0.81 and a proximal femur shaft-epiphysis angle greater than 116°, indicating abnormal skeletal development. Various genetic tests, including amniocentesis, high-throughput gene sequencing, prenatal screening, chromosome microarray analysis, and Sanger sequencing for the FGFR3 gene c.1138G > A variations, showed no abnormalities. By the time these results were available, the fetus was 29 weeks gestational age, and the family declined further genetic testing. The girl was delivered at 39+2 weeks via cesarean section with Apgar scores of 9, 10, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes, respectively. She was breastfed for ten months, with supplementary food introduced at 6 months. The child had a poor appetite from birth. Her birth weight was 3300 g (P55.8, Z score 0.15) and length was 48 cm (P40.5, Z score -0.24). At 6 months, her weight was 6.13 kg (P7.5, Z score -1.44), height was 59.5 cm (P0.3, Z score -2.76), and cranial circumference was 45.6 cm (P97.1, Z score 1.9). At 12 months, her weight was 7.62 kg (P9.0, Z score -1.34), length was 65.5 cm (< P0, Z score -3.33), and cranial circumference was 47.5 cm (P97.1, Z score 1.9). The ratio of crown-rump length to height was above the normal upper limit. Routine tests showed an increase in d-3-hydroxybutyric acid to 2.66 mmol/L (reference value: 0–0.27 mmol/L), while other parameters including routine blood tests, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, blood glucose, blood lactate, blood ammonia, pyruvic acid, ceruloplasmin, insulin-like growth factor-1, insulin-like growth factor-1 binding protein 3, thyroid stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, free triiodothyronine, and parathyroid hormone levels were normal. X-ray findings indicated decreased bone mineral density in the tubular bones and spinal column, thick and short humeri, and irregular metaphyses with a cup-shaped deformity. Brain cranial MRI findings were normal. The patient achieved head control at 5 months, could sit with assistance at 8 months, and began climbing at 12 months. The Gesell Developmental Schedules test indicated mild motor development delay due to malnutrition. Fetal DNA extracted from amniotic fluid and panel Sanger sequencing for FGFR3 gene c.1138G > A variations were negative.
test_results: The c.1620C > A pathogenic variations was detected in exon 12 of the proband, which is a pathogenicity variant leading to an amino acid change, p.Asn540Lys. No relevant variants were identified in the parents, whose genotypes were normal. Testing for the variant in the proband and her parents was performed by Sanger sequencing, and the variant met the criteria to be identified as a pathogenic variant, PS1 + PS2 + PS3-Supporting + PS4 + PM2-Supporting + PP3, according to the 2015 ACMG guidelines.

case_report: A 34-year-old nulligravid Caucasian woman with a history of infertility due to bilateral tubal occlusion and oligoovulation underwent an in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycle using a Gonadotropin Releasing Hormone agonist (GnRH-a) long protocol. Following down-regulation with leuprolide acetate, controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) was conducted with recombinant Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (rFSH) at a daily dose of 225 IU for eleven days. Ovulation was induced with recombinant human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (rhCG) (250 mcg s.c.) when three follicles reached 17 mm in diameter. On the trigger day, estradiol levels were 27,496 pmol/L. Ultrasound-guided transvaginal follicular aspiration was performed 35 hours post-rhCG administration, retrieving eight mature oocytes. Biochemical evaluations of hematocrit, coagulation, serum albumin, liver, and renal functions were within normal ranges. The patient was asymptomatic, and two day-3 embryos were transferred. Luteal phase support was provided with vaginal progesterone at 200 mg twice daily. Twelve days post-embryo transfer, the patient developed nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dyspnea, and oliguria. Physical examination showed paleness, dehydration, abdominal tension, and lung hypoventilation, with normal temperature, blood pressure, pulse rate, and oxygen saturation. The patient's weight was 86.5 kg. Transvaginal sonography indicated ovarian enlargement (left ovary 84 × 63 mm, right ovary 79 × 61 mm) and significant ascites. Blood analysis showed hemoconcentration (hematocrit 46.1%, white blood cells 19,010/ml, platelets 855,000/ml), hyperkalemia (5.1 mmol/l), and hypoproteinemia (total protein 59 g/l, albumin 27 g/l). Renal and hepatic functions were normal. Serum b-hCG was 182 U/L. The patient was admitted to the hospital and received continuous monitoring and supportive therapy, including oral and intravenous hydration, colloid fluids, crystalloid fluids, human albumin infusion, and prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. Fluid intake and urine output were recorded daily. Despite conservative treatment, symptoms worsened, with increased dyspnea and abdominal tension, and weight increased to 87.5 kg. After four days, the patient experienced dyspnea, tachycardia, and sweating, and was treated with oxygen, furosemide (10 mg/day), and cabergoline (0.5 mg/day), and underwent abdominal paracentesis. The patient was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) due to mild hydropericardium and moderate pleural effusion. Cabergoline therapy was discontinued due to severe asthenia. In the ICU, the patient received parenteral nutrition, continuous dopamine infusion (3 γ/kg/min), intravenous hydration, and plasma expanders. Paracentesis was repeated, and albumin therapy was initiated for ascites and mild pleural and pericardial effusions. As respiratory and abdominal symptoms worsened, beta-hCG levels were 1057 U/L. Ultrasound showed a single gestational sac with a fetus at 5 weeks of gestation. Laboratory tests indicated reduced hemoconcentration (hematocrit 41.5%, white blood cells 13,000/ml, platelets 385,000/ml) but increased aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (0.67 ukat/l and 1.17 ukat/l, respectively). Over the next 15 days, ovarian size, ascites, and pleural and pericardial effusions gradually reduced, and the patient was transferred to the Obstetric Unit. A new transvaginal ultrasound revealed two gestational sacs, one with a fetus at 6 weeks of gestational age and the other a blighted ovum, along with reduced ascites and ovarian volume.

case_report: A 12-year-old girl visited the maxillofacial department of Shar hospital with a history of painless, bilateral, slow-growing posterior jaw swelling for 3 years. She had undergone multiple consultations and treatments without resolution. Clinical examination revealed symmetrically swollen parotid glands that were firm, non-movable, non-pulsatile, and non-tender to palpation, with normal-colored, intact overlying facial skin. The other two major salivary glands showed no palpable changes. Intraoral examination indicated signs of reduced salivary flow rate, including multiple cervical caries, large restorations on the permanent molars, and remnants of food debris due to decreased saliva washing action. Her parents reported that she drinks plenty of water during meals to aid swallowing. Systemically, her parents denied any symptoms such as fever, malaise, cough, shortness of breath, loss of appetite, or weight loss. The child reported dryness in her eyes, for which she was prescribed eye drops by an ophthalmologist. Her past medical history included an episode of bilateral painful knee joint swelling at age 8, which was treated with aspiration and painkillers.

case_report: An 11-year-old male presented with asymptomatic, dark-brown, spiny, hyperkeratotic, verrucous scales and ridges covering the body since birth. The patient reported that the scales shed after scrubbing and reappear within 5-7 days. He was born at full term via normal vaginal delivery. There was no history of parental consanguinity, collodion presentation at birth, blistering, or erythroderma. No family members were affected. Physical examination revealed symmetrically distributed, generalized, thickened, verrucous, dark-brown cobblestone-like lesions. The scalp and central part of the face were spared, but the ears were involved. The axillary region, dorsum of the hands, popliteal fossa, and antecubital fossa were less affected. Severe palmoplantar keratoderma and fissuring were observed. Examination of hair, nails, teeth, mucosa, and other systems was normal.
test_results: Skin biopsy showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis with thick granular layer. Perinuclear vacuolization and coarse keratohyaline granules were seen in upper spinous layers.

case_report: A 28-year-old female was referred to a cardiomyopathy clinic for screening after her father's unexpected passing. At 23 years old, she was identified with a hypokinetic non-dilated cardiomyopathy based on various investigations. During her initial clinic visit, she had a New York Heart Association (NYHA) score of 1 and reported no cardiac symptoms. She maintained an active lifestyle, participating in activities like Zumba and circuit training without any notable symptoms. She worked in accounting, which involved mostly sedentary tasks. Physical examination revealed normal vesicular breath sounds, normal first and second heart sounds without additional sounds, and no lower limb oedema. Her pulse was regular at 80 beats per minute, and her non-invasive blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. Her body mass index (BMI) was 39 kg/m2, placing her in the obese category. She was on anti-heart failure therapy, including enalapril 10 mg at night, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, and empagliflozin 10 mg daily, which led to a significant improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) to 50% on transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE). Further dosage increases were limited due to hypotension. Her N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) level was 76 pg/mL (normal range: 5–125 pg/mL).
test_results: Electrocardiogram showed poor R-wave progression, left anterior fascicular block (QRS axis of −40), low QRS voltages in the precordial leads, and T-wave inversion in V1–V6, III, and AVF. Her first TTE showed mildly reduced LV systolic function of 46% (based on Simpson’s biplane). A 24-h ambulatory ECG monitor recorded a modest ventricular ectopic (VE) burden of 3.1% (n = 3058), without any malignant arrhythmias. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging reported LV systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction (EF) of 40% and normal LV wall thickness of 8 mm. There was circumferential mid-wall and subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in the basal to mid-ventricular LV free wall segments, consistent with a non-ischaemic aetiology. Cardiopulmonary exercise test reported a low VO2 max of 16.6 mL/kg/min [75% of predicted maximum for age, body surface area (BSA), and ethnicity] with VEs at peak (including two couplets). Repeat CMR reported normal LV dimensions with an improved systolic function (LVEF 47%). Thin subepicardial to mid-myocardial linear LGE was demonstrated in all LV basal segments on CMR, as well as the mid-ventricular anterior, anterolateral, and inferior walls. The degree of scar was similar to the previous CMR. Right ventricular (RV) size and global systolic function were normal. Cardiopulmonary exercise test showed an improved VO2 max of 18.7 mL/kg/min (90% of predicted maximum for age, BSA, and ethnicity) with some isolated VEs at peak exercise. The patient was found to harbour a pathogenic splice site variant in FLNC, c.7384+1G>A (heterozygous).

Histopathological examination showed spindle-shaped fibroblastic and collagenous stromal tissue, characteristic of the NOF.

case_report: A 48-year-old Asian woman presented with a chronic mild headache. Imaging of the head revealed a small mass within the sella turcica. Laboratory tests indicated elevated serum GH levels at 6.83 ng/ml (normal range: 0–2.47 ng/ml) and IGF-1 levels at 517 ng/ml (normal range: 82–219 ng/ml). The patient had no neurological deficits, hypertension, or diabetes mellitus, and surgery was not initially recommended. She had no family history of cancer or endocrinological diseases, occasionally consumed alcohol, and did not smoke. She worked as a school janitor, and routine medical checkups showed blood pressure readings of approximately 110/70 mmHg. Follow-up imaging showed no significant change in the size of the mass, and serum GH and IGF-1 levels remained stable at 6.99 ng/ml and 476 ng/ml, respectively. Five years later, her baseline blood pressure increased to 140/80 mmHg, she gained 8 kg, and her shoe size increased by 1.5 cm. She was then referred for surgical intervention.
test_results: Endocrinological examination showed high concentrations of serum GH (6.83 ng/ml; normal range, 0–2.47 ng/ml) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) (517 ng/ml; normal range, 82–219 ng/ml). Head MR imaging incidentally detected a small mass lesion inside the sella turcica. Head MR imaging showed that the tumor was slightly enlarged (11 × 16 × 16 mm) and sparsely enhanced with gadolinium. A roentgenogram showed cauliflower-like enlargement of the distal phalanx of the fingers. Serum concentrations of GH (7.33 ng/ml) and IGF-1 (606 ng/ml) had further increased. A preoperative 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) showed no suppression of serum GH concentration. Postoperative histological examination of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor specimens demonstrated sheet-like proliferation of monomorphic round cells with H&E staining, and tumor cells showed diffuse immunoreactivity for GH.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman underwent screening mammography, which revealed an abnormal finding in her left breast. A stereotactic biopsy was conducted, and the pathology results showed DCIS. Given her strong family history of breast cancer, a bilateral mastectomy was performed. Previous imaging from several years ago at another hospital showed stable right intraocular calcifications over time. The patient has a history of chronic vision loss in the right eye and was born prematurely.

case_report: Patient 4 is an 11-year-old boy who has exhibited pendular nystagmus and intense photophobia since he was 3 months old. His medical history is unremarkable, and there is no family history of significant ophthalmologic conditions or consanguinity. At the age of 5, his best-corrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 in both eyes. He had a mild hypermetropic refractive error (+1.00 in the right eye and +1.50 in the left eye). Examination revealed a 5 prism diopter exotropia in the left eye. The ocular fundus examination was completely normal. Over time, his VA has decreased. Currently, at 11 years old, his best-corrected VA is 20/200 in both eyes.
test_results: The first electrophysiological test performed at the age of 3 revealed DA adapted ERGs within normal limits, but the LA 3.0 ERG and LA 30-Hz flicker ERG were nonrecordable. These results indicated a cone dysfunction and normal rod function. Farnsworth-Munsell 100 Hue Test presented multiple errors is the 3 axes. The boy recognized plates number 1 and 14 and partially plates 5 and 7–8 plates.

case_report: A 35-year-old male patient (height: 179 cm, weight: 49 kg) with severe mitral regurgitation (MR) was referred for elective minimally invasive mitral valve repair. He had no relevant medical history. Preoperative laboratory blood test results were normal. A preoperative transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) revealed severe MR due to a prolapsed anterior leaflet (A3) and a hypoplastic posterior leaflet. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 75 bpm. After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was intubated with a left-sided 37 Fr double-lumen tube for one-lung ventilation (OLV). Ventilator settings during OLV included pressure control ventilation (PCV) with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) set to 0 cmH2O and an inspiratory to expiratory ratio of 1:2. Percutaneous arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) > 95% was maintained under 100% oxygenation with a maximum airway pressure of 15 cmH2O and tidal volume of approximately 300 mL. Immediately after intubation, a TEE probe was inserted, and a central venous catheter and a pulmonary artery catheter were placed in the left internal jugular vein. Under echocardiographic guidance, a 16 Fr venous cannula was inserted through the right internal jugular vein. Another 16 Fr cannula was inserted into the right femoral artery, and a 27 Fr cannula was inserted into the right femoral vein, which threaded through to the right atrium, guided by TEE. The conventional procedure for cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) was subsequently performed. After establishing the CPB, direct aortic clamping was performed using the Chitwood technique. Subsequently, mitral valve repair via four thoracic ports in the left chest wall using the da Vinci surgical system XI was conducted. Cardiac surgeons performed mitral valve leaflet repair through the anterior leaflet neochord reconstruction reinforced with a standard 32-mm MEMO 4D mitral ring mitral annuloplasty band. After completing the leaflet repairs, the aorta was declamped, autonomous heart activity was re-established, and the patient was weaned from CPB without incident. TEE showed no residual mitral regurgitation (MR). Using PCV with a maximum airway pressure of 15 cmH2O and PEEP of 0 cmH2O during the closure of the thoracic port incisions on the chest wall under OLV to avoid parenchymal lung injury, premature ventricular contractions occurred. The patient’s hemodynamic parameters abruptly decompensated to arterial, pulmonary artery, and central venous pressures of 46/24 mmHg, 9/1 mmHg, and 10 mmHg, respectively. After suspecting hemorrhage with cardiac tamponade, the thoracic drain placement was verified and aspirated at −20 mmHg. However, no blood was aspirated. TEE was reperformed to determine the cause of the shock. Four-chamber TEE images showed deformity of the left ventricle, distinctly pronounced motion of the left ventricular apex during the cardiac cycle, and absence of pericardial fluid. Transgastric short-axis TEE images showed left ventricular swing; however, wall motion asynergy could not be accurately evaluated. After frequent phenylephrine dosing (total amount administered, 1 mg), the patient’s hemodynamic parameters gradually stabilized at arterial, pulmonary artery, and central venous pressures of 92/45 mmHg, 20/10 mmHg, and 10 mmHg, respectively.
test_results: Postoperative chest radiography in the operating room revealed a protrusion of the right cardiac border.

case_report: A 29-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with a high-grade fever. She was pregnant, Gravid V, Para II, Aborta II, at 18 weeks and 6 days of gestation. She reported a fever of 105°F, lower abdominal pain, and increased urinary frequency with burning for four days. The fever was continuous and accompanied by chills and rigors, with no factors making it better or worse. Her symptoms worsened to include vomiting and diarrhea, prompting her visit to the ED. She experienced four episodes of vomiting and was unable to tolerate oral intake, along with eight episodes of watery, non-bloody diarrhea in one day, accompanied by lower abdominal pain. She had no recent travel history or contact with sick individuals. On examination, she was well-oriented but lethargic and in obvious distress. Her temperature was 101°F, blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse was 75 beats per minute, and her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 15/15. Chest examination revealed no added heart sounds or murmurs, no wheezes or crackles, and clear and equal breath sounds bilaterally. Vaginal speculum examination was deferred. Rubella and toxoplasmosis immunoglobulin G titers were insignificant. Screens for syphilis, hepatitis A, B, and C, dengue, and rapid malaria test were negative. C-reactive protein level was elevated at 103.3 mg/L. Blood and urine samples were collected for culture and sensitivity. The patient was initially treated with intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone. However, her fever persisted, and her condition worsened with continued rigors, chills, and diarrhea. Laboratory results during hospitalization are presented in Table. Routine urine examination and urine culture results were unremarkable. Blood Gram stain showed the presence of Gram-negative rods. After consultation with an infectious disease specialist, the patient was started on meropenem (2 g IV immediately, 1 g every eight hours) before receiving the results of the blood culture report.
test_results: The blood culture and sensitivity report was positive for S. Typhi (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase).

case_report: The patient is a 17-year-old male who presented with an elevated serum CK level of 8599 U/L (normal range: <175 U/L) discovered during preoperative evaluation for left esotropia surgery one month prior. He was born to non-consanguineous parents following a full-term normal delivery, with a birth weight of 3.2 kg. According to his parents, he achieved early motor milestones on time, walking independently and speaking by age 1 year, with no signs of mental retardation. Throughout his growth, no motor function abnormalities were noted. He performed well in physical education classes and had the same ability to run and climb stairs as his peers. At 1 year of age, a physical examination revealed mild esotropia of the left eye without diplopia. He was noted to be thin with long, thin feet. A manual muscle test showed normal muscle strength without obvious muscle atrophy. He could walk on his toes but had difficulty walking on his heels. Electromyographic evaluation indicated a pattern consistent with muscle lesions. Both electrocardiogram and ultrasonic cardiogram showed no cardiac abnormalities.
test_results: MRI of the bilateral thighs did not show abnormalities. MRI of the bilateral leg muscles showed an abnormal signal of the bilateral soleus and musculi flexor pollicis longus (increased signal on the T2-weighted image and isointensity on the T1-weighted image).

case_report: A 73-year-old woman presented with abnormal posture and gait disturbance. Since the age of 63, she had a slight stooping posture and a pushed-out waist. At 68 years old, she began using a walking stick due to an unstable gait. She was treated with 25 μg/day levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, but her symptoms did not improve. By age 70, she had difficulty climbing stairs, and at 71, she was admitted to another hospital where elevated serum CK levels were noted. She visited our hospital with prominent paraspinal muscle atrophy and mild proximal limb weakness. Her levothyroxine dose was increased to 50 μg/day, but her symptoms remained unchanged. She had a family history of bent spine in her elder sister, mother, and maternal aunt. Physical examination revealed marked atrophy of the paraspinal muscles, abnormal posture, right ptosis, dysarthria, bilateral cataracts, and hearing loss. Eye movements were normal, but there was moderate neck flexion weakness and mild proximal limb muscle weakness. Tendon reflexes were symmetrical, Babinski’s sign was absent, balance was poor with tandem gait, and there was no limb ataxia. Sensory systems were intact, and Romberg’s sign was negative. She scored 25 points on the Mini-Mental State Examination, indicating poor performance on attention and calculation tests. Laboratory data showed a serum CK level of 290 IU/l (normal range 45–163 IU/l), normal resting blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate levels, and slightly low thyroid-stimulating hormone levels at 0.47 μIU/ml (normal range 0.5–5.0 μIU/ml). Under 50 μg/day levothyroxine administration, antithyroglobulin antibody levels were 7.0 U/ml (normal range <0.3 U/ml), antithyroid peroxidase antibody levels were 46.5 U/ml (normal range <0.3 U/ml), rheumatoid factor levels were 152.3 IU/ml (normal value <15.0 IU/ml), and antinuclear antibody levels were mildly elevated (titer of 1:80). Autoimmune analyses, including anti-Jo-1, anti-RNP, anti-SS-A, and anti-SS-B, were negative. The oral glucose tolerance test (75 g) was normal, but Holter monitoring showed high-frequency premature contractions. Pure-tone audiometry indicated sensorineural and high-frequency hearing loss.
test_results: Needle electromyographic findings of the biceps brachii and rectus femoris muscles indicated mild myopathic features. Computed tomography (CT) of the thoracic spinal nerve 10 (T10) revealed severe atrophy and fatty degeneration of the paraspinal muscles. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging showed moderate cerebellar and temporo-parieto-occipital lobe atrophy. MR spectroscopy revealed the absence of increased lactate peaks. 123I-IMP single photon emission CT revealed hypoperfusion that was indicative of atrophic brain lesions.
diagnosis: Mitochondrial disease characterized by familial late-onset predominant axial myopathy and encephalopathy

case_report: An 8-year-old Chinese boy was admitted to the hospital due to delayed growth. He was born full-term, weighing 2.45 kg and measuring 48 cm in height. At 8 months gestational age, a fetal B-ultrasound indicated short limbs. His mother had hypothyroidism during pregnancy and was treated with levothyroxine sodium tablets, maintaining normal thyroid function for the remainder of the gestational period. His height measurements were 67 cm (–3.52SDS) at 1 year, 75 cm (-3.97SDS) at 2 years, 82 cm (-3.89SDS) at 3 years, and 84.5 cm (-5.02SDS) at 4 years. He began speaking at 14 months and walking at 16 months, with developmental milestones delayed by about 1 month compared to typical children. He is currently in grade two of primary school with good academic performance and has an appropriate vaccination status. He experienced recurrent respiratory infections until the age of 4 years. His parents reported no consanguinity. The patient has an elder brother who had intrauterine growth retardation and short limbs as indicated by fetal B-ultrasound. The brother was born full-term, weighing 2 kg and measuring 46 cm in length, but died at 50 days old, possibly due to pneumonia. Upon admission, the child had a height of 86 cm (-5.81SDS), weighed 15 kg (< P3r), and had a BMI of 15.6 kg/m2 (P25–50t). His head circumference was 51 cm, finger distance 90 cm, and sitting height 59 cm. The skin on the inner side of his upper limbs and thighs showed signs of livedo. He exhibited various facial features including zygomatic arch dysplasia, a high forehead, low anterior and posterior hairline, short and down-slanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, a long nasal tip and columella, and a small mouth. Additionally, he had irregular teeth, short limbs, a 2 cm long webbed penis, and testicular volume of 0.5 mL.
test_results: The whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in the proband’s POLE gene. One variant was a splicing variant (c.5811 + 2T > C). The other variant was defined as a nonsense variant (c.2006G > A), resulting in a truncated protein (p.W669X).

case_report: An 85-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with rapid breathing, noisy breathing, and reduced consciousness. Her medical history included coronary artery bypass graft, tissue aortic valve replacement, heart failure, chronic left pleural effusion due to a past left empyema, rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate, total hip replacement, and thoracic compression fractures. She had a COVID-19 infection six weeks prior. Initial observations showed oxygen saturation at 99% on 15 liters of oxygen via a non-rebreather mask, a respiratory rate of 45 breaths per minute, a heart rate of 80 beats per minute, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7/15. Arterial blood gas analysis indicated hypercapnic respiratory failure on 60% oxygen with a pH of 7.19, pCO2 of 10.4, pO2 of 17.1, and HCO3 of 30.4. Her COVID-19 test was negative. A recent echocardiogram showed moderate-severe tricuspid regurgitation, a non-dilated left ventricle, grade 1 diastolic dysfunction, and preserved systolic function. Blood tests indicated moderately elevated infection markers, and a chest X-ray showed right lower zone consolidation.

case_report: A thirteen-month-old boy presented with neurodevelopmental delay. He is the second child of consanguineous parents (first cousins) of Moroccan origin, with a history of two previous miscarriages. Pregnancy and early life were unremarkable. At four months, the patient exhibited eye nystagmus and growth stunt. By six months, nystagmus resolved, but neurological examination revealed mild neurodevelopmental delay, global hypotonia, and hyporeflexia. Cerebral MRI showed myelination delay and a thin corpus callosum. Electroneuronography at 13 months indicated a defect in nerve conduction consistent with demyelinating sensorimotor neuropathy; brainstem auditory evoked potentials documented peripheral and retrocochlear hearing impairment. Additional findings included tubulopathy with low molecular weight proteinuria, reduced electrolytes excreted fractions, cardiac wall thickness, non-autoimmune subclinical hypothyroidism, and normocytic anemia. Over time, the patient developed coarse facial features (short nose and neck, prominent forehead, epicanthal folds, telecanthus, macroglossia, full lips, pronounced philtrum), scaphocephaly, pectus carinatum, lumbar kyphosis, and umbilical hernia. The patient also showed developmental delay, achieving sitting at 10 months, babbling at 11 months, and walking with aid at 22 months. Fine motor skills were limited due to joint stiffness and claw fingers, resulting in clumsiness and difficulty manipulating objects. Exertional dyspnea affected endurance, and moderate cognitive delay was evident. Multiple metabolic investigations were conducted; urinary oligosaccharides and mucopolysaccharides were normal, while excretion of conjugated sialic acid was increased (479 mmol/mole of creatinine, normal value < 148), as well as urinary sulfatides. Molecular analysis for mucopolysaccharidosis IV and enzymatic analysis for mucolipidosis I and II were negative.
test_results: At 23 months of age, the whole exome sequencing was performed, and a homozygotic mutation (p.R498W) in the VPS33A gene was detected.

case_report: A 2-year-old male patient underwent surgery at the Department of Orthopaedics, Tianjin Paediatric Hospital. The right hand and left foot exhibited specific characteristics, and there was skin webbing between the 3rd and 4th fingers of the left hand. Among four other affected family members (great-grandmother, granduncle, grandfather, and father), variations in physical presentation were observed. Their hands showed similar characteristics. test_results: A novel autosomal dominant heterozygous GLI3 variant, NC_000007.14(NM_000168.5):c.1622C > T; p.(Thr541Met), located in exon 11, was identified by Sanger sequencing of the patient’s gDNA sample. This variant was predicted to be most likely damaging, with a score of 1 (sensitivity: 0; specificity: 1) by Polyphen 2. case_report: A 13-year-old girl presented to the Department of Pedodontics and Preventive Dentistry with a primary concern of missing teeth. The patient had a history of vision loss and hearing impairment. Intraoral examination revealed pale oral mucosa and a small sequestrum on the left side of the mandible. Abdominal sonography indicated spleen enlargement measuring 16.28 × 8.6 cm with a homologous echo texture. The liver, gallbladder, and kidneys were of normal size, and no lymphadenopathy was observed. Histopathologic examination of the soft tissue attached to a malformed tooth suggested a dentigerous cyst. Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin at 9 mg%, white blood cell count at 2.3 × 10^9/L, differential leukocyte count with 70% neutrophils and 30% lymphocytes. Serum chemistry results included chloride at 106 mg/L and alkaline phosphatase at 8.0 KA unit/dL.
test_results: The skull radiograph and radiograph of left mandible (oblique lateral view) showed increased bone density. The OPG showed that all permanent tooth bud remained totally or partly embedded in basal bone. Vertical growth of alveolar ridge was very limited. Where a fenestration of overlaying mucosa had occurred, a localized, progressive osteitis developed leading to soft tissue inflammation.

case_report: A 51-year-old male reported a 3-year history of a mass in his right foot, which had recently increased in size and was causing pain. Imaging identified a soft tissue mass located in the plantar arch of the right foot, positioned anterior to the calcaneus and beneath the fascia. Further imaging indicated no signs of disease spread. The mass was surgically removed.
test_results: Histologic sections revealed a cellular tumor with scattered ectatic and hyalinized vessels composed of spindle-shaped cells focally arranged in intersecting fascicles admixed with islands of epithelioid cells. The spindle cells have vesicular nuclei of variable shape and contour and indistinct cytoplasmic borders with occasional mitoses. The epithelioid cells have round to ovoid nuclei with occasional bi-nucleation, and ample eosinophilic cytoplasm, some with focal vacuolation, with distinct cytoplasmic borders. No significant necrosis was observed. Immunohistochemical analysis showed tumor cells positive for S100, specifically the spindle cells were strongly positive while the epithelioid cells were weakly positive. Tumor cells were also positive for TFE3 and vimentin. Immunostains were negative for desmin, MSA, AE1/3, A103, SOX10, MelanA, HMB45, MITF, Tyrosinase and BRAF. Molecular testing reported the tumor as negative for fusion of the EWSR1 (22q12) and ATF1 (12q13) loci, negative for rearrangement of the TFE3 (Xp11) locus, and negative for fusion of the EWSR1 (22q12) and CREB1 (2q33.3) loci. Additionally, no SS18/SSX1 or SS18/SSX2 fusion transcript was detected by RT-DNA amplification. Hybrid capture-based comprehensive next-generation sequencing revealed a fusion between MTAP exons 1–7 and RAF1 exons 8–17. Presence of the fusion was supported by both DNA evidence (150 supporting read pairs) and RNA evidence (437 supporting read pairs). The fusion product disrupts MTAP activity but conserves the RAF1 tyrosine kinase domain with loss of the autoinhibitory N-terminal domain. Next-generation sequencing also reported a low tumor mutation burden of two mutations per megabase and lack of an ultraviolet (UV)-signature as measured by C → T mutations at dipyrimidine sites.
diagnosis: fusion-positive soft tissue sarcoma, not otherwise specified

case_report: A 27-year-old woman presents with complaints of dyspepsia and abdominal distension persisting for several months. Her medical history is unremarkable. Laboratory tests reveal an elevated CA 125 level of 1,309 UI/ml. Physical examination indicates significant abdominal distension and dullness in the lower abdominal quadrants, consistent with the presence of ascites.
test_results: A transabdominal ultrasound confirms the ascites in all peritoneal recesses and reveals a bulky mass, which occupies almost entirely the abdominal cavity and the pelvis. It appears predominantly solid, with few cystic components and heterogeneous echotexture. Internal blood flow is demonstrated on ultrasound color Doppler. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis confirms the findings highlighted on the ultrasound: diffused ascites and a multiloculated, voluminous solid mass with definite margins measuring 20 × 10 cm on the axial view, with cranio-caudal extension of 23 cm. The mass occupies partially the abdomen and entirely the pelvis, and presents contextual cystic components, the largest of which was 6 × 4 cm, and calcifications, the largest of which measured 14 mm. It shows heterogeneous vascularity during the arterial phase and presents few septa and pseudosepta, which have a lively enhancement on postcontrast images, especially during the portal/venous phase. The mass dislocates the intestinal loops but does not show signs of local invasion. There are no enlarged lymphnodes. The uterus is normal; the ovaries are not viewable.

case_report: A 23-month-old female presented to the emergency department with multiple episodes of bloody diarrhea. The symptoms had persisted for 40 days and worsened over the last four days, during which the patient experienced 26 episodes of bloody diarrhea, along with hypoactivity, weakness, weight loss, dry skin, and dry mouth. The mother reported no alleviating or aggravating factors, recent travel, or contact with individuals with similar symptoms. The patient's medical history included anemia unresponsive to iron supplementation, failure to thrive, and multiple antibiotic treatments due to recurrent infections over the past two months, including acute otitis media, forearm skin abscess, and acute enteritis. Antibiotic treatments included metronidazole for 10 days, amoxicillin-clavulanate for seven days, and vancomycin for seven days. There were no complications during pregnancy. The patient was breastfed until six months of age, transitioned well to formula, and currently follows an irritant-free diet. Developmental milestones were appropriate for age. Family history included autoimmune diseases in the father (rheumatoid arthritis and uveitis) and autoimmune hypothyroidism in the paternal grandfather. The parents denied smoking, substance abuse, and alcohol consumption. The mother did not use antibiotics during pregnancy. Vital signs were normal at the time of evaluation. Physical examination revealed pallor and dry mucous membranes. The abdominal examination showed present bowel sounds in all quadrants, a soft and depressible abdomen with voluntary guarding, and bright red blood per rectum on rectal examination. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with a normal differential, hemoglobin decreasing from 11.1 g/dL to a low of 8.1 g/dL, and thrombocytosis. The comprehensive metabolic panel indicated stable renal function, normal liver enzymes, and hypoalbuminemia without major electrolytic disturbances. Inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP) were elevated. Iron studies showed elevated ferritin levels. Tests for Clostridium difficile toxin and antigen, stool ova and parasites, and stool cultures for viruses and pathogenic bacteria were negative. Stool analysis revealed elevated white and red blood cells, and increased stool calprotectin and lactoferrin levels. Immunological testing, including Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry, lymphocytic analyses, and immunoglobulin levels, showed no immune deficiencies but revealed elevated lymphocytic and absolute neutrophil counts. Vaccine titers indicated a deficiency in the diphtheria component due to missed vaccine doses.
test_results: The colonoscopy with biopsy revealed an exudated, friable, erythematous mucosa at the rectosigmoid junction with superficial erosions and decreased vascular pattern and erythematous and edematous mucosa at the transverse and descending colon. case_report: A 50-year-old circumcised male presented with a growth on the glans penis that had been present for 6 months. The patient had undergone circumcision for phimosis 8 months prior. Two months after the circumcision, the patient noticed a scaly lesion on the glans penis, which gradually increased in size and became dry, rough, and elevated. There was no history of trauma, localized skin conditions, or systemic diseases. The patient reported no exposure to sexually transmitted diseases (STD) and exhibited no symptoms or signs of STD. The patient's partner also had no significant illnesses. Clinical examination showed a well-defined, dry, rough, hard, mica-like scaly, verrucous, and hyperkeratotic plaque measuring 4 × 3 cm on the glans penis, around the urethral meatus. The shaft of the penis, scrotum, and inguinal area appeared normal. There was no regional lymphadenopathy. Blood tests for Venereal Disease Research Laboratory and HIV were negative. Hematological, biochemical, and radiological examinations did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination revealed skin with epidermis displaying massive hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and pronounced epithelial hyperplasia without cellular atypia. The dermis showed mild lymphocytic infiltrate.

case_report: A 36-year-old woman with no previous pregnancies visited the hospital due to heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB). She had a history of leiomyoma, which was treated with hysteroscopic myomectomy four years ago. Following the surgery, her HMB resolved but had returned shortly before her current visit. She reported no pain during menstruation or irregularities in her menstrual cycle. Laboratory tests showed anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL, but no other abnormalities were found in the blood tests related to HMB. Levels of serum LH, FSH, PRL, and E2 were within normal ranges. Pelvic examination and ultrasonography indicated a normal uterus, and color Doppler showed normal blood flow. The HMB persisted despite undergoing dilatation and curettage, and the pathological examination of the removed endometrial tissue showed normal results.
test_results: MRI revealed normal uterine size, with a long axis of 84.4 mm, short axis of 50.4 mm, and width of 65.2 mm; JZE thickness was 9.4 mm.

case_report: A 16-year-old male presented with a history of limited movement in his elbows, thumbs, and great toes since early childhood. He experienced knee and ankle pain following physical activities and had minor deficits in fine motor skills. Physical examination revealed pectus excavatum, a high-narrow palate, and a bifid uvula. The patient had dental braces to address crowded teeth, crossbite, and to widen the palate. He exhibited large hands and feet, long fingers with bilateral fifth finger clinodactyly, reduced thumb flexion, and slightly medially deviated halluces bilaterally. There was an absence of skin creases over the distal interphalangeal joints of the toes, halluces, and thumbs. His mental development, growth, hearing, and male genitalia (Tanner stage 4) were within normal limits.
test_results: Radiographs revealed a bilateral radial head dislocation of the elbows and partial bilateral fusion of the thumbs' interphalangeal joint. A similar pattern was seen in the feet with a fusion of the interphalangeal joints of dig I and of the distal interphalangeal joints of dig II-V. Radiographs raised suspicion for a bilateral calcaneonavicular coalition, and the lumbar spine showed a fusion of the dorsal portions of the vertebrae L3 to S1 with reduced height of the disc L3-L4 and L4-L5.

case_report: The patient is a 23-year-old male with a four-year history of walking difficulties and frequent falls. He also experiences clumsiness in his arms and hands and has had speech difficulties for the past six months. He was born to consanguineous parents via successful vaginal delivery with normal birth parameters. He left school at age 14 due to learning difficulties. At age 18, during a routine examination before military service, he was found to have gynecomastia and small testicles. Physical examination revealed eunuchoid body proportions, short stature, gynecomastia, poor facial hair growth, and generalized jaundice. Neurological examination showed dysarthria and severe ataxia, making walking impossible without assistance. He exhibited appendicular dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, particularly in the lower extremities, slightly generalized chorea while talking, hypomimia, mild bradykinesia, slight dystonia in the left hand, and brisk deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. Eye examination revealed fragmented pursuit eye movements with slow hypometric saccades, vertical gaze palsy, and square wave jerks in horizontal pursuit. Psychiatric examination showed regressed speech, a smaller appearance compared to peers, no delirium, no suicidal or homicidal thoughts, and no euthymic perception deviation. An IQ test indicated borderline mental capacity, with a Kent EGY intelligence test verbal performance score of 85.71. He was unable to obtain a calculable score on the Porteus maze test.
test_results: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed progressive cerebellar, vermian, and cerebral cortical atrophy, and periventricular confluent white matter hyperintensities in 2022 compared to 2018. Mild mesencephalic atrophy is similar in both dates. Basal ganglia hyperintense lesions began to appear in 2022. Pituitary MRI showed a normal pituitary gland height (4 mm) for his age. Testicular atrophy detected on ultrasound (right testis 12 × 6 × 15mm, 0.56 ml, left 10 × 4.5 × 14 mm, 0.32 ml). In the X-ray evaluation of his hands at 24, it was noted that the growth plate of the distal radius, which normally starts at the age of 17 to 19 and should fuse at the most at the age of 20, did not fuse.

case_report: A 29-year-old male presented with a serum creatinine level of 1.40 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 70 mL/min/1.73 m2. He had a history of mild hypertension managed with 8 mg of candesartan. Urinalysis indicated microalbuminuria with an albumin/creatinine ratio of 36 mg/g. Renal ultrasound revealed medullary nephrocalcinosis. The patient also exhibited mild nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, characterized by isosthenuria and a daily urine output of 3 to 4 liters. Historical medical records indicated that the patient experienced failure to thrive at three months old, with a total serum calcium level of 4.2 mmol/L, hypercalciuria, and nephrocalcinosis. At that time, he was receiving 800 IU of vitamin D3 daily, which was discontinued after his serum 25(OH)D3 level was found to be 123 ng/mL. Treatment included prednisolone and a calcium-free formula, leading to normalization of serum calcium levels. Subsequent development on a low calcium diet was normal. Total serum calcium levels remained in the upper normal range or slightly elevated (2.4–2.6 mmol/L), while hypercalciuria persisted (0.35–0.45 g calcium/g creatinine). Intact PTH levels were consistently suppressed. During the first four years of life, 25(OH)D3 levels were elevated (110–609 ng/mL) but later normalized. At 13 years of age, 1,25(OH)D3 levels were in the upper normal range (65 pg/mL). Current assessments of calcium and vitamin D metabolism are provided. Bone density measured by DEXA was normal, with lumbar spine density at 1.247 g/cm2 (T score 0.2) and femoral neck density at 1.175 g/cm2 (T score 0.7).
test_results: Sequencing analysis revealed that the patient was homozygous for three common DNA polymorphisms (rs2296241, rs2762934 and rs6022987) and additionally for a yet undescribed nonsynonymous mutation in exon 4 (c.628T>C), causing tryptophan to be replaced with arginine in codon 210 (W210R).
diagnosis: Idiopathic Infantile Hypercalcaemia with a novel CYP24A1 mutation

case_report: An 11-month-old Iranian girl from a consanguineous family was evaluated in October 2020. The patient exhibited multiple traumas without any signs of discomfort. She had various lesions and injuries, including those on the oral cavity and tongue. Eye issues such as nystagmus were noted as the initial indication of visual abnormalities. Additionally, the patient had dry skin without sweating and experienced recurrent unexplained fevers. A general examination revealed multiple scars and non-tender ulcers on the limbs and face. Neurologic examination showed a loss of reflexes and a general absence of pain and temperature perception. The parents provided informed consent for the study.
test_results: The variant filtration strategy was initiated by excluding variants with an allelic frequency higher than 0.01 in extensive normal population databases, including gnomAD, ExAC, and an in-house variant frequency dataset derived from an extensive cohort of over 12 000 samples representative of the Iranian population. Subsequently, the integration of homozygous variants based on familial pedigree data further refined the candidate variants. To prioritize variants associated with neuropathy disorders, a meticulously curated gene list was curated by the Genomics England PanelApp (Hereditary neuropathy ID: 85), leading to the identification of a potential causative variant within the PRDM12 gene. Following the stringent guidelines set by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG), the allelic frequency of the c.826_840dupTGCAACCGCCGCTTC (p.Cys276_Phe280dup) variant in exon 5 of the PRDM12 gene was observed to be notably low in the normal population (PM2). Computational analysis utilizing the PaPI tool predicted a deleterious impact for this variant, assigning it a high score of 0.904 (PP3). Notably, missense and in-frame shift variants within this specific region of PRDM12, known as the zinc finger domain ‘C2H2-type 2,’ have been documented as likely pathogenic and uncertain of significance, respectively, with a conspicuous absence of benign variants. (PM1). Protein coding length changes as a result of in-frame variant in gene PRDM12, and this variant is not located in a repeat region (PM4). Collectively, this variant has been identified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG guideline. Crucially, the identified in-frame variant does not locate with any repeat regions, enhancing its significance. Finally, the detected mutation was confirmed using Sanger sequencing. Both parents were heterozygote for PRDM12 mutation.
diagnosis: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type VIII
Orpha_name: Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type VIII

case_report: A 52-year-old perimenopausal caucasian woman, gravida 3 para 3, presented with a 10-week history of vaginal bleeding, bloating, fatigue, weight gain exceeding 7 kg, and a hypogastric mass. She was admitted to the local emergency room due to epigastric pain and mild dyspnea. Additionally, she reported breast tenderness over the past 3 months. Her medical history includes appendectomy, amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism, chronic atrial fibrillation, and a breast abscess, but no history of hypertension. Her last childbirth was 23 years ago, and she stopped taking oral contraceptive pills at least 18 months ago. She experienced hot flashes and irregular menstrual cycles with longer durations, with her last menstrual period occurring 4 months ago.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showed a uterine enlargement (15 × 12 cm axial) with a heterogeneous hypodense endometrium punctuated with nodular areas enhanced by iodinated contrast. Neither fetus nor adnexal mass was detected. Diffuse bilateral pulmonary nodules were observed. Her serum hCG level was 0.96 × 106 IU/L. An endometrial trans-cervical biopsy showed two non-malignant chorionic villi.

case_report: A 5-day-old female infant was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit due to refusal to breastfeed, poor responsiveness, weak cries, and cold extremities. Physical examination revealed the following: Weight 3100 g (SDS = −0.56), Height 49.5 cm (SDS = −0.37), Heart rate 125/min, Respiratory rate 36/min, Blood pressure 71/32 mmHg, Rectal temperature 37°C, SpO2 99%. Auscultation indicated no lung crackles or heart murmur. Palpation showed the liver edge about 2.5 cm below the costal margin, and the spleen was not palpable. The skin exhibited mild jaundice. Genital examination confirmed female characteristics. Two days later, the infant developed severe dehydration and vomiting. Biochemical laboratory tests indicated severe hyperkalemia with K+ 10.1 mmol/L, Na+ 105 mmol/L, Cl− 83 mmol/L, pH 7.31, BE(B) −10.8 mmol/L, and a trans-tubular potassium gradient (TTKG) of 4. The infant was immediately given a supplement of 10% NaCl.

case_report: A 26-year-old male reported experiencing painful urination and blood in the urine for approximately one month. During a digital rectal examination, a large, hard mass with an uneven surface was detected. The serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level was measured at 0.44 ng/mL, which is within the normal range. Additional tumor markers were also found to be within normal limits.
test_results: MRI revealed an uneven multinodular mass located mainly within the central zone of the prostate and extending to the right peripheral gland at the bottom level of the central gland mass. The mass showed homogeneous low signal intensity on T1-weighted imaging and heterogeneous high signal intensity with pseudocapsule on T2-weighted EPI. In DCE-MRI, the central gland portion of the mass showed a weak gradual enhancement containing cystic areas, whereas the right peripheral gland showed a moderate gradual enhancement. DWI showed the prostatic mass as an area of marked high signal intensity. Coronal T2-weighted imaging demonstrated enlarged internal iliac lymph nodes. The resected specimen predominantly comprised elongated ducts and cellular stroma that contained areas of necrosis with calcification. Hypercellular stroma without glands was specifically detected. Although epithelial components did not show malignant changes, stromal cells showed ovoid, spindle-shaped and hyperchromatic nuclei in cellular areas, and spindle-shaped nuclei in myxomatous areas. An average of two mitoses per high-powered field was counted. Epithelial cells showed positive immunostaining for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3, CAM5.2). In stromal cells, positive immunostaining was detected for vimentin, CD34, and progesterone receptor; whereas, negative results were obtained for pan-cytokeratin, CD31, S-100, HHF-35, desmin, α smooth muscle actin, MyoD1, c-kit, and estrogen receptors. The MIB-1 labeling index was elevated to > 50%.

case_report: A 67-year-old male former smoker presented with 3 months of voice changes without any breathing difficulties. His medical history included mandibular dental implants with cadaveric bone graft and rhBMP-2 in 2017, 18 months prior to presentation, though the dose information was unavailable. Additionally, he had a history of lumbar spine surgery without rhBMP-2 and a resolved case of Guillain–Barre syndrome from decades ago. Laryngostroboscopy images at the time of presentation showed erythematous thickening of the right anterior vocal fold and a smaller reactive lesion on the left vocal fold.
test_results: Findings at surgery confirmed a firm right vocal fold lesion, that was epithelial in origin. The lesion was described as hyperplastic mucosa with a superficial, circumscribed focus of metaplastic bone formation. Surface epithelium was inflamed and exhibited mild atypia in the form of basilar hyperplasia, increased mitotic figures and occasional pleomorphic nuclei.

case_report: A 6-year-old Chinese boy presented to the stomatology department with a primary concern of dental caries, which had been noted since he was 4 years old and had progressively worsened. The patient had a history of intracranial decompression surgery at 1 year old due to hydrocephalus, followed by posterior cranial vault distraction at 2 years old. At 3 years old, he underwent a ventriculoperitoneal shunt operation for hydrocephalus, and at 4 years old, cranial vault remodeling was performed. He was born full-term via cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, with a birth height of 48 cm and weight of 2.35 kg, alongside his fraternal twin sister who had a birth height of 48 cm and weight of 1.8 kg. Family history over three generations was negative for similar conditions, and his twin sister had no medical issues. Physical examination revealed normal height (108 cm) and weight (20.4 kg) for his age. Hands and feet appeared clinically normal. Extraoral examination showed a prominent forehead, eyelid ptosis, ocular proptosis, shallow eye sockets, hypertelorism, midface hypoplasia, and a retrusive upper lip with a protrusive lower lip. Intraoral examination indicated early mixed dentition with all deciduous canines and molars present in both the maxillary and mandibular arches. The eruption chronology and status were appropriate for his age. Oral hygiene was poor, with scattered pigmentation on the teeth. Permanent teeth 36 and 46, along with deciduous teeth 54, 55, 65, 74, 75, and 85, were mostly decayed. Eruptive permanent teeth 11, 21, 36, and 46 exhibited enamel hypomineralization. The maxillary arch was constricted, and there was an anterior cross bite and open bite.
test_results: Sanger sequencing showed that the pathogenic variant c.1026C>G (p.Cys342Trp) was present on the FGFR2 gene for the patient.
