case_report: Mrs. Kim, age 57, presented with a recently enlarging neck mass and hoarseness that began 5 days prior to hospital admission. She reported a very hard, fixed lump on the right side of her neck that had been present for months. She had a history of intermittent treatment for hyperthyroidism over the last three decades and had previously taken antithyroid agents prescribed by a private hospital. On admission, she showed no symptoms associated with thyrotoxicosis. She had no other symptoms or medical problems. The patient was conscious and in no acute distress, with stable vital signs: blood pressure of 130/90 mm Hg, pulse of 76 beats per minute, respiration rate of 20 breaths per minute, and a temperature of 36.5℃. Physical examination revealed no globe protrusion, scleral icterus, or conjunctival anemia. There were no enlarged cervical lymph nodes or jugular vein engorgement. A hard and fixed thyroid nodule measuring approximately 5×4 cm was palpated without neck tenderness. Normal heart and breath sounds were observed on auscultation, and no pitting edema was noted in her extremities. Laboratory results showed a white blood cell count of 6,460/mm3 (neutrophil 57.4%, lymphocyte 36.6%, monocyte 7.7%, eosinophil 0.6%), hemoglobin of 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit of 35.2%, and platelet count of 295×103/mm3. Urine test results were normal. Serum biochemical examination revealed blood urea nitrogen/creatinine of 25/0.6 mg/dL, total protein/albumin of 7.4/4.3 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase/alanine aminotransferase of 22/20 IU/L, Na/K/Cl of 142/5.1/105 mEq/L, Ca of 4.6 mEq/L (normal range, 4.5 to 5.2), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 19 mm/hr, and C-reactive protein <0.2 mg/day. Thyroid function tests showed thyroid stimulation hormone of 0.07 µIU/mL (normal range, 0.4 to 4.5), free T4 of 3.86 ng/dL (normal range, 0.7 to 2), TBII of 51% (normal range, 0 to 15), thyroglobulin of 493 ng/dL (normal range, 2 to 60), antithyroid microsomal antibody of 3.1 U/mL (normal range, 0 to 8), and negative thyroglobulin antibody of 22 U/mL (normal range, 0 to 55). Imaging revealed normal sinus rhythm, signs of emphysema, and a right to left shift of the trachea due to the thyroid nodule. A well-defined irregular and hypoechoic nodule measuring 4 cm in diameter with large scattered dense calcifications was observed in the right thyroid lobe. No enlarged cervical lymph nodes or invasion into the parathyroid glands were noted. An aspiration technique yielded a very small amount of cytologic specimen, which showed no malignant cells. A 4.3×4.0 cm nodular lesion occupied most of the right lobe of the thyroid, with peripheral calcified lesions and severe marginal calcification in the inferior portion of the nodule. Unilateral fixed vocal cords were observed in a paramedian position, suggesting vocal cord paralysis on the right side. A total thyroidectomy was performed, revealing a 4.5-cm solid mass in the right thyroid lobe closely adhered to the surrounding airway and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The resected mass was covered by a thin capsule, with a cut surface showing mixed strips of white, yellowish-brown, and pink colors, along with peripheral dense calcification.
test_results: Thyroid follicles were replaced by extensive inflammatory and fibrous tissue. Inflammation was also noticed in the vein, which was encased in fibrous tissue, but no malignant cells were found.

case_report: A 21-year-old female dental student residing in a hostel experienced occasional rashes on her thighs, which improved with local ointments prescribed by her dermatologist. She later noticed loss of eyelashes and slight eversion of the eyelid, treated as blepharitis. She also had reddish streaks in the bulbar conjunctiva and eye watering, treated as allergic conjunctivitis. Subsequently, she developed fever and cough lasting about fifteen days, which improved with treatment at a local hospital. Following this, she experienced severe insomnia and extreme fear, which she reported to her parents. She also had a brief period of unawareness at night, with unclear details as she was in the hostel. During bathing, she experienced severe panic and ran from the second floor to the ground floor of her hostel. She was admitted to a local hospital under psychiatric care and treated with antipsychotics, but did not improve. She was then referred to the psychiatric department of our institution, where she again did not improve and was subsequently referred to Neurology. Upon examination, the patient was slightly confused, had absent eyelashes, mild reticular changes in her conjunctiva, and restricted extreme lateral movement of the right eye. Speech and language assessment indicated aphasia, evidenced by word-finding difficulty, circumlocution, paraphasic errors, and naming defects. Mild asymmetry of reflexes was noted on the right side. The next day, the patient developed tonic-clonic seizures.
test_results: Her investigation showed strongly positive anti RO52, Strongly positive anti body to Sm antigen (Smith antigen), Antibody to SS-A(RO) and Antibody to UI-nRNP/Sm. Ultrasound abdomen showed ascites. Her renal functions, liver functions, hematological workup were normal. Vitamin B12 level were 88.7 pg/mL (normal range180-914 pg/mL). MRI showed atrophy of frontal and temporal regions with multiple periventricular white matter signal changes. There was mild medial temporal hyper intensity on both sides.

case_report: A 24-year-old G2A1 woman at 35+3 weeks gestation presented with intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, and headache for six days. She was treated with injection zofer, injection Pantop, and tablet Dolo 650 mg SOS at a private facility. On physical examination, she was alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Her vital signs included a blood pressure of 140/90, heart rate of 124/min, respiratory rate of 20/min, and temperature of 99°F. She exhibited pedal edema, icterus, and urine albumin of +1. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and respiratory system evaluations were positive. There was no organomegaly, and the abdomen was soft. Fetal heart sounds were absent, and the fundus measured 32 weeks in height. The uterus was well relaxed at 32 weeks, and an intrauterine fetal demise was noted. Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin of 13.7 g/dL, WBC of 15,450/cumm, and platelet count of 80,000/cumm. Liver function tests showed AST of 213 U/L, ALT of 217 U/L, total bilirubin of 12.30 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 534 U/L, serum albumin of 1.5 g/dL, and serum globulin of 4.8 g/dL. Renal function tests indicated urea of 61 mg/dL, serum creatinine of 2.44 mg/dL, random blood glucose of 68 mg/dL, and serum ammonia of 73 mmol/L. Serum LDH was 1077 mg%, INR was 1.3, and D-Dimer was over 10,000. Serological tests for HIV, HCV, and HBsAg were negative, as were tests for viral hepatitis and malaria. The patient received a loading dose of Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) and was transferred to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) for further management. Cervical examination showed a cervical os of 1 cm, 30% effacement, and a station of -2. Labor was induced with two doses of 50 mcg misoprostol administered intravaginally, six hours apart. The patient had sluggish deep tendon reflexes (DTRs), decreased urine output with hematuria, and a respiratory rate of 36 breaths per minute. Artificial rupture of membranes was performed at os - 3 cm. The patient received 10 units of vitamin K intravenously and delivered a 1.87 kg male stillborn baby. Post-delivery, Pitocin drip was initiated to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), and the placenta was removed by controlled cord traction. The patient was administered intravenous albumin, injection piptaz, injection metronidazole, injection Meropenem 1 g, and tablet febuxostat.
test_results: Moderate ascites and a changed liver echo pattern were seen on abdominal ultrasound.

case_report: A 71-year-old male presented with a primary complaint of reduced ability to perform routine activities and difficulty walking, accompanied by weakness and muscle cramping. His medical history includes coronary artery disease, gastroesophageal reflux with Barrett’s esophagus, and a previous lacunar stroke. He reported no current or past tobacco use but had a history of alcohol consumption. Laboratory results revealed elevated creatinine kinase (CK) at 748 Units per Liter (U/L) and aldolase at 8.2 U/L, with negative results for Lyme disease and Rickettsia antibodies. Atorvastatin was discontinued due to suspected medication-induced myopathy, and a follow-up was scheduled to reassess symptoms. However, muscle weakness and gait difficulties persisted despite the discontinuation of the medication.
test_results: Electromyography (EMG) studies suggested findings consistent with myopathy attributed to polymyositis. A left thigh biopsy showed denervation atrophy. Computed tomography (CT) scans of the chest, abdomen and pelvis were negative for paraneoplastic disease. The workup showed elevated muscle acetylcholine receptor antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, and positive antinuclear antibodies.

case_report: A 21-year-old male arrived at the emergency department with a two-day history of purulent discharge from his umbilicus. He did not report any pain. He mentioned a similar episode one year earlier, which had resolved with oral antibiotics. Since childhood, he had recurrent episodes of a 'pulling sensation' in the umbilicus and suprapubic areas, for which multiple specialist consultations had yielded unremarkable results. The patient had no significant medical or surgical history, and his family and social history were also unremarkable. He was not on any medications and denied the use of drugs and alcohol. Upon presentation, his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 139/82 mmHg, heart rate 55 beats per minute, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, and an oral temperature of 98.5 degrees Fahrenheit, with a pulse oximetry reading of 100% on room air. Physical examination revealed yellowish discharge from the center of the umbilicus, with erythema and mild tenderness around the area. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and basic metabolic panel, were within normal limits, and the urinalysis was unremarkable.
test_results: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast revealed an urachal remnant arising from the anterior/superior margin of the bladder and extending to the umbilical region. The remnant consisted of a thin fibrous band of tissue measuring up to 4.6 mm in thickness near the umbilicus. The band narrowed to a minimum of 2 mm along its course. No umbilical fluid collection was identified. The abdominal fat posterior to the umbilicus showed no inflammatory reaction.
diagnosis: Infected umbilical-urachal sinus due to urachal remnant

case_report: A 24-year-old female visited the outpatient department with a 6-month history of headache, double vision, dizziness, and reduced vision in the right eye. She experienced multiple falls resulting in injuries. She did not report seizures, altered consciousness, nausea, vomiting, or trauma. On examination, she was alert and oriented. Cranial nerve examination was normal. Vision in both eyes was reduced to finger counting, but extraocular movements were normal bilaterally. Muscle tone, bulk, and power were normal in all four limbs, and sensations were intact. No cerebellar signs were noted. Hormonal levels were within normal limits. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain revealed a well-defined hyperdense lesion in the sella without bony erosion. MRI showed a well-defined rounded lesion in the pituitary fossa, isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with thick peripheral enhancement on postcontrast sagittal images. She underwent endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary mass. Intraoperatively, a grayish-green, jelly-like tumor was removed, and the diaphragma sella was damaged, resulting in a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. The sella was packed with fat and fascia from the abdomen, reinforced with bone and a nasoseptal flap. Postoperatively, she developed panhypopituitarism and presented with CSF rhinorrhea on the 9th postoperative day. She underwent endoscopic CSF leak repair using fat, flap, bone, and Hadad flap, with fibrin glue applied and a nasal pack inserted. Two days later, she developed a severe headache, altered sensorium, and fever, and was treated with antibiotics. She gradually improved but experienced another CSF leak on the 5th day post-CSF leak repair. A lumbar drain was inserted and kept until the 6th postprocedure day, resolving the CSF leak. She was observed for an additional day, her symptoms improved, and she was discharged. The nasal pack was removed on the 8th postoperative day in the outpatient department. On follow-up, she has fully recovered.
test_results: Her histopathology showed abundant hemorrhage and proteinaceous material along with spindle cells. It was glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) negative and thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF1) positive. On pathological examination, the sample showed a hypocellular lesion, composed of ovoid to spindle cells, arranged in short bundles and sheets. Tumor cells were bland in appearance and showed no cytological atypia or mitoses. Cytoplasmic granularity or oncocytic changes were absent. The background was fibrillary. Immunohistochemically, nuclear expression of TTF1 was demonstrated, whereas GFAP, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), and S100 were negative.

case_report: A man in his late 40s visited the outpatient department due to weakness in his lower limbs. He first noticed this symptom at age 12 when he struggled to keep up with his peers while running, and it gradually worsened over time. Despite being able to walk, he had trouble climbing stairs. His family history revealed that his male siblings and maternal uncle, aged between 40 and 60 years, experienced similar muscle weakness. He had no intellectual impairment. Physical examination showed a waddling gait, enlarged calf muscles, and wasting of the quadriceps and gluteal muscles, resulting in pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles. Knee jerks indicated weak quadriceps contractions (grade 1) upon tapping, and ankle jerks were absent. The patient used his arms to rise from the ground, demonstrating a positive Gower’s sign. Laboratory results showed a total leukocyte count of 5.7 cells/109 (reference range: 4.5-11), with neutrophils at 62% and a hemoglobin level of 11 gm/dl. Creatine kinase level was 1148 U/L (reference range: 22-172 U/L).
test_results: A molecular genetic test (multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification [MLPA]) showed duplication of exon 2 in the dystrophin gene.

case_report: A 27-year-old white man with no significant medical or family history came to the emergency department with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, a fever of 38.8°C, and bloody-mucoid diarrhea occurring 10 to 13 times daily over the past 2 days. During this time, Salmonella was identified in some meat samples in the city center of Sivas, and a similar endemic diarrhea was reported. The patient mentioned consuming the contaminated meat. His blood pressure was 120/70 mmHg, and his pulse rate was 78/minute, with no other abnormal physical examination findings. Initial biochemical analysis showed leukocytosis at 21.6×10^3/mm3. Stool microscopy revealed 7 to 8 red blood cells per high-power field and 1 to 2 white blood cells in some fields. Blood and stool cultures showed no growth. He was admitted to the infectious diseases clinic for gastroenteritis and started on ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily. One week later, laboratory results indicated blood urea nitrogen at 75 mg/dL, serum creatinine at 10.4 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at 1539 U/L, total protein at 4.5 g/dL (normal range 5.7 to 8.2), and albumin at 2.8 g/dL (normal range 3.2 to 4.8). Urine analysis was normal. He was transferred to the nephrology department due to anuria. At that time, his blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, pulse rate was 84/minute, and body temperature was 36°C, with no abnormal physical examination findings. Specific stool culture for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli showed no growth. Two days later, his hemoglobin concentration dropped to 10 g/dL, the direct Coombs test was negative, his reticulocyte ratio was 6%, and schistocytes were present in his peripheral blood smear. Serologic tests were negative for anti-nuclear antibodies, cytoplasmic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen, antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen, antibodies to hepatitis C virus, and human immunodeficiency virus, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and anti-glomerular basement membrane. His C3 level was 0.511 g/L (normal range 0.9 to 2.1) and C4 level was 0.151 g/dL (normal range 0.1 to 0.4).
test_results: A renal biopsy specimen stained with hematoxylin and eosin revealed six glomeruli with increased mesangial cells and matrix, and minimal focal interstitial lymphocytic inflammation. There was no pathologic finding in the tubules and blood vessels. Direct immunofluorescence staining of the tissue sections revealed a total of eight glomeruli, which showed only mild to moderate mesangial granular staining for C3; no immunofluorescent staining was detected with immunoglobulin A, immunoglobulin G, immunoglobulin M, C1q, and fibrinogen. Congo red staining was negative.

case_report: A 4-year-old female patient presented with complaints of discolored teeth, pain in the lower jaw, and significant wear of all teeth. The patient's father reported that the discoloration had been present since the teeth first erupted. Family history indicated that the patient's mother, maternal grandfather, two aunts, and their sons also experienced similar dental issues. The mother and her sisters had not sought dental treatment, resulting in progressive tooth substance loss. There was no reported history of bone abnormalities in the family. Clinical examination showed extensive loss of enamel and dentin, with teeth exhibiting hard brown dentin and worn incisal and occlusal surfaces, in some cases down to the gingival level. The mandibular first molars were exposed, and an abscess was noted in relation to the mandibular right first molar.
test_results: Orthopantomograph revealed obliterated pulp chambers in most of teeth and constricted in some teeth. Full mouth IOPA radiographic survey also showed the same findings.

case_report: This female infant was born to a 20-year-old mother and 26-year-old father by normal vaginal delivery at 37 weeks' gestation. The parents are healthy first cousins. The family history is non-contributory. The couple had a subsequent boy who died a few days after birth due to growth retardation and multiple congenital heart anomalies. During the gestation of the patient, the pregnancy was complicated by threatened abortion in the first trimester. Intrauterine growth retardation and weak fetal movements were also documented. The birth weight was 1,600 g. The birth length and head circumference were not recorded but mentioned to be small. She was referred to the Clinical Genetics Department at the age of 4 months due to poor weight gain and for genetic counseling. On clinical examination, she was noted to have a head circumference of 31.5 cm (−5 SD), weight of 2,800 g (−6 SD), and length of 48 cm (−5 SD). The patient had a high forehead, prominent eyes, depressed nasal bridge, short philtrum, tented upper lip, bulged alveolar ridge, and prominent ear lobule. Her neurological evaluation revealed hypertonia, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, with flexor plantar responses. Radiological examination at that age showed unossified pubic bones, proportionately short femora, and broad metaphyses of the femora and tibiae. The tibiae and fibulae were short and equal in length. At the age of 10 months, she developed seizures with only partial response to valproate and lamotrigine. EEG records revealed low voltage slow waves (3–6 cycles/s) mixed with sleep spindle. At the age of 20 months, her weight, length, and head circumference were 3,500 g (−6.5 SD), 55 cm (−9.5 SD), and 32 cm (−10.7 SD), respectively. The girl was spastic with contracture deformity in the elbows and hands. Her neurological evaluation revealed hypertonia, brisk deep-tendon reflexes, with flexor plantar responses. She had not acquired any developmental milestones and never recognized her mother. Abdominal ultrasonography and echocardiography showed normal results. Ophthalmological examination showed bilateral optic atrophy.
test_results: Chromosomal examination revealed normal female karyotype 46,XX. Cranial MRI showed partial agenesis of corpus callosum, and abnormal gyral pattern most pronounced posteriorly.

case_report: A 12-year-old boy from the Northwest Gondar Amhara regional state presented with left flank swelling for the past 3 months. Three days prior to admission, he began experiencing pain in the left flank, accompanied by high-grade fever, chills, rigor, and vomiting. He did not report any urinary or respiratory symptoms. His maternal pregnancy course and medical history were unremarkable, and he was born at a health center. His past medical history was also unremarkable. He has seven siblings, none of whom exhibited similar symptoms. His mother had no history of radiation exposure, use of traditional medicine, or chemotherapy during pregnancy. No dysmorphisms were observed in his general appearance. Vital signs were as follows: pulse rate 142 beats/min, respiratory rate 33 breaths/min, temperature 38.5 °C, and blood pressure 105/65 mmHg. Anthropometric measurements indicated severe stunting. Abdominal examination revealed a distended abdomen, asymmetry with bulging on the left flank, a visible horizontal line, an upward umbilical slit, and absent rectus abdominis muscles. The abdomen was soft with a tender cystic mass on the left flank, measuring 13 × 11 cm, palpable bimanually. Both testes were undescended. The patient also had scoliosis and developmental dysplasia of the hips with a waddling gait. Urinary analysis showed many red blood cells and positive leukocyte esterase. Renal function tests were normal with a creatinine level of 0.72 mg/dl and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 44 mg/dl. Hemoglobin was normal at 12.7 gm/dl, and electrolyte levels were normal.
test_results: Ultrasound showed a large cystic mass in his left kidney area with echo debris. His right kidney had normal echo texture and size. An X-ray of his hips showed bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hip. His left kidney is cystic and enlarged; there is no parenchyma tissue, both testes are intraperitoneal just below the kidneys, tortuous left renal vein, enlarged bladder reaching above umbilicus, and left megaureter.

case_report: A six-year-old boy from Texas presented with global developmental delay, aggressive behavior, insomnia, microcephaly, strabismus, facial dysmorphic features, vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), bilateral congenital renal dysplasia, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), hypotonia, failure to thrive, dysphagia, and status post-gastrostomy tube. He was referred to Children's Health in Dallas for evaluation. The patient was born at 39 weeks via spontaneous vaginal delivery. The pregnancy was normal with regular prenatal visits and unremarkable laboratory tests, but there was an umbilical cord rupture at delivery. He did not have difficulty breathing but was unable to breastfeed and was started on expressed breast milk and formula. At five weeks old, he was hospitalized and diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) and VUR. Further evaluation revealed bilateral congenital renal dysplasia. At seven months old, he was hospitalized for intractable projectile vomiting and was found to have GERD and oral/pharyngeal dysphagia. At 10 months old, he underwent G button placement with Nissen fundoplication due to persistent GERD. At three years old, he underwent bilateral ureteral reimplantation due to recurrent UTIs. During this period, he exhibited aggressive behavior with self-inflicted injury (head banging), insomnia, and noticeable global developmental delay. Oxcarbazepine was prescribed for aggressive behavior, and trazodone and clonidine for insomnia. Physical examination revealed a hypotonic infant with bilateral ptosis, hypertelorism, a hypopigmented lesion on the left neck, Mongolian buttock spots, and pes planus. Neurology recommended extensive tests, including basic metabolic screening, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and genetic tests due to severe global developmental delay and facial dysmorphic features. The non-contrast brain MRI showed thinning of the corpus callosum with no structural abnormalities. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) revealed a gain in 1q44 copy number. The father was found to have the same chromosomal abnormality, but this did not explain the patient's findings, prompting further tests. A leukodystrophy panel for lysosomal enzymes and gene/DNA testing were unremarkable, ruling out lysosomal storage disorders, trisomies, and Fragile X syndrome.
test_results: A whole-exome genome sequencing was performed revealing a de novo pathogenic heterozygous mutation in the ASXL3 gene in chromosome 18q12.1.

case_report: A four-month-old female infant was brought to a private pediatric hospital in Port Harcourt, Nigeria, by her mother due to concerns about poor feeding and inadequate weight gain. The infant weighed 4.5 kg (<3rd percentile) at the time of presentation and 2.8 kg at birth. There was no history of rapid breathing, cough, cyanosis, or excessive sweating. She is the only child of a non-consanguineous couple and was delivered by emergency caesarean section at term due to a cord around the neck. The mother reported no intake of herbs or drugs during early pregnancy. The father passed away in a road traffic accident during the pregnancy. On physical examination, the infant had a left precordial bulge. Her heart rate was 140 beats per minute, and the apex beat was located at the 4th left intercostal space, midclavicular line. A grade 3/6 ejection systolic murmur was noted. The patient exhibited mild respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 64 cycles per minute. There was no hepatomegaly. A chest X-ray revealed situs solitus, levocardia, mild cardiomegaly, and pulmonary plethora. An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, extreme right axis deviation, and left ventricular hypertrophy.
test_results: Echocardiography revealed a dilated left atrium and a hypertrophied left ventricle. There was a left ventricular—right atrial shunt through an aneurysmal septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve restricting the perimembranous VSD. Effective perimembranous VSD size was 7 mm. The LV to RV to RA mean velocity was 50.5 cm/s and TV gradient was 50 mmHg. Color flow Doppler of a 4-chamber view showed systolic flow into right atrium from the adherent septal and anterior leaflets of the tricuspid valves and restricted 7 mm perimembranous VSD shunting left to right. Color flow Doppler showed the tricuspid leaflet with no tricuspid regurgitation.

case_report: A 79-year-old woman presented with increasing weakness and severe low sodium levels (114.8 mEq/L). In the preceding months, she experienced attention deficits and mild memory loss. Her only medication was a calcium channel blocker for mild hypertension. Both the patient and her family denied excessive water consumption. She had a history of liver disease related to HCV for the past 10 years. Physical examination showed no signs of dehydration or swelling, with a BMI of 20.5 kg/m2, blood pressure at 145/90 mmHg, a regular heart rate, and no palpable lymph nodes. Laboratory tests revealed low plasma osmolarity (253 mOsm/L) and a urinary sodium concentration of 151 mEq/L. Other laboratory values, including blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, thyroid and adrenal hormones, urinary catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine), and chromogranin A, were within normal limits. Chest X-rays indicated an abnormal enlargement in the mediastinum.
test_results: CT scan showed a large solid inhomogeneous mass originating in the anterior mediastinum and abutting into the left pleural space (about 10 × 8 × 7 cm), as well as a nodular lesion in the 3rd liver segment, but was negative at the encephalic level. An 18F-FDG-PET/CT displayed positive uptake in the mass (SUVmax = 10). At immunohistochemistry tumor cells were positive for neuroendocrine markers: CD56, neuron specific enolase (NSE), synaptophysin, and chromogranin A.

case_report: A 68-year-old Japanese woman, with no notable medical history, was found to have a low-echoic nodule in the pancreatic head during an abdominal ultrasound. There is no family history of endocrine tumors or diseases, though her father passed away from stomach cancer. She does not smoke or consume alcohol. Her blood pressure is 127/69 mmHg, managed with antihypertensive medication. She has a body mass index of 25.8 kg/m2, indicating slight obesity. Physical examinations revealed no abnormalities. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no lesions in the stomach or duodenum.
test_results: Endoscopic ultrasonography revealed a 21.6 mm diameter, low-echoic nodule in the pancreatic head. No dilation of the biliary or pancreatic duct was detected. On contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scans, the above-described lesion was peripherally enhanced during the arterial phase and was weakly and heterogeneously enhanced during the portal phase. In addition, CT scans identified an 8-mm mass in the pancreatic tail with a well-defined border and marked enhancement, and a 12-mm mass in the left adrenal gland with heterogeneous enhancement. On fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F–FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, the mass in the pancreatic head demonstrated a high 18F–FDG uptake with a maximal standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 4.8. The masses in the pancreatic tail and the left adrenal gland exhibited negative 18F–FDG uptake. Needle biopsies from the pancreatic head and tail did not provide a sufficient amount of materials for a pathological diagnosis. Macroscopic examination revealed a poorly demarcated, solid, yellowish-white tumor, measuring 22 × 22 × 17 mm, in the head of the pancreas. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of an admixture of three cell types: epithelioid cells, ganglion-like cells, and spindle cells. The epithelioid cells, the major component of the tumor, were rather uniform in size and formed small nests, exhibiting fine granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and round-to-ovoid nuclei with stippled chromatin. This component of the tumor showed vascular, perineural, and peripancreatic adipose tissue invasion. The ganglion-like cells, the smallest component of the tumor, had vesicular nuclei, conspicuous nucleoli, and an abundance of cytoplasm. The spindle cells exhibited thin, elongated, wavy-shaped nuclei resembling Schwann cells and were arranged in intertwining fascicles. Mitosis was not conspicuous, and foci of intratumoral necrosis were not observed. The surgical margins were negative for tumor cells. Tumor tissue, composed of all the three cell types, also showed metastasis to a peripancreatic lymph node. The epithelioid cells were positive for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) but negative for catecholamine-synthesizing enzymes (tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine β-hydroxylase, dopa decarboxylase, and phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase). The ganglion-like cells were positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin A. Some of these cells were weakly positive for neurofilament, pancytokeratin, and phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase. The spindle cells were positive for S-100 protein and neurofilament. The Ki-67 labeling index (LI) of the tumor cells was 0.3%, with no apparent difference among the three cell types. The immunohistochemical features of the metastatic lesion were identical to those of the primary tumor. Somatostatin receptor (SSTR) 2A was expressed on the cell membranes of more than 50% of epithelioid cells, which was defined as a score of 3. SSTR2A expression was also detected in a small number of ganglion-like cells. The epithelioid cells and some ganglion-like cells were positive for progesterone receptor (PgR). All the three cell types were negative for pancreatic polypeptide (PP). A well-demarcated, grayish-white tumor, 7 × 7 mm in size was found in the pancreatic tail. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of round-to-columnar cells with uniformly round nuclei, a salt-and-pepper chromatin pattern, and an eosinophilic, finely granular cytoplasm, arranged in trabecular and ribbon-like patterns and accompanied by fibrous stroma. There was no evidence of mitotic figures, necrosis, or lymphovascular invasion. Immunohistochemical examination showed that the tumor cells were diffusely positive for chromogranin A and synaptophysin. The Ki-67 LI was 0.5%. The tumor cells were diffusely positive for glucagon and PgR, but negative for PP. Macroscopic examination showed that the nodular lesion in the left adrenal gland was 15 × 12 mm in size, well-circumscribed, and with a yellowish-tan coloring. Microscopically, the tumor was composed of both spongiocytic cells with a clear lipid-rich cytoplasm and lipid-poor compact cells with an eosinophilic cytoplasm. There was no evidence of mitosis, tumor necrosis, or vascular invasion. The pathological diagnosis was an adrenocortical adenoma. The surgical margins were negative for tumor cells. DNA analysis of a peripheral blood sample showed no mutations in exons 2–10 of the MEN1 gene, exons 1–3 of the VHL gene, and exon 16 of the RET gene.

case_report: A 45-year-old male patient was referred for examination of whitish lesions in the mouth. The patient reported that these oral lesions, along with thickened nails and callosities on the palms and soles, had been present since the age of 10. These conditions appeared spontaneously and had gradually worsened over time. The soles were particularly affected, causing discomfort and pain while walking. Excessive sweating of the soles and palms was also noted. The whitish plaques in the mouth were asymptomatic. The patient was born to non-consanguineous parents, and his dental and medical histories were non-contributory. Family history indicated that his father, brother, and son had similar conditions but declined clinical examination. The patient reported no tissue-abusing or parafunctional habits. General examination showed that the patient was moderately built and nourished for his age, with an altered gait. The nails were extremely hard, thickened, opaque brown, lusterless, and the free edges were raised by thick horny masses of subungual keratosis. Palmoplantar keratosis was more pronounced on pressure areas and elbows. All vital signs were within normal limits. Extraoral examination revealed no abnormalities. Solitary right and left submandibular lymph nodes were palpable, 1 cm × 1 cm, mobile, and firm. Intraoral examination showed a full complement of teeth. The labial mucosa, ventral surface of the tongue, floor of the mouth, vestibular mucosa, and oropharynx revealed no abnormalities. Leukokeratosis, characterized by diffuse whitish, non-tender, and non-scrapable plaque-like lesions, was present on both right and left buccal mucosae, the left retromolar region, the dorsal aspect of the tongue, the hard and soft palate, and the gingivae. Bilateral angular cheilosis was also observed. Routine investigations, including a complete hemogram, urine analysis, and fasting blood sugar, were within normal limits. Potassium hydroxide examination of nail clippings and fungal culture of the nails were negative. A biopsy from a palmar lesion indicated palmoplantar keratoderma.
test_results: Histopathological features were suggestive of oral leukokeratosis.

case_report: A 56-year-old male patient experienced chest discomfort during meals and was found to have middle thoracic esophageal cancer (cT3N1M0, cStage IIIb). He received neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by thoracoscopic-assisted subtotal esophagectomy with three-field lymph node dissection and retrosternal gastric tube reconstruction. During the gastric tube preparation, an injury to the splenic artery occurred, necessitating a switch from laparoscopic to open surgery for hemostasis. The bleeding was controlled, but ischemic changes in the spleen were noted, leading to a splenectomy. Postoperative findings indicated middle thoracic esophageal cancer (pTisN0M0, pStage 0). At a follow-up 3 years and 6 months later, a plain CT scan revealed a 12 mm retrosternal nodule near the reconstructed gastric tube. The nodule had smooth margins, a round shape, and homogeneous density. A retrospective review of postoperative contrast-enhanced CT showed a corresponding nodule with gradual enlargement and homogeneously high density, indicating homogeneous contrast enhancement. No similar nodules were seen in the abdomen or anterior mediastinum on preoperative CT.
test_results: 99mTc-Sn-colloid (115 MBq) was administered intravenously, and 15 minutes later, planar images of the chest and abdomen and SPECT/CT images of the chest were acquired using a SPECT/CT scanner (Symbia T2; Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a low-energy high-resolution collimator. Intense accumulation was observed in the chest, and the fused SPECT/CT images confirmed that the accumulation corresponded to the nodule of interest.

case_report: A 5-month-old female presented with a 3-day history of coughing and recurrent vaginal discharge, along with poor weight gain over the past 3 months. case_report: An 87-year-old woman residing in a nursing home presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain, cough, and high-grade fever that began four days prior to admission. Her medical history included polymyalgia rheumatica, giant cell arteritis, and mild cognitive impairment. She had no history of abdominal surgery or gastrointestinal symptoms. The patient had no known contact with individuals at high risk for SARS-CoV-2 infection, but a real-time PCR test of a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2. Upon admission, her blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse was 100 bpm and rhythmic, and oxygen saturation was 95% in ambient air and 97% with 40% oxygen. Physical examination of the chest showed reduced breath sounds at the pulmonary bases bilaterally. The abdomen was distended, diffusely tender, and positive for Blumberg’s sign, with no audible bowel sounds. Rectal examination revealed rectorrhagia. Laboratory results were as follows: white blood cell count 5990 cells/mm3, hemoglobin 15 g/dL, platelet count 233,000 109/L, C-reactive protein 290 mg/dL, INR 1.22, aPTT 29.2 s, fibrinogen 790 mg/dL, D-Dimer 2.1 mg/LFEU, and fecal calprotectin 290 mg/kg. Renal, liver, and pancreatic function tests were within normal limits. During clinical monitoring, the patient’s condition rapidly deteriorated, leading to septic shock.
test_results: The abdominal CT showed wall thickening of the lower third of the rectum associated with free perivisceral air; perivisceral fat stranding and thickening of the mesorectal fascia were also seen. On the chest CT, typical imaging features of COVID-19 interstitial pneumonia were clearly visible, with patchy bilateral ground-glass opacities associated with interlobular and intralobular septal thickening.

case_report: A 48-year-old male presented with rapidly worsening headache and nausea. Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) of the head revealed a left frontal lesion with a variegated appearance. Subsequent contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed a heterogeneous mass lesion in the left frontal area, which appeared hyperintense on T1-weighted images and relatively hypointense on T2-weighted images, accompanied by mass effect and perilesional edema. The patient underwent gross total resection of the lesion, which measured approximately 7 by 5 cm, was blackish in color, vascular, lacked dural attachment, and was confined to the left frontal lobe.
test_results: The tumor consisted of epithelioid cells, arrayed in sheets, with abundant melanin pigment deposits in the cytoplasm. The tumor was hypercellular with some signs of pleomorphism. Mitoses were present. Foci of hemorrhage and necrosis were seen. Both melanin and hemosiderin pigment were identified by Masson-Fontana stain and iron stain, respectively. The neoplastic cells were stained positively with human melanin black-45 (HMB-45) antibody.

case_report: A 21-year-old nonsmoking woman was admitted with a 3-month history of worsening shortness of breath and cough. She also reported feeling generally unwell, experiencing loss of appetite, and losing weight. Initially, she was treated for asthma with inhaled corticosteroids and β2-agonists, but there was no notable improvement. She had no history of using other medications or alternative treatments. On examination, the patient appeared ill and had a frequent dry cough. Lung auscultation revealed coarse crackles and generalized wheezing. Laboratory tests showed severe eosinophilia, with eosinophils making up 21.2% of the total peripheral white blood cell count (2450 /µL), and elevated levels of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and immunoglobulin E (IgE). There were no signs of parasitic infestation in fecal tests. Tests for antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) were negative. Chest radiography showed bilateral patchy, ill-defined infiltrations. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest revealed RHS in the right upper lobe and a few ill-defined peripheral air-space consolidations, with no abnormalities in the mediastinum or pleura.
test_results: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) analysis revealed a marked increase in the number of cells with a high proportion of eosinophils (45.4%). Charcot-Leyden crystals were seen indicating eosinophil activation. There was no evidence of bacterial pathogens or malignant cells. Cytomorphology of BALF was not in favor of extrinsic allergic alveolitis or cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP).

case_report: A 15-year-old male reported having poor vision in his left eye since birth. His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was measured at 20/63 in the right eye and finger counting close to face (FCCF) in the left eye. The left eye exhibited enophthalmos and a 30° exotropia. The anterior segment appeared normal in both eyes. Examination of the right fundus revealed mild temporal dragging of the optic disc, straightening of the temporal vessels, subretinal exudations, and scarring at the periphery of the temporal retina. The left fundus showed dragging of the optic disc, a falciform retinal fold, and an abnormal retinal vascular pattern, along with pigmentation and scarring of the retina. There was no history of prematurity, and the patient's parents and four siblings were reported to be normal.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiography showed abrupt cessation of vasculature at the temporal retina of right eye. There was brush like anastomoses and shunts at the vascular-avascular border with mild leakage from the vessels. Left eye showed mild leakage from the disc and falciform retinal fold.

case_report: A 43-year-old South Asian male, with no known past medical history, presented with an eight-month history of asymptomatic, hyperpigmented patches, characterized by discrete central atrophy. The lesions were violaceous in color and ovoid in shape, appearing gradually over the dorsal aspect of hands bilaterally, and over the medial aspect of both thighs. Small multiple unilateral lesions were also noted over the lateral aspect of the right lower limb. There was no history of any recent or distant trauma, tick bites, new medication use, or any recent fungal infections reported by the patient. The patient reported that these lesions had shown the same form, texture, and color since their initial appearance, with slow and nominal growth in size noted over the course of the past eight months. Both his prior medical and familial history was deemed unremarkable. With the exception of these dermal lesions, the patient’s general health and overall physical condition were exceptional. On dermatological examination, there were two large hyperpigmented violaceous patches with atrophic changes noted on the bilateral dorsum of hands, measuring 3 x 4 cm and 4 x 6 cm in size. Small, multiple, brownish, and hyperpigmented patches with a depressed shiny center were noted over the lateral aspect of the right lower limb as well as on the medial aspect of both thighs. All patches were observed to be ovoid in shape, with a central atrophic, “cigarette paper”-like appearance, conserved pathognomonic “cliff-drop” borders, and minimal surrounding peripheral desquamation. The patient reported a lightly diminished sensation within the patches, and hence a pinprick examination was performed in and around the lesions. The sensation was deemed to be intact in all areas.
test_results: Histopathologic findings of this specimen revealed focal basal hyperpigmentation. The dermis displayed marked dermal atrophy, with mildly thickened collagen fibers and minor perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. There was no obvious dermal sclerosis appreciated nor any absence of the dermal appendages. There were no signs of epidermotropism or any evidence of epidermal infiltration. The rest of the skin adnexa was unremarkable. Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stains were negative for fungal elements.
diagnosis: Idiopathic Atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini

case_report: A 30-year-old female presented with blurred vision in her left eye for the past year. She had a history of glaucoma surgeries in both eyes 13 years ago, and her right eye had been blind (no light perception) for more than 10 years. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/100 in her left eye with a refractive error of -16.0D. The intraocular pressure (IOP) was measured at 54 mmHg in the right eye and 49 mmHg in the left eye. Examination revealed a very shallow anterior chamber in the right eye with significant lens opacity, making the retina unviewable. In the left eye, the anterior chamber was extremely narrow with a forward-bulging iris. The optic disc in the left eye appeared pale with a cup-to-disc (C/D) ratio of 0.99. Visual field testing using the Humphrey field vision test showed an extremely narrow tubular field of vision in the left eye. Due to the patient's history of glaucoma surgery, elevated IOP, small cornea, and extremely narrow anterior chamber, aggressive therapy was deemed necessary. A trabeculectomy was performed on the left eye, and atropine ointment was used to dilate the pupil. On the first postoperative day, the IOP in the left eye was reduced to 20 mmHg. The equator of the lens was visible through the dilated pupil, revealing a small, spherical lens with a slight upward dislocation. The suspensory ligaments were clearly visible under high magnification.
test_results: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed a microspherophakic lens with horizontal diameter of approximately 9 mm and anteroposterior diameter of approximately 8 mm. General physical examination demonstrated short stature (145 cm) and brachydactyly.

case_report: A 27-year-old man reported discomfort in the right testis in early September 2021 and subsequently visited our department. Physical examination of the scrotum revealed no abnormalities. Ultrasound imaging showed a heterogeneous lesion in the central part of the right testis. MRI indicated a 2.7 cm mass with clear boundaries and a smooth margin located centrally in the testis. Laboratory results were as follows: alpha-fetoprotein level at 1.38 ng/ml, human chorionic gonadotropin level below 1.0 mIU/l, human chorionic gonadotropin-β subunit level below 0.1 ng/ml, and lactate dehydrogenase level at 178 U/l. CT imaging showed no abnormalities. A right radical orchiectomy was performed in mid-September 2021 due to the presence of a right testicular tumor. Examination of the excised tissue revealed a solid mass measuring 1.5 cm in diameter. The lesion contained areas of bleeding necrosis and granulation tissue, but no viable tumorous cells were observed. Granulation tissue was present at the boundary between necrotic and existing testicular tissue, with no additional findings.
test_results: The lesion contained atypical cells that were observed in the seminiferous tubules from the spermatic cord. The atypical cells were like spermatogonia, large, and had clear reticulum. The nucleus had large irregularity and included a clear nucleolus. These cells were arranged like lining the basement membrane. The collapse of the basement membrane or extravasation was not recognized. No extension to epididymis, vas deferens, and spermatic cord of atypical cells was seen. The surgical stump was negative for a tumor. The atypical cells were stained positively with immune-histochemical staining MIB-1, CD117 (c-kit) and D2-40, but negatively with alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin, and human chorionic gonadotropin-β subunit.

case_report: A 39-year-old woman with a history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) visited the outpatient clinic with a 3-day history of petechiae following vaccination with ChAdOx1 nCov-19. The patient was diagnosed with ITP during her teenage years and underwent splenectomy at the age of 15. Her platelet count remained stable post-splenectomy, with steroid treatments administered before and after childbirth. From February to August 2017, she was treated with eltrombopag, an orally administered thrombopoietin receptor agonist. Since 2018, her platelet count has been stable during regular outpatient examinations, although she experienced intermittent transient thrombocytopenia due to viral infections in the past. At the outpatient visit after vaccination, she did not present with fever, headache, abdominal pain, dyspnea, or limb edema. She had no history of anticoagulant use, including heparin. Severe thrombocytopenia was noted with a platelet count of 22,000/µL at the initial examination on the day of admission. The international normalized ratio (INR), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), fibrinogen, and D-dimer levels were within normal ranges.
test_results: The PF4-heparin ELISA performed during hospitalization showed a weakly positive result with an optical density (OD) value of 0.81.
diagnosis: Subclinical thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura  after vaccination with ChAdOx1 nCoV-19
Orpha_name: Rare hemorrhagic disorder due to a platelet anomaly

case_report: A 55-year-old male presented with pain extending down the left leg. He had no history of corticosteroid use, endocrinopathy, or radicular pain. Physical examination revealed obesity (height 165 cm, weight 86 kg) with a body mass index (BMI) of 31.6 kg/m2. The patient exhibited significant limitation during the straight leg raise test and demonstrated motor weakness in the left extensor hallucis longus and peroneal muscles, although sensation remained intact. Plain radiographs did not show any abnormalities, including instability or other pathological findings.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an epidural mass posterior to the L5 vertebral body that was isosignal to subcutaneous fat, and it compressed asymmetrically on the left side of the cauda equina and the exiting left L5 nerve root on sagittal and axial T1 weighted images (T1WI). Severe arthritis of the left facet joint and edema of the left pedicle bone marrow were also demonstrated. There was no evidence of spinal stenosis. The result of electromyography was compatible with radiculopathy in the left fifth lumbar root.

case_report: A one-year-old girl was examined by a dermatologist in 2016 due to dense yellow-orange formations on the knee joints, elbow joints, and gluteal folds. Laboratory tests revealed hypercholesterolemia with a maximum total cholesterol level of 16.0 mmol/L. Echocardiography showed no structural or hemodynamic abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound indicated no hepatosplenomegaly or fatty liver. Thrombocytopenia was not present. Extracranial color triplex scanning of the brachiocephalic arteries was not performed. Both parents had no dyslipidemia or signs of premature coronary artery disease. Plasmapheresis was conducted but did not show marked efficiency.
test_results: Targeted sequencing revealed that the patient was homozygous for a missense variant in the ABCG8 gene rs769576789 NM_022437.3:c.1715T>C p.(Leu572Pro). These variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and parents were heterozygous.

case_report: A 42-year-old woman with a history of asthma and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes presented to the hospital with knee pain, swelling, fever, and rash for four days. Prior to admission, she experienced a fever of 103.9 F, followed by a generalized non-pruritic rash mainly on the lower extremities, and later developed swelling and erythema in her right foot and both knees. She reported unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner a week before the presentation. Upon admission, her vitals were: blood pressure 137/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats per minute, temperature 97.8 F, respirations 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination revealed diffuse vesiculopustular, non-tender, non-pruritic rashes on the skin. The right foot was erythematous with ankle edema, and the left knee showed mild swelling with a reduced range of motion due to tenderness. Laboratory results on admission indicated a white blood cell count of 21,000/microL. HIV antigen and antibody tests were negative. HbA1c was 8.2. Two sets of blood cultures were negative. The urine nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) was indeterminate. She was started on intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone.
test_results: Right knee swelling confirmed joint effusion on imaging which was aspirated, revealing monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid analysis and the culture growing gram-negative diplococci.

case_report: Patient 1 is a 16-year-old male born at 40 weeks of gestation to non-consanguineous Italian parents. The mother was 25 years old and the father was 30 years old at the time of birth. The patient was delivered at term via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Birth weight was 3.750 kg (50–75th percentile) and length was 51 cm (75–90th percentile). Physical growth was consistent with age norms, but the patient exhibited psychomotor delay and significant language impairment. Milestones included independent sitting at seven months, walking at 16 months, babbling after 12 months, and first words after 24 months. Sphincter control was achieved around three years of age. At the age of 14, cognitive and behavioral assessments indicated moderate intellectual disability with severe expressive language impairment. The WISC-IV scale measured an IQ of 40. Speech was severely disordered, characterized by stuttering, speech dysfluency, articulation difficulties, and limited vocabulary. Neuropsychological evaluation revealed communication and executive function difficulties, short attention span, and behavioral issues including problems with verbal inhibitory control. Despite these challenges, the patient was relatively cooperative. No sleep disturbances were reported, and there was no diagnosis of autism. Feeding and gastrointestinal functions were normal. Physical examination revealed mild pectus carinatum and moderate craniofacial features including protruding supraorbital ridges, bushy eyebrows, deep-set eyes, bulbous nasal tip, short philtrum, and wide mouth. Neurological examination was largely normal, with the exception of mild global dyspraxia and fine motor skills impairment. The patient had no history of seizures, and both EEG and brain MRI results were normal.
test_results: His initial diagnostic examinations included a complete metabolic workup, conventional karyotyping, and Comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array (40 kb resolution) as well as Fragile X testing, which were all negative.
Orpha_name: Facial dysmorphism-developmental delay-behavioral abnormalities syndrome due to WAC point mutation

case_report: A 65-year-old female presented with a 3-year history of gradually enlarging, periorbital, asymptomatic lesions. One of the lesions had been surgically removed 2 years ago at another hospital, but it recurred within a few months, accompanied by new, larger nodules. There was no history of ulceration or involvement of other sites, nor any eye complaints or significant systemic symptoms. The patient's medical history was unremarkable. On examination, multiple yellowish-brown, firm nodules were observed symmetrically in the periorbital area, ranging from 3 to 7 cm in their widest dimensions. The surface of the nodules exhibited a few telangiectasias and mild atrophy. Mild right-sided ectropion was also noted.

case_report: A 55-year-old male presented to the hematology department with a 5-month history of recurrent fever, severe jaundice, and fatigue. Initial thoracic CT scans from another hospital showed multiple high-density opacities and nodules in both lungs. Treatment with cefoperazone and levofloxacin did not result in clinical or radiological improvement. A follow-up thoracic CT scan revealed worsening lung opacities and nodules in both lungs without cavitations. The patient had no history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, autoimmune disease, hepatitis, or AIDS. Physical examination revealed severe anemia, noticeable jaundice, and sporadic petechiae and ecchymosis. His temperature was 38.9°C, with no enlarged superficial lymph nodes in the cervical, axillary, or inguinal regions. The liver and spleen were not palpable. The rest of the physical examination, including the respiratory system, was unremarkable. Laboratory results showed bicytopenia (leukocytes 6.93 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 53 g/L, and platelets 13 × 10^9/L) and significantly elevated serum ferritin (5,350 μg/L) and β2-microglobulin (13.1 mg/L). Additional laboratory tests indicated triglycerides (TG) of 7.95 mmol/L (normal range: 0.56–1.70 mmol/L), fibrinogen 1.13 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 475 U/L, total bilirubin 118 μmol/L (normal range: 3.4–20.5 μmol/L), direct bilirubin 89.4 μmol/L (normal range: 0.0–6.8 μmol/L), albumin 22.8 g/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 120 U/L, aspartate transaminase (AST) 176 U/L, procalcitonin (PCT) 3.48 ng/ml, and serum creatinine (Scr) 149 μmol/L (normal range: 57–97 μmol/L). Blood cultures for aerobic bacteria, anaerobic bacteria, and fungi, T-spot test, Beta-D-Glucan assay (G test), galactomannan assay (GM test), and cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA serological tests were all negative. Serological tests for EBV-related antibodies showed positive EBV-capsid antigen-IgG (EBV-CA-IgG) and EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA)-antibody, with normal EBV-DNA copy levels. The absolute count of CD4+ T cells was 0.31 × 10^9/L, and the CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio was 0.76. The autoantibody profile was normal. Chest CT scans showed scattered patch-like opacities with minimal bilateral pleural effusion and multiple enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. Transabdominal ultrasound revealed moderate splenomegaly with the spleen measuring 16 cm in length and 5.7 cm in thickness. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) demonstrated irregularly-shaped hypermetabolic nodular lesions in the anterior segment of the superior lobe of the right lung with a maximum standard uptake value (SUV) of 5.8 g/ml. FDG-PET CT scan also showed multiple hypermetabolic nodular lesions with a maximum SUV of 4.7 g/ml in the anterior segment of the superior lobe of the right lung, middle lobe of the right lung, apico-posterior segment of the superior lobe of the left lung, bilateral pleura, and the liver. Intense FDG uptake was observed in the lymph nodes of the posterior region of the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, right internal mammary region, hilums of both lungs, and mediastinum. Multiple bone lesions with hypermetabolic FDG uptake (maximum SUV of 5.6 g/ml) were noted in the skull, maxillae, bilateral humerus, bilateral clavicle, bilateral scapula, sternum, some vertebrae, some ribs, bilateral femurs, and the pelvis.
test_results: Histopathologic examination of lung biopsy specimen demonstrated proliferation of fibrous tissue and infiltration of chronic inflammatory cells interspersed with atypical large B-lymphocytes. Immunohistochemistry results showed that the large atypical lymphocytes stained strongly positive for CD20, LCA, Ki67, Pax-5, latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1), while completely negative for AE1/AE3, ALK1, CD3, CK7, P40, P63, TTF, CD15, CD4, CD8, EBNA2. In situ hybridization for EBV encoded small RNA (EBER) was strongly positive in numerous large atypical lymphocytes (>50/high power field).
diagnosis: Pulmonary Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis  with secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis
Orpha_name: Acquired hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis associated with malignant disease

case_report: A 6-year-old girl visited the pediatric nephrology outpatient clinic due to proteinuria detected during a school health screening. Physical examination showed no significant abnormalities, including in her external genitalia. Her spot urine protein/creatinine ratio (UPCR) was 1.34 g/g, and her 24-hour urine protein was 0.66 g. Renal sonography indicated increased echogenicity in both kidneys. Two months later, proteinuria persisted with a UPCR of 2.1 g/g. The patient sought a second opinion at another medical center, where a renal biopsy showed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in two out of seven glomeruli. The patient received several sessions of methylprednisolone (MTP) pulse therapy followed by daily oral steroids, but heavy proteinuria continued. Another renal biopsy two years later still showed FSGS (4/67 glomeruli). Over the next two years, multiple treatments were tried, including MTP pulse therapy, oral prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and abatacept, but proteinuria worsened, with UPCR rising to 4.01 g/g. Regular medical treatment was stopped at age 12, and the patient began alternative herbal therapy. At age 14, she visited a gynecology clinic for a prolonged menstrual period lasting up to one month (menarche at age 12). Preliminary sonography revealed a left ovarian tumor, and she was referred to our hospital. Sonography confirmed a heterogeneous adnexal mass, and a CT scan showed a lobulated mass (maximum diameter: 10.1 cm) with cystic and solid components in the pelvis. Serum tumor markers were: CA-125, 77.96 unit/mL (normal: <35.0 unit/mL); CA-199, 57.01 unit/mL (normal: <34.0 unit/mL); alpha-fetoprotein, 94.88 ng/mL (normal: <7 ng/mL). Serum albumin was 2.2 g/dL, cholesterol 183 mg/dL, and triglyceride 133 mg/dL. The patient underwent cytoreductive left salpingo-oophorectomy one week after the CT scan. Pathology revealed a malignant mixed germ cell tumor in a gonadoblastoma of the ovary, composed of 75% dysgerminoma, 10% immature teratoma, 10% embryonal carcinoma, and 5% yolk sac tumor. Further analysis showed a chromosome karyotype of 46, XY, with the SRY gene present in PCR tests, although the patient had normal female external genitalia.
test_results: A genetic analysis that revealed a point mutation in intron 9 of the WT1 gene, c.1447 + 4 C > T.

case_report: A 53-year-old Chinese woman experienced a gradual onset of unsteady gait over a period of 3 years, without any additional symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable except for mild chronic rhinitis. During the physical examination, she was unable to perform heel-toe walking, but no other neurological abnormalities were observed. Blood tests showed normal results. There was no family history of malignancies.
test_results: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a 3 cm × 2.9 cm × 2.9 cm intraventricular cystic lesion in the fourth ventricle which was causing moderate hydrocephalus. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed ring enhancement with mural nodules. An intralesional T2W hypointense dependent fluid level with susceptibility artifact suggested history of tumoral hemorrhage. Restricted diffusion was absent. MRI of the whole spine showed no cerebrospinal fluid tumor seedling or synchronous spinal cord tumor. Histopathological examination showed cords and clusters of eosinophilic tumor cells in a myxoid background, with mild lymphocytic infiltrate. Pericellular clearing reminiscent of chondroid pattern was focally observed. There was no abnormal mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, or necrosis. Immunohistochemical analysis showed positive staining for S-100, Olig2, vimentin, and CAM5.2. EMA (epithelial membrane antigen) was focal. Staining was negative for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), CD34, PR, brachyury, neurofilament protein, synaptophysin, and somatostatin receptor (SSTR). INI1 staining was preserved. IDH1 and IDH2 mutation were absent.

case_report: A 37-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was found to have grade III esophageal varices and significant gastropathy during an endoscopy performed for dyspepsia. Laboratory tests showed normal results except for a mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase of 135 U/L (normal range 30–110) and a platelet count of 137,000 mil/L (normal range 150,000–400,000). The patient did not exhibit symptoms such as jaundice, ascites, or encephalopathy. A colonoscopy revealed diffuse vascular congestion indicative of portal hypertensive colopathy. Abdominal MRI identified seven focal hepatic masses, a patent portal vein, and a recanalized umbilical vein. An ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the largest liver lesion indicated focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) without surrounding cirrhosis. Over the following 16 months, the patient was treated with nonselective beta-blockers and underwent four additional upper endoscopies with banding. Despite these interventions, she continued to have persistent and recurrent large varices. The patient was eventually referred for surgical evaluation. After consulting with her rheumatologist, the patient discontinued AZA, but there was no improvement in her portal hypertension. Due to the refractory nature of her varices, she underwent a side-to-side portacaval shunt with an 8 mm polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) graft.
test_results: The final pathology demonstrated multiple hypercellular nodules centered on portal triads without fibrosis.
Orpha_name: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver

case_report: A 55-year-old female teacher, an ex-smoker with a history of 45 pack years, was referred to the emergency department after experiencing a notable reduction in exercise tolerance over the past two months, decreasing from running 5 km to only 1 km. She reported mild shoulder discomfort and a dry, non-productive cough without hemoptysis or dyspnea. She also mentioned recovering from a mild COVID-19 infection three months ago, which was managed at home. Her medical history includes nine years of thyroxine replacement therapy following a thyroidectomy. Upon admission to the Department of Respiratory Medicine, the patient was afebrile and normopnoic. Physical examination revealed psoriatic-like rashes on the extensor surfaces of the elbows. Cardiac examination was normal, but auscultation detected velcro-like crackles at the bases of both lungs. Peripheral lymph nodes were normal, and no muscular weakness was observed. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Arterial blood gas analysis indicated hypoxemic respiratory failure with an elevated alveolar-arterial gradient, requiring oxygen supplementation. The patient was hemodynamically stable but exhibited tachycardia with a heart rate of 116 beats per minute. Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood cell count and biochemical panel, except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). A chest X-ray revealed an asymmetrical basal predominant reticular pattern with a few areas of alveolar infiltrates bilaterally.
test_results: A high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) showed bilateral ground glass opacities and patchy consolidations with a central irregular peribronchovascular and perilobular distribution. Bronchoscopy demonstrated no endobronchial abnormalities. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the right lower lobe revealed no alveolar hemorrhage. The polymerase chain reaction for acid-resistant bacteria and acid-fast stains was negative. Additionally, the BAL differential cell count showed lymphocytic predominance. A complete immunological panel was conducted.
diagnosis: Anti-NXP2 amyopathic idiopathic inflammatory myopathy  presenting as interstitial lung disease with anti-Ro52 progressive phenotype

case_report: A 59-year-old male presented with a history of progressive muscle weakness starting in his late twenties at the outpatient department of the rehabilitation center, Daejeon St. Mary's Hospital (Daejeon, Republic of Korea). He was born healthy at full-term and had no health issues during childhood and early adulthood, including completing mandatory national military training. In his late twenties, he experienced frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs, with progressive muscle weakness primarily in the pelvic girdle and proximal legs, while the motor function of the upper extremities remained normal at that time. By the age of 38, he noticed muscle weakness in the upper extremities, a waddling gait, hyperlordosis of the lower back, and anterior pelvic tilt. His gait disturbance and muscle weakness continued to progress slowly. By the age of 55, he was unable to walk and required a wheelchair for mobility. His family history indicates a genetic background of autosomal recessive inheritance related to his muscle condition. One of his elder brothers exhibited similar symptoms and was diagnosed with progressive muscular dystrophy in his twenties. The patient is married to a healthy woman and has healthy children with no signs of muscle weakness.
test_results: The electrodiagnostic study revealed myopathy, normal values in the motor and sensory nerve conduction study, and short-amplitude muscle unit action potentials with early recruitment in needle electromyography. Quantitative electromyography also showed a myopathic pattern. In the laboratory findings, the serum creatine kinase (CK) level was elevated in 2042 IU/L.
diagnosis: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2B  with DYSF mutation

case_report: A 31-year-old female presented with complaints of oligomenorrhea and worsening headaches. She described an 11-year history of intermittent headaches, rated 4 out of 10 on a visual analog scale, which were typically triggered by fatigue and relieved by rest or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Recently, the headaches increased in both frequency and intensity, accompanied by mild nausea, and persisted for a week without relief from NSAIDs, prompting her to seek medical care. She reported no issues with vision, visual field, excessive urination, lactation, central obesity, or abnormal growth. Both general physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable, with no focal neurological signs observed.
test_results: A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan with contrast was performed, demonstrating a 19 mm × 24 mm × 23 mm irregular suprasellar lesion with slight intrasellar extension. The lesion signal characteristics were isointense on T1-weighted imaging and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging. No obvious gadolinium enhancement was noted.

case_report: A 10-month-old male infant with significant anxiety observed for one day was admitted. The patient had a history of surgery at 8 months for a Morgagni-Larrey hernia and was under cardiology care for a ventricular septal defect type 2 and ENT care for bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Complete blood counts and routine biochemical tests conducted two and four months prior showed no abnormalities. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination noted pale skin, postoperative scars, a Mongolian spot in the sacral region, a flat forehead, a broad nasal bridge with a tendency to form epicanthal folds, single transverse palmar creases, persistent fetal pads, aphthous stomatitis, an umbilical hernia, and a systolic murmur along the left sternal border. Initial laboratory tests indicated agranulocytosis, monocytosis, anemia, and elevated C-reactive protein levels. Abdominal radiographs and ultrasound showed no abnormalities in abdominal organs except for the umbilical hernia. On the second day, a tender and painful mass approximately 2 × 2.5 cm was palpated in the right submandibular area, and ultrasound suggested an abscess formation. Empiric antibiotic therapy with amoxicillin and clavulanic acid was initiated following a laryngological consultation but showed no improvement. On the seventh day, surgical incision and drainage of the abscess were performed under general anesthesia, and pus culture identified methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Immunological, genetic, and hematological consultations were conducted due to agranulocytosis. Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus infections were ruled out. Lipid profile, lactate, and uric acid levels were normal. Elastase I and stool fat concentrations were normal, excluding exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Urine organic acid analysis by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) did not indicate inborn errors of metabolism. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry showed reference ranges for peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets, and immunoglobulin classes A, G, M, complement component 3, and complement 4 were within normal limits.
test_results: Anti-human neutrophil antigen-1 (HNA-1) antibodies were detected in serum using the granulocyte immunofluorescence test (GIFT).

case_report: A six-year-old boy presented with a one-month history of abdominal distension and facial puffiness. Two weeks prior, he experienced a brief episode of low-grade fever with general symptoms. Physical examination showed jugular venous distention, significant hepatomegaly, and ascites. His ECG results were normal, but a chest X-ray indicated cardiomegaly with right atrial enlargement and normal pulmonary vascularity. Transthoracic echocardiography identified a large solid mass with inhomogeneous echo texture occupying the entire right ventricle, including the outflow tract, leaving only a few millimeters of residual lumen. This mass was indistinguishable from the myocardium and bordered by the tricuspid and pulmonary valves. The right atrium was enlarged, and the left-sided cardiac chambers were compressed. A small pericardial effusion was also noted. Systemic evaluation did not reveal any extracardiac disease. Cardiac MRI did not provide additional information. Due to obstructive symptoms, an urgent palliative resection was planned. The tumor was approached through an atriotomy and the pulmonary artery, confirming its intracavitary nature as suggested by echocardiographic findings. The entire mass was resected, and a Glenn shunt was performed, leaving the foramen ovale patent. The immediate postoperative period was uneventful. However, the patient expired on the first postoperative day, likely due to an air embolism.
test_results: Histology and histochemistry of the operative specimen revealed a malignant small round cell tumor with abundant intracytoplasmic glycogen. Immunocytochemistry was positive for vimentin and MIC2 (CD99). Negativity for smooth muscle actin, desmin, and myogenin ruled out rhabdomyosarcoma. Lymphoblastic lymphoma and neuroblastoma were ruled out by negativity for leucocyte common antigen, chromogranin and synaptophysin.
diagnosis: Primitive Neuroectodermal Tumor  of the myocardium

case_report: A 15-month-old first-born female toddler presented with a history of generalized body swelling since birth and neurodevelopmental delay. The initial presentation occurred at 2 weeks of age following a full-term normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 2.3 kg. The mother was HIV-positive during pregnancy and received anti-retroviral drugs. The mother reported unsatisfactory growth of the newborn, with delays in motor and speech development. The child was breastfed until 4 months of age and then fed with infant formula. On examination, the child was below the 3rd percentile for height and weight (weight 6.5 kg; length 64 cm; head circumference 44.5 cm). Despite having Harrison’s sulci, the child appeared un-distressed with no dysmorphic features. There was generalized edema and hypoplastic teeth. Central nervous system examination showed delayed social and motor milestones, with no smiling, reaching, or sitting, decreased muscle tone and power, and normal reflexes.
test_results: The urine dipstick resulted with 3+ for proteinuria, no signs of haematuria. Blood testing showed a significant depressed C3 level of 0.638 g/L (reference interval 0.9-1.8 g/L) and hypoalbuminaemia of 2.0 g/L (reference interval 27-43 g/L). Whole blood count revealed anaemia with haemoglobin of 8.0 g/L and there was thrombocytosis with 656 × 109/L. Plasmatic coagulation tests were found within normal ranges, as well as liver enzymes and renal function testing and electrolytes. Total- and LDL cholesterol levels were markedly increased; TSH and PTH were also significantly elevated together with hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphatemia. Serologic testing for active infections including hepatitis, toxoplasmosis, anti-streptolysin-O titer, cytomegalo virus and syphilis gave negative results, HIV-antibody ELISA was negative and HIV-RNA was not detectable. A renal biopsy showed mesangial hypercellularity, focal microcystic dilatations of the tubules and a mild interstitial inflammatory infiltrate. 4+ foot process effacement and increased tubular lipid droplets were visualised on electron microscopy. Immunofluorescence displayed focal 1+ IgM mesangial positivity.

case_report: A 79-year-old male presented with a painless swelling in the posterior region of the mandible, with an uncertain onset. Examination revealed expansion of the mandible in the left molar region to both the buccal and lingual sides. There was no fluctuation of the mandible or hypoesthesia of the lower lip. The patient's medical history included a frontal intradiploic meningioma 16 years prior, for which he underwent bifrontal craniotomy with complete tumor excision and cranioplasty. No clinical or imaging signs of recurrence were noted. A recent brain MRI confirmed the absence of tumor recurrence. Orthopantomography indicated a large, round, well-circumscribed radiolucency in the mandible. CT imaging showed an expansive lesion with thinning and partial interruption of the cortical bone margins, involving the mandibular canal.
test_results: An incisional biopsy of the lesion revealed the presence of spindle cells and collagen bundle without atypical or mitotic figures.
