case_report: A 70-year-old Greek man was referred to the Neurology Department of the Papageorgiou Hospital in Thessaloniki. The primary observation was choreatiform tongue movements, which were initially noted by the haematology unit. These movements were recently observed and were thought by the family and the patient to be due to his ill-fitting denture. The patient also exhibited slight generalized restlessness with frequent changes of posture, but without any specific tic-like or choreiform movements in other parts of his body, except for his tongue and face. Neurological examination revealed chorea of the face and tongue, along with lower limb muscle weakness and muscle wasting. His medical history includes severe progressive skeletal deformities starting after the age of 50, with bilateral osteoarthritis of the knees leading to severe varus deformities. The patient had a brother who passed away at the age of 60, who had severe facial dyskinesias, chorea, and schizophrenia-like psychosis. His sister, who died at the age of 70 following an acute ischemic stroke, was reported to be healthy until that event. His 38-year-old daughter and 35-year-old son are both healthy. There is no additional family history of neuropsychiatric diseases.
test_results: The haematology unit detected a weak expression of K red blood cell antigens, acanthocytosis, haemolysis, and a form of Factor IX deficiency.

case_report: A 37-year-old male with a 2-year history of cerebellar ataxia presents with an unsteady walk, difficulty swallowing, and slurred speech. He is the offspring of first-cousin consanguineous parents. His parents did not exhibit gait issues, but detailed neurological assessments were not conducted on them. case_report: A 46-month-old male patient with a history of recurrent bronchiolitis, inability to walk, inability to speak, and seizures presented to the clinic with respiratory distress. Physical examination showed delayed neuromotor development, fever, and rales and rhonchi on lung auscultation. The parents were second cousins. Laboratory results were: WBC: 3320 /mm3, ANC: 2870/mm3, ALC: 130/mm3, Hb: 11.4 g/dL, PLT: 284000/mm3, UA: 0.6 mg/dL, IgG: 741 mg/dL, IgA: 28 mg/dL, IgM: 38 mg/dL, LP: CD3 4.2%, CD19 0.46%, CD4 2.2%, CD8 2.7%, CD3-CD16/56 90%, CD3 HLA DR 2.4%. CMV viral load (DNA quantitative) was 3311 IU/mL. Respiratory virus panel indicated influenza, and stool examination showed rotavirus. During ICU hospitalization, tracheal aspirate culture and skin lesion tissue fungal examination revealed Candida albicans. HRCT indicated bronchiolitis obliterans. Anemia developed during follow-up, and a direct Coombs test was (+++). Resistant convulsions occurred during follow-up. Cranial computed tomography showed cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and deepening of cerebral sulci. A fully suitable HSCT from the father was planned, but the patient was lost before it could be performed due to resistant fever, septic shock, and multiorgan failure despite multiple antibiotherapy, antifungal, and antiviral treatments.
test_results: A homozygous p.R58X stop codon mutation was found in the patient, and the parents were found to have heterozygous c.172 C>T (p.Arg58Ter) mutations.

case_report: A 37-year-old male reported experiencing reduced vision in the right eye for a duration of 4 months. His overall health history was without notable issues. The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) measured 20/60 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Upon ocular examination, the pupils were round and responded normally to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and the visual axes were aligned. The anterior segment examination of both eyes showed no abnormalities. Examination of the posterior segment revealed dilated and twisted blood vessels with arteriovenous (AV) communication in both eyes, along with hard exudates in the macular area of the right eye. The AV malformations (AVMs) in the right eye were classified as grade II, while those in the left eye were classified as grade I. The peripheral regions of both eyes appeared normal.
test_results: Fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA) showed normal arm-to-retina time and rapid transit time in both the eyes, non-leaky retinal AV communications in the left eye, and late leakage in the perifoveal area in the right eye. Magnetic resonance neurogram finding included tortuous vertebral arteries in close approximation with left-side complex of cranial nerves VII and VIII and bilateral multiple tiny cavernous and capillary hemangiomas in supra- and infratentorial compartments with predominant involvement of brainstem and cerebellum. Optical coherence tomography examination showed hyporeflective lesions in the inner retinal layers of the perifoveal and peripapillary region suggestive of dilated vessels in both the eyes; hyperreflective lesions suggestive of hard exudates, intraretinal edema, and neurosensory detachment involving the fovea in the right eye; while the left eye showed no macular edema.

case_report: A 3-year-old boy, the only child of non-consanguineous parents, exhibited widespread warty eruptions covering the body, including the genital area, but excluding the scalp, face, palms, and soles. The skin changes began at 3 weeks of age, initially appearing symmetrically on the anterior thighs, then spreading to the axillae, and over approximately 6 months, progressed to the current widespread distribution. There was no history of blisters or generalized redness at or after birth. The condition showed improvement during summer and worsened in winter. The child was otherwise in good health with no developmental delays or visual or hearing difficulties. There was no significant family history. Physical examination revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, verrucous plaques following the lines of Blaschko, extensively involving the trunk and extremities. The plaques were oriented transversely on the trunk and longitudinally on the limbs. Hair, nails, and oral cavity appeared normal. Systemic examination showed no abnormalities.
test_results: Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis. Focal epidermolytic hyperkeratosis was evident in the form of perinuclear vacuolization of keratinocytes of the upper epidermis with coarse keratohyaline granules.

case_report: A 12-year-old Japanese girl with a normal birth and developmental history, and no significant family or medical past history, experienced swelling in both knee joints at the age of 2 without any apparent cause. Initial examination revealed no rest pain in either knee, but pain on motion in the right knee and joint effusion in both knees. The right knee had full extension but limited flexion to 130°, while the left knee had a normal range of movement. Aspiration of clear yellow joint fluid showed a negative culture result. Laboratory findings included a white blood cell (WBC) count of 10,700/μL, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 0.45mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 21mm/hour. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed small masses in the knee joints. Symptoms did not improve after several joint aspirations, leading to arthroscopic synovectomy for both knees. During the procedure, rice bodies and thickening of the synovial membrane were observed. Pathological examination of the rice bodies showed acidophilic tissues with lymphoid infiltration. Post-operation, the pain and swelling in the knees improved, and the patient remained asymptomatic for 10 years, negating the need for annual medical examinations. At 12 years old, the left knee again showed swelling without any cause. Several joint aspirations and intra-articular steroid injections did not alleviate the symptoms. The patient did not experience pain in the left knee. Full extension was observed, but flexion was limited to 130°. Laboratory findings at this time included a WBC count of 4,300/μL, CRP of 0.10mg/dL, ESR of 12mm/hour, rheumatoid factor (RF) of < 5IU/mL, matrix metalloproteinase-3 of 95.1ng/mL, and an antinuclear antibody (ANA) test result of 1:80 positive.
test_results: Contrast-enhanced MRI showed joint effusion and thickening of the synovial membrane. Pathological findings revealed the presence of a villiform structure, increased blood vessels, chronic inflammatory cells, and lymphocyte infiltration.

case_report: A nine-month-old girl was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fever, cough, diarrhea (11-12 episodes daily), and failure to thrive. She was born at term via normal delivery with a birth weight of 3200 grams following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the second child of a non-consanguineous Turkish couple, with a healthy 5-year-old sister. Upon admission, her body weight was 4.7 kg (SD: -3.5), height was 62.5 cm (SD: -1.7), and head circumference was 39 cm (3rd percentile). Relative index was 71.2. Physical examination revealed pallor, thin and weak hair, and decreased subcutaneous adipose tissue. Auscultation detected rales in the middle zone of the left lung. Her abdomen was distended with prominent bowel loops, and she had umbilical and bilateral inguinal hernias. Dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, frontal bossing, triangular face, and retromicrognathia. She had complete head control but could not sit without support. Deep tendon reflexes were normoactive. Laboratory results showed a hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL, leukocyte count of 14820/mm3, and platelet count of 363000/mm3. Serum transaminases were mildly elevated with aspartate aminotransferase at 105 U/L and alanine aminotransferase at 112 U/L. Vitamin D concentration was 11.6 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase was 99 u/L, calcium was 9.03 mg/dL, phosphorus was 3.15 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone was 60 mg/L. TORCH screen was negative, and infections from hepatotropic viruses or HIV were ruled out. Coagulation tests, renal functions, and electrolytes were normal. The patient had been hospitalized three times for bronchiolitis. Cystic fibrosis was considered due to malnutrition, recurrent bronchiolitis, and elevated liver function tests, but molecular genetic analysis of the CFTR gene was normal. Stool examination showed no reducing substances but revealed fat droplets. Tests for pathogenic bacteria or parasites were negative. Normal levels of anti-endomysial antibodies ruled out celiac disease, and basic metabolic tests including ammonia, lactate, pyruvate, blood acyl carnitine profile, amino acid analysis, urinary organic acid analysis, homocysteine, and biotinidase activity were normal. Congenital immune deficiency was ruled out, and immunoglobulin profile (IgA, IgM, IgG, IgE), CD markers (CD3, CD19, CD56), and fagotest were normal. Cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations were low with TC at 26 mg/dL and TG at 9 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear revealed acanthocytosis. Vitamin E concentration was 0.87 mg/L, vitamin A was 71 ug/L, and vitamin D was 11.6 ug/L, all very low. Abdominal ultrasonography showed multiple small stones (<3 mm) in both kidneys, and ophthalmologic examination was normal.
test_results: MTTP gene analysis revealed a novel homozygous pathogenic variant [c.506A>T (p. D169V)].

case_report: A 30-year-old male presented with persistent proteinuria. His medical history included hypertension and dyslipidemia. He was treated with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, statins, and a trial of oral steroids, but there was no change in proteinuria levels. Family history revealed familial dyslipidemia among several first-degree relatives. His sister had end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and was on hemodialysis, with the cause of ESRD undetermined. The patient reported no symptoms except for lower-limb edema at initial presentation. On examination, his blood pressure was 159/95 mmHg, pulse 82/min, and he was afebrile. He denied urinary symptoms, loin pain, or analgesic use. Physical examination showed a healthy-looking young male of average build with a body mass index of 24.8 kg/m2. Cardiovascular, chest, neurological, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Notably, bilateral corneal ring opacities were observed. Laboratory results showed serum creatinine at 1.31 mg/dl, normal serum electrolytes, hemoglobin at 13 g/dl, and platelets at 200 × 109/L. Serology for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV 1 and 2 antibodies were negative. Serum total cholesterol was 309 mg/dl, triglycerides 545 mg/dl, LDL 177 mg/dl, and HDL 23 mg/dl. Liver enzymes and coagulation profile were within normal limits. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) was negative, and complement C3 and C4 levels were normal. Urinalysis indicated protein 3+ and red blood cells 20-30 per high power field. The 24-hour proteinuria was 3.55 grams. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral echogenic kidneys with the right kidney measuring 10.1 cm and the left kidney 10.4 cm.
test_results: Light microscopy with periodic acid-Schiff stain revealed glomerular mesangial matrix expansion and irregular thickening of the glomerular basement membranes. When stained with Jones Methenamine Silver, it further illustrated the glomerular basement membranes with an irregular vacuolated appearance. Immunofluorescence microscopy was negative for immunoglobulins and complement components. Electron microscopy revealed lipid deposits appearing as abundant lacunae. The lacunae contains electron-lucent deposits with an electron-dense core involving the mesangial matrix as well as the glomerular basement membranes.

case_report: A 63-year-old African American female arrived at the emergency room experiencing progressively worsening shortness of breath, new-onset difficulty breathing while lying down, swelling in both lower legs, and weight loss over the past month. Approximately 20 years ago, a mediastinal mass was incidentally discovered, but no further action was taken at that time, and it remained untreated due to its slow progression. Physical examination revealed rapid heart rate, labored breathing, reduced breath sounds with crackles and rhonchi in both lungs, and severe pitting edema in the lower extremities. Laboratory tests showed a brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) level of 2709 pg/mL, albumin level of 2.6 g/dL, and hemoglobin level of 9 g/dL. An initial chest X-ray identified a solid mass in the mediastinum. A chest CT scan revealed a large mass in the upper anterior mediastinum, measuring 16.4 x 12 x 15.3 cm, displacing most of the left lung tissue, exerting pressure on the heart, and encasing the ascending aorta and main pulmonary trunk. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed a significantly reduced ejection fraction of 28.7%. Coronary angiogram indicated 90% narrowing of the ostial left main coronary artery and a large branch from the proximal right coronary artery (RCA) supplying the mediastinal mass. An initial plan for tumor removal via thoracotomy was halted due to a significantly increased risk of bleeding and other potential complications.
test_results: A CT-guided biopsy of the mass showed nesting of small blue cells with salt & pepper chromatin pattern, abundant vasculature, and lack of mitosis. Immunostain strongly expressed synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and cluster of differentiation (CD)56 marker. A proliferation marker, Ki-67, was less than 2% and there was no evidence of necrosis within the tumor.

case_report: A healthy two-year-old white boy experienced a blunt injury to his right eye after hitting a sideboard in September 2008. He remained without symptoms until a month later when he presented to a local Casualty Department with a red and painful right eye. Upon referral to a children's hospital, he had light perception vision in his right eye and strongly resisted covering his left eye. Examination of his right eye under anesthesia showed conjunctival injection, corneal stromal haze, a significant anterior chamber reaction with fibrinous reaction and iris deposits, lens opacity, and elevated intraocular pressure of 30 mmHg. The corneal diameters were 12 mm bilaterally. Examination of the posterior segment was challenging due to significant media opacity, but the retina appeared attached. Examination of his left eye was normal. He was otherwise systemically well with no previous medical or ophthalmic history. An anterior chamber tap revealed small round cells in clumps, but the specimen was poorly preserved, preventing further evaluation. No mass lesion was seen on a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the right orbit. An ultrasound scan showed clumps of hyperechogenic material over the temporal lens surface, adjacent to but not in contact with the ciliary body, and extruding into the anterior vitreous. This was associated with a cataractous lens and the presence of cyclitic membranes. Intensive topical steroid therapy was initiated to treat the inflammation. He later underwent a right lensectomy and anterior vitrectomy in January 2009 (four months after initial presentation) and was left aphakic. Postoperatively, the intraocular pressure in his right eye became increasingly difficult to control despite the use of gutt Cosopt and Travatan. The cup-disc ratio in his right eye was noted to be 0.5 (compared to 0.1 in the left) and the right axial length was 23.6 mm (compared to 21.2 mm in the left). The angle was closed in all four quadrants, and an ectropion uvea was observed. There was no rubeosis. A limited trans-scleral cyclodiode laser was performed on the right eye two weeks later. He then underwent a right Baerveldt shunt (350 mm2) with 0.4 mg/mL Mitomycin-C in September 2009 due to further glaucoma progression, as indicated by an increase in the cup-disc ratio (0.7), axial length (25.8 mm), corneal diameter (14 mm), and intraocular pressure measurement (39 mmHg).
test_results: Ultrasound imaging revealed an irregular-surfaced mass with heterogeneous echogenicity measuring 8 mm in length by 11.3 mm in width by 5.4 mm in thickness.

case_report: A 59-year-old Vietnamese woman arrived at the emergency department (ED) following a motor vehicle accident (MVA) after a syncopal episode, with a recent history of gastrointestinal illness. She did not report any pre-syncope, palpitations, chest pain, or dyspnea. There was no evidence of urinary incontinence or tongue biting. She experienced vomiting and abdominal pain for 2 days prior, without fever or diarrhea. She had received her first COVID-19 (Pfizer) vaccine 2 weeks before the MVA. At ED triage, her heart rate was 114 beats per minute, oxygen saturation was 98% on room air, respiratory rate was 16, blood pressure was 120/77, and she was afebrile. She was alert, oriented, euvolemic, and had no murmurs on examination. Her medical history included thalassemia, but she had no known cardiovascular risk factors, no prior history of seizures, and no significant family history. Initial electrocardiogram (ECG) in the ED showed Q waves, fixed ST elevation anteriorly, and low QRS voltages. Cardiac troponin I was 24,000 (normal range <12). Inflammatory markers were mildly elevated—C-reactive protein 10 and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12. Her chest x-ray was unremarkable except for a calcified granuloma in the right apex. Her first transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) at 20 hours demonstrated normal left ventricle (LV) size, moderate-severe global systolic dysfunction, and an ejection fraction (EF) of approximately 30% by visual estimation. There was a mild concentric increase in wall thickness and severely reduced tissue Doppler velocities. The right ventricle (RV) size and function were normal. Mild-moderate aortic regurgitation and a moderate pericardial effusion were observed. The patient deteriorated overnight with symptomatic hypotension and bradycardia to 30 beats per minute. The ECG revealed high-grade atrioventricular block and a left bundle branch block. The initial TTE findings, along with worsening AV block, led to the patient being started on an isoprenaline infusion and transferred to the coronary care unit. The patient had an expedited Cardiologist review the next morning, which resulted in expedited permanent pacemaker insertion. The next day, the patient remained persistently hypotensive with a systolic blood pressure of 60 mmHg, became oliguric, and was started on a dopamine infusion. She experienced conscious, symptomatic episodes of brief accelerated idioventricular rhythm noted on telemetry. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for management of persistent hypotensive shock. TTE on day 4 revealed severe LV dysfunction, an EF of 10% with global hypokinesis, severely impaired RV systolic function, and a dilated inferior vena cava. Right heart function was limited to visual assessment only on subsequent TTEs due to limited imaging windows and significant difficulties in obtaining on-axis imaging.
test_results: On day 4, an EMB revealed florid infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, fewer plasma cells, and scattered eosinophils, which was associated with marked oedema and cardiomyocyte necrosis. There were occasional poorly formed granulomas consisting of loose aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes and a few multinucleated macrophages with foamy appearing cytoplasm.

case_report: This case report details a 70-year-old Caucasian man who exhibited neuromyotonia with notable autonomic and psychological symptoms, including insomnia, anxiety, and suicidal behavior, followed by effective treatment. In April 2014, the patient experienced pain in the crural region and legs, chills, tingling sensations, hypersensitivity to mechanical stimuli, and mild weakness in the lower limbs accompanied by slight foot-drop. These symptoms developed rapidly without an identifiable cause. By June 2014, the patient showed signs of insomnia, anxiety, confusion, auditory hallucinations, and attempted suicide by slashing his left wrist. He was briefly admitted to a psychiatric ward. The patient was later referred to a neurological clinic due to muscle weakness with significant fasciculations and myokymia.
test_results: An EMG confirmed fibrillations, positive waves, fasciculations, and multiple myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges, occasional high frequency fasciculations, doublets and multiplets. Contraction curve was reduced with unstable motor unit potentials with neurogenic changes. A motor nerve conduction study showed multiple afterdischarges with long-lasting repetitions, which prevented F-waves assessment. His blood test showed high levels of creatine kinase (CK) 12.26 (nkat/L; normal value 3.60), CK myocardial bound 0.52, but no other abnormalities. No antibodies (contactin associated protein-like 2, CASPR2; leucine-rich glioma inactivated 1 protein; contactin 2; anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase) were found in his blood or in his cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Oligoclonal protein synthesis was not confirmed. Cancer was not detected (oncological markers were negative; the results of chest X-ray, ultrasonography of abdomen, endoscopic investigation of gastrointestinal tract and urological examination were negative). His CSF showed borderline results: protein 0.40g/L and 1 mononuclear cell/1mm3.
diagnosis: Morvan’s syndrome of an autoimmune type with undetected specific antibodies

case_report: A 19-year-old male arrived at the emergency department after sustaining an injury to his left eye from a palm leaf that fell from approximately 10 meters. Earlier in the day, a piece of the stalk had been extracted from the wound at a local hospital. Upon examination, his vision was 20/20, the globe was intact, and ocular movements were unrestricted. A superficial wound was observed at the left infraorbital margin, with no signs of any remaining foreign body. The wound was dressed, and the patient was advised to follow up in the outpatient department. The patient returned 18 months later with swelling at the same location. Examination revealed his vision remained 20/20. There was a non-axial proptosis of the left eye with restricted elevation. The globe was displaced 3 mm forward and 2 mm upward. A firm, non-tender mass measuring 2 × 1 cm was detected at the infraorbital margin, with its posterior extent not clearly defined. A small scar was noted on the skin overlying the mass.
test_results: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbit obtained in axial and coronal planes depicted a medium-sized soft tissue density mass in the inferomedial aspect of the left orbit. The mass involved the retrobulbar, intra and extraconal spaces, abutting and slightly displacing the optic nerve superiorly. An incision biopsy of the mass at the infraorbital margin was done. Histopathological examination showed features of chronic inflammation with fibroblastic proliferation. Complete blood count, ESR, Mantoux test and Chest X-ray were within normal limits. The discharge from the sinus was sent for culture and sensitivity. It grew Enterobacter species, sensitive to ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, lomefloxacin and gentamicin.

case_report: A 73-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with trismus, which led to sudden respiratory distress and cyanosis. The trismus had begun three days prior to hospitalization, initially without any signs of respiratory failure. The patient had no significant medical history and was taking macrogol, escitalopram, mometasone, indapamide, and lorazepam. There was no use of antipsychotic or antiemetic agents, and her vaccination history was unknown, with no vaccinations recalled in the past decade. She had no history of alcohol, nicotine, or drug abuse and was socially active and enjoyed gardening. Upon arrival, the medical team noted an unsafe airway, which was stabilized with a Mayo tube, leading to rapid stabilization of oxygen saturation. Neurological examination showed trismus and mild neck muscle rigidity, but the patient was alert with normal motor function, sensibility, and reflexes. General physical examination was unremarkable except for small wounds in the oral mucosa from an ill-fitting dental prosthesis. Laboratory tests, brain and neck CT scans, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were all normal, with sterile cultures. Treatment included antibodies, vaccinations, and metronidazole. The patient's condition remained stable with persistent trismus (mouth opening limited to a few millimeters) during the first 12 hours of hospitalization. Twenty-four hours after admission, she experienced a sudden respiratory collapse and a 2-minute hypoxic cardiac arrest. Post-sedation evaluation showed persistent trismus and the need for ventilation, with no change in her general condition compared to before the cardiac arrest. In the following days, her condition worsened with the development of non-stimulus-induced myoclonus in all limbs.

case_report: A 12-year-old male patient, with no prior medical history, came to the emergency department after experiencing pain in the left iliac fossa for 20 days, which had progressively worsened. The patient did not report any fever, weight loss, blood in urine, or other urinary symptoms. During the physical examination, pain was noted upon palpation of the left flank, and fist percussion on the same side was also positive.
test_results: Abdominal ultrasound and contrast abdominal MRI showed a left renal mass, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathies in renal hilum and paraaortic location, with no evidence of metastasis. CT of the chest ruled out pulmonary metastasis. Frozen section biopsy of the renal mass and lymph nodes suggested malignant neoplasia, with an absence of INI1 expression, and positive for EMA, AE1/AE1, and vimentin. Hb electrophoresis confirmed a Hb SC disease.

case_report: A 13-year, 8-month-old Chinese Han boy was seen in the endocrinology department due to short stature observed over the past 7 years. He had a normal birth weight and length following an uneventful pregnancy. There were no reports of back or joint pain, or scoliosis. His motor and cognitive functions were within normal limits. Physical examination revealed a height of 126.4 cm (-4SD), sitting height of 70.5 cm, and weight of 22.5 kg. The boy exhibited disproportionate short stature with a relatively short trunk and barrel chest. His arm span measured 138.0 cm, exceeding his height by 11 cm. He had no dysmorphic facial features and was at Tanner stage 2. No other family members exhibited short stature, abnormal arm span, or a history of degenerative joint disease or hip joint replacement. Serum levels of insulin-like growth factor 1 and thyroid hormone were within normal ranges. Growth hormone stimulation tests (L-dopa and arginine) showed a peak growth hormone level of 22.6 ng/ml, indicating no growth hormone deficiency.
test_results: Radiographs revealed lumbosacral platyspondyly with characteristic superior and inferior humping of the vertebral bodies seen on lateral view. The pelvis was somewhat narrow, and the femoral necks were short. Osteoarthritic changes such as joint space narrowing, extensive osteophytes, were not observed in all involved joints including shoulders, wrists, and knees. His bone age (BA) was 11-year, 2-month old estimated by G-P BA assessment, extremely younger than chronological age. Targeted next-generation sequencing revealed a novel missense variant c.260A>C in the TRAPPC2 exon5 localized to ChromosomeXp22 in the proband, causing p. His87Pro mutation. His mother was found to be heterozygous for the c.260A>C substitution, confirming her carrier status, whereas the father was found to be normal.

case_report: Patient 1, a female aged 10 years and 4 months, is the first of two children of a healthy 38-year-old woman and a non-consanguineous 48-year-old man, with no notable family history. She was conceived naturally. The fetal ultrasound scan at gestational week (gw) 12 was normal. At gw 21, a choroid plexus cyst and echogenic intracardiac focus were detected, and the biparietal diameter was at the 95th centile at gw 21 and greater than the 95th centile at gw 33 with normal cerebral morphology. She was born at the 34th gw with a weight of 3080 g (90-97th centile), length of 49 cm (90th centile), and head circumference of 35.6 cm (97th centile). At birth, a diffuse capillary malformation involving the trunk and limbs was observed, along with cutaneous syndactyly of the 2nd and 3rd toes. During the first year of life, a plantar epidermal nevus and a small hemangioma, which later disappeared, were noted, along with left hemihyperplasia (detected at the age of 3 months). Cardiac and abdominal ultrasound scans were repeatedly normal.
test_results: Brain MRI scans detected increased peritrigonal signal of white matter at the age of 10 months and focal hemimegalencephaly with perisylvian polymicrogyria at the age of 7 years.

case_report: A 59-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric or neurological history presented to the emergency department with significant anxiety related to unemployment. Communication was possible only after administering lorazepam. Clinical examination revealed delusional thoughts, including the belief that her thoughts were being controlled and audible. The patient was transferred to the Department of Psychiatry, Social Psychiatry, and Psychotherapy. She reported that her mother had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease at age 50 and died at age 65. No other family members had neurological or psychiatric conditions. Laboratory tests showed mild hypothyroidism post-hemithyroidectomy, for which levothyroxine was prescribed. Hyponatremia was also found, and sodium chloride tablets were given, along with advice to reduce excessive water intake. Complete blood count was normal, and there were no deficiencies in folic acid, vitamin B12, or ceruloplasmin, nor infections with HIV, Borrelia burgdorferi, or Treponema pallidum. Antipsychotic treatment with risperidone was started, but delusional thoughts persisted. Due to sleep disturbances, chlorprothixene was initiated, and risperidone was stopped. Neurological examination showed dysdiadochokinesis (mainly in the left hand), mild hyperkinetic movements (notably restlessness), bradykinesia in the finger-tapping test, and a broad-based gait, without rigidity, tremor, or postural instability. The patient became increasingly disoriented and exhibited long-term memory deficits, fear, agitation, and perseverations, indicating cognitive impairment. Cognitive function tests (CERAD+) revealed deficits in verbal recognition, severe visuospatial impairment, reduced semantic and phonological fluency, and decreased cognitive flexibility, confirmed by the Trail Making B test. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMST) and frontal assessment battery (FAB) scores were 22/30 and 10/18, respectively, indicating reduced mental flexibility, motor programming, environmental autonomy, and inhibitory control. The SCID-II showed no personality disorder, and the patient refused the Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II).
test_results: Genetic testing revealed 42 CAG repeats in the HTT gene.

case_report: A 63-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of dry cough and fatigue. Initial symptoms included dry cough and fatigue without an apparent cause. The patient did not report fever, headache, or night sweats. A chest CT scan performed at a local hospital identified a solitary solid pulmonary nodule in the right lower lobe. The patient received a 10-day course of intravenous cephalosporin without improvement. His medical history included a 20-year history of asthma. He had worked as a miner in Mexico for 6 months, one year prior to his hospital visit. Laboratory tests indicated decreased levels of total protein (60.6 g/L), albumin (33.6 g/L), and alkaline phosphatase (33 IU/L), with other routine laboratory results within normal limits. A follow-up chest CT scan showed a 1.4 × 1.3 × 1.1 cm solitary solid nodule with a smooth margin in the right lower lobe and multiple small nodules measuring 0.1 to 0.2 cm with mild ground-glass opacity in both lungs.
test_results: Histological examination of biopsy tissue from a thoracoscopic right lower lobectomy revealed multiple granulomas with caseous necrosis, in which scattered thick-walled spherules containing endospores were observed following PAS and GMS staining.

case_report: A 15-day-old female infant was referred for evaluation of an umbilical swelling and noticeable pulsations in the epigastric region, both of which had been observed since birth. case_report: A 73-year-old male with a history of non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction managed with medical therapy, hemorrhagic rectocolitis diagnosed in 2002 under anti-TNF-α therapy currently in histological and endoscopic remission, and an epidermoid cyst infection, presented with ongoing inflammatory abdominal pain. The patient resided in a semi-rural area and did not report any specific contact with livestock. Computed tomography angiography (CTA) identified an infra renal abdominal aortic aneurysm with a maximum diameter of 42 mm, featuring anterior parietal thickening and extension to the left common iliac artery. An [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18FDG-PET/CT) scan showed significant uptake in the aneurysm wall, with no evidence of large- or medium-vessel vasculitis. The patient was assessed for zoonotic infections.
test_results: Immunofluorescence assay revealed significantly elevated C. burnetii immunoglobulin titers: IgG phase I of 1:512, IgM of <1:32, and IgG phase II of 1:256.

case_report: A 49-year-old male of Chinese descent presented with proteinuria, indicated by a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) of 153.8 mg/mmol during routine lab tests. His creatinine level was 109 µmol/L, with an estimated GFR of 68 mL/min/1.73. He was asymptomatic except for newly diagnosed hypertension, for which he was prescribed perindopril 4 mg daily a week before his first nephrology visit. His medical history included dyslipidemia diagnosed six years prior, and he had been taking rosuvastatin 10 mg daily for the past 3–6 months. He was a current smoker with a 30-year history of smoking. There was no family history of kidney disease; his father had died of pancreatic cancer and his mother of liver cancer. Other immediate family members were healthy. On examination, his blood pressure was 136/80 mmHg, and the physical examination was otherwise normal with no signs of connective tissue disease or lipoidosis. Laboratory results showed serum creatinine at 109 µmol/L and serum albumin at 39 g/L. He had subnephrotic range proteinuria with an ACR of 153.8 and 24-hour urine protein of 2.66 g/day. Urinalysis was positive for 0.3 mg/L hemoglobin, but urine microscopy revealed only 1–3 erythrocytes per high power field. Antinuclear antibody was weakly positive, but an autoimmune review was negative. Tests for C3, C4, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, glomerular basement membrane antibodies, hepatitis B and C serology, HIV, and cryoglobulins were all negative. Hemoglobin A1C was 5.6%. Serum protein electrophoresis showed no monoclonal protein. A fasting lipid profile revealed total cholesterol at 8.82 mmol/L, LDL at 6.16 mmol/L, HDL at 1.12 mmol/L, and triglycerides at 3.38 mmol/L. An ApoE level was ordered but not processed. The patient's perindopril dosage was increased to 16 mg daily, but the ACR remained elevated at 173.8 mmol/L.
test_results: Renal biopsy contained up to 20 glomeruli by light microscopy. The biopsy showed that most glomeruli were enlarged and had markedly dilated capillary lumina filled with amorphous to mesh-like material that stained pale with hematoxylin and eosin, Periodic Acid Schiff, Jones’, and Masson trichrome, but positive with Oil-Red-O. No foam cells were seen. There was mild-to-moderate mesangial expansion with hypercellularity (segmentally up to 8–9 nuclei). Segmental sclerosis was noted within up to 2 glomeruli in a perihilar distribution. Silver stained sections showed variable thickening and duplication of the glomerular basement membrane in some areas with no epimembranous spike formation. Chronic tubulointerstitial injury (fibrosis and atrophy) was seen in 5% of sampled cortex. There were no red blood cell casts. Interlobular-sized arteries and arterioles were unremarkable, and peritubular capillaries were unaffected. Direct immunofluorescence showed no significant staining for IgG, IgM (trace), IgA, C1q, C3, kappa, lambda, fibrin/fibrinogen, or albumin. Immunofluorescence on paraffin-embedded tissue after pronase digestion showed segmental mesangial and capillary wall staining for IgM (1+), kappa (1+), and lambda (1+) in segmentally sclerosed glomeruli. The intracapillary material did not stain for any of the immunoreactants tested. On electron microscopy, there were large extracellular vacuolated particles that focally showed a laminated structure. Glomerular basement membranes surrounding this material were thickened, with flocculent material expanding the subendothelial space and focally containing granules and vacuoles. There was mild-to-moderate podocyte foot process effacement. A segment without intracapillary material was unremarkable with normal basement membrane thickness, preserved podocyte foot processes, and no immune deposits.

case_report: A 37-year-old female patient was referred to Hacettepe University, Pediatric Genetics Department due to unusual facial characteristics. She is the second child of healthy parents who are not related by blood. She was born at term via spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birthweight of 1,500 g (below the 3rd percentile). Her birth length and head circumference were not documented. The patient experienced delayed psychomotor development, beginning to walk and speak after the age of 3 years. She learned to read and write following participation in a rehabilitation program. During childhood, she was assessed for developmental delay, short stature, learning disability, recurrent upper respiratory infections, and constipation, but no diagnosis was established. Laboratory evaluations, including cranial imaging, echocardiography, and blood biochemistry, were normal except for subclinical hypothyroidism and osteoporosis. Since adolescence, she has had generalized anxiety disorder and hypochondriasis, with symptoms worsening over time. In the past five years, she has had difficulty falling asleep. Her family described her as overly friendly. On physical examination, her weight was 42 kg (below the 3rd percentile), height was 145 cm (below the 3rd percentile), and head circumference was 52 cm (−2 standard deviations). Notable facial features included a long face, long neck with sloping shoulders, low-set ears, periorbital fullness, short nose, wide mouth, small jaw, and malar flattening. She was talkative and sociable, with prolonged eye contact and phases of staring during the examination.
test_results: Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis revealed 46,XX.ish del(7)(q11.2 q11.2) (ELN-).

case_report: An 84-year-old man visited the Neurology clinic due to worsening symptoms of restless legs syndrome (RLS) that did not improve with a total daily dose of 4 mg ropinirole. He had been initially prescribed 0.5 mg ropinirole nightly by his primary care provider (PCP) about 4 years earlier, which had initially improved his symptoms significantly. However, over the past year, his symptoms worsened and began occurring earlier in the day. His ropinirole dosage was increased to 2 mg during the day and 2 mg at night, but this provided only minimal relief. His medical history included major depressive disorder managed with sertraline and a history of prostate cancer diagnosed at age 65. He was a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history. case_report: A 60-year-old man was brought to the emergency room at Aichi Medical University Hospital from an outpatient clinic due to difficulty breathing the day after receiving the second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (Pfizer/BioNTech). He had no prior history of respiratory or allergic conditions. He was a current smoker with a 40 pack-year history and had not changed cigarette brands. For the past two years, he had been keeping seven budgerigars (Melopsittacus undulatus) and four cockatiels (Nymphicus hollandicus) indoors. He was admitted to the hospital and started on sulbactam ampicillin for suspected pneumonia. His body temperature was 36.3°C, and his partial pressure of arterial oxygen was 68.7 Torr while receiving 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula. Chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) revealed bilateral ground glass opacities without nodules or mosaic attenuation. Laboratory tests indicated normal peripheral white blood cell and eosinophil counts, but elevated levels of serum LDH, C-reactive protein (CRP), Kreb von den Lugen-6, and SP-D. Pulmonary function tests showed restrictive changes with reduced diffusing capacity.
test_results: The results of BALF obtained from the B5 right middle lobe (46% of recovery rate) showed elevation of total cell counts (5.27 × 105/mL), eosinophils (37%), and lymphocytes (34%) with a low CD4/CD8 ratio (0.37). No bacterium or fungus was isolated from cultures of BALF. A TBLB specimen obtained from the B8 right lower lobe showed lymphocytic alveolitis without granuloma and eosinophilic infiltration. The serum immunoglobulin (Ig) E level was low, and IgE specific for feathers and droppings of budgerigars were negative. Moreover, tests for autoimmune antibodies were negative.

case_report: A 66-year-old female experienced pain on the right side of her tongue, starting a day after receiving her first AZD1222 vaccination. Her medical history includes hypertension, osteoporosis, hyperthyroidism, and headaches. Prior to visiting our clinic, she was given chlorhexidine gluconate solution (0.12%), which worsened her symptoms. At another dental clinic, she was prescribed clonazepam (0.5 mg/day) and gabapentin (200 mg/day) for neuralgia, but these medications did not alleviate her pain. The pain was described as throbbing and persistent throughout the day. Additionally, she reported a burning sensation when food or toothpaste came into contact with the affected area. The pain intensity varied, typically ranging from NRS 3 to 7 during flare-ups.

case_report: A 32-year-old man presented with episodes of headache and dizziness over the past month and an unusual rhythm observed in the ECG. Despite a normal clinical workup for headaches and symptomatic treatment, there was no improvement. The patient reported no cardiac symptoms such as palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, or syncope and was able to engage in strenuous physical activities like climbing and playing football without difficulty. His past medical history and physical examination were unremarkable. Notably, his mother experienced a cerebrovascular accident at the age of 35 and received a permanent pacemaker. Additionally, his brother had a permanent pacemaker implanted at the age of 13 following several episodes of seizures.
test_results: In echocardiography, both atria were mildly enlarged and no A wave was observed in the tricuspid and mitral inflow pulse in Doppler recording. Tissue Doppler imaging also confirmed no visible atrial contracture. In a 24-hour electrocardiogram Holter monitoring, the patient’s minimum, maximum, and mean heart rates were 44, 45, and 59 bpm, respectively. The patient’s electrophysiological study revealed a wide complex QRS bradycardia (40 – 45 bpm) without any discernable P wave. Also, no potential for the right atrium could be recorded, and electrical stimulation failed to provoke atrial depolarization. There was a lack of atrial capture during high output, right atrium and coronary sinus pacing, without His potential around the His bundle. No ventricular arrhythmia could be induced during programmed ventricular stimulation.

case_report: A 39-year-old Chinese male presented with a 9-year history of progressive weakness in all four limbs. At the age of 30, he initially experienced difficulty holding objects with his right hand. Over time, he developed increasing weakness in his limbs, an unsteady gait, numbness, and mild speech difficulties. He underwent treatments including glucocorticoid pulse therapy, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasma exchange, but his condition continued to deteriorate. Physical examination revealed muscle strength of 4/5 in the proximal upper and lower extremities and 3/5 in the distal extremities. There was noticeable atrophy in the bilateral interphalangeal muscles, thenar and hypothenar muscles, and the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. Additional findings included muscle fasciculations, absent deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral positive Babinski signs. The patient's Barthel index score was 85.
test_results: Analysis of CSF showed elevated protein levels of 0.69 g/l but normal cell counts and glucose levels. Oligoclonal bands were negative. The value of arylsulfatase A was 133.97 nmol/17 h/mg (normal range: >58 nmol/17 h/mg). Nerve conduction studies revealed severe motor and sensory demyelinating polyneuropathy associated with axonal damage. The needle EMG showed fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves in the right biceps and tibialis anterior. Wide duration, high amplitude, and polyphasic form were observed in the right biceps during mild voluntary activity, which indicated neuropathy. MRI of the brain showed asymmetric consecutive hyperintensity along bilateral corticospinal tracts (from the precentral gyrus down to the pons on the left and in the level of the centrum semiovale on the right) and in the optic radiation and corpus callosum on T2W and T2W FLAIR images. MRI of the spinal cord revealed inconsecutive lesions with high signal intensity in the cervical cord at C1–C5 on T2W images. WES detected two missense GALC mutations in this patient: c.461C>A (p.P154H) and c.1065G>C (p.W355C).

case_report: A 12-year-old male with no notable birth or medical history presented with concerns about lower abdominal distention and had reduced his food intake over the past 3 months. He engaged in excessive exercise relative to his food intake. Despite significant weight loss, he expressed concerns about his abdominal size. During the initial consultation, he was observed to be very lean with a body mass index (BMI) of 11.5 kg/m2 and had a heart rate of approximately 40 beats/min, indicating sinus bradycardia. Enteral nutritional supplements were administered to improve his weight. Seven days after the first visit, he was emergently hospitalized due to disorientation. On admission, his height was 145 cm, weight was 20.9 kg (BMI: 9.9 kg/m2), and he presented with impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) E3V4M6), bradycardia (heart rate ~40 beats/min), and slow breathing (respiratory rate ~10 cycles/min). Blood gas analysis and blood tests showed hypercapnia, hypoglycemia, and elevated levels of creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and transaminases. His movements were slow but not paralytic, and his cranial nerves were intact. Due to chronic hypoglycemia and dehydration, rapid correction was avoided to prevent complications such as refeeding syndrome, heart failure, pleural effusion, and ascites. Hypoglycemia and dehydration were corrected slowly (glucose infusion rate: 0.6–1.0 mg/kg/min; water: 20 mL/kg/day). On the second day of admission, he developed further impaired consciousness (GCS E1V1M1) and low blood pressure, necessitating transfer to the intensive care unit (ICU). After correcting hypoglycemia and dehydration, his consciousness improved, and he was transferred to the general ward on the third day. On the fourth day, hepatic transaminases peaked with aspartate transaminase (AST) at 4,782 U/L and alanine transaminase (ALT) at 2,265 U/L, along with coagulopathy (prothrombin time (%): 28%). Liver support therapy, including glucose infusion and enteral nutrition, was provided, leading to gradual improvement in AST and ALT levels.
test_results: T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images showed a localized high-signal area from the cortex to the white matter of the fusiform gyrus to the parahippocampal gyrus near the left hippocampus. The cortex in high-signal lesions is thickened, the boundary between white matter and cortex is indistinct and localized, and there is no tendency for invasion into the surrounding white matter. There was no contrast enhancement.
Orpha_name: Isolated focal cortical dysplasia type II

case_report: A 58-year-old male with a history of end-stage heart failure due to dilated cardiomyopathy, who had received a left ventricular assist device (LVAD) as a bridge to transplant, presented with recurrent fever episodes, abnormal fatigue, and elevated infection parameters, along with kidney retention measures in laboratory tests. Despite empiric intravenous antibiotic therapy with Ampicillin/Sulbactam, and subsequent switches to Ciprofloxacin and Fosfomycin, the infection persisted. Upon transfer to our center, positron emission tomography (PET-CT) identified an anterior intrapericardial inflammation process involving the outflow graft of the LVAD and caudal parts of the pacemaker lead. Blood cultures revealed Staphylococcus aureus, leading to an adaptation of antibiotic therapy to Flucloxacillin based on the antibiogram. During treatment, the patient experienced new fever episodes (38.9 °C / 102 °F), mental confusion, and visual disturbances described as “dots and stars.” Neurological examination revealed left homonymous hemianopsia without other notable findings.
test_results: Cerebral computed tomography (CCT) constituted spheres of atypical bleeding in both hemispheres and extra-axial blood formations in the left hemisphere with no dynamics in repeated CCT after six hours. Contrast CCT found two hypointense parietal and occipital areas with scalloped microvascular blood impurities, with a hyperintense 2.5 cm ring enhancement with poorly definable circumvent at the right upper parietooccipital region including a surrounding edema.

case_report: A 33-year-old male presented with difficulty in mouth opening since childhood. There was no history of head-and-neck trauma or maternal exposure to harmful agents. No signs of cognitive impairment were observed. The medical history was unremarkable, with no congenital heart diseases. The patient's family history included similar complaints in his brother. Physical examination showed facial asymmetry with the angle of the mouth deviating to the left and loss of malar prominence. The left eye had epibulbar dermoids, preauricular tags, and an elevated orbital floor. There were no disturbances in the central nervous system, cleft lip/palate, dental development, cognitive function, vertebral structure, heart, growth, lungs, labyrinth, tracheoesophageal region, kidneys, or genitourinary system. Intraoral examination revealed a mid-line deviation to the left, a tilted occlusal plane, and lower anterior crowding.
test_results: OPG revealed mandibular deficiency on the left side, with steeping of the gonial angle and reduction in the size of the left mandibular ramus region with hypoplasia of the condylar and coronoid region. CBCT scan measurements were in agreement with OPG findings.

case_report: A 29-year-old male presented to the emergency department in July 2019 with pain in the left foot, specifically around the second and third metatarsal heads, which began after playing football. The patient, originally from the Indian subcontinent, had been living and working as a healthcare worker for several years. An initial radiograph of the left foot was normal. One month later, a repeat radiograph showed a subtle periosteal reaction at the neck of the second metatarsal. The patient was treated conservatively for a stress fracture. Six months later, he returned with persistent pain that had not resolved. He was fully weightbearing and reported no systemic symptoms such as fever or night-sweats. Physical examination revealed a firm mass over the forefoot without pain on palpation. A subsequent radiograph showed an expansile lesion at the distal diaphysis of the second metatarsal with extensive periosteal erosion. Urgent outpatient CT and MRI of the foot were performed. CT confirmed an expansile lesion centered on the second metatarsal neck with several foci of increased attenuation within the lesion. MRI showed the lesion with low signal on T1 and heterogeneous increased signal on T2 weighted sequences, along with avid enhancement within the lesion and the marrow of the second metatarsal diaphysis. Staging CT of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed calcified mediastinal lymph nodes and prominent left inguinal nodes, while the lungs were clear.
test_results: Histology demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with a single acid fast bacillus within the necrotizing debris.

case_report: A 60-year-old woman visited the outpatient clinic after a lung mass was incidentally found on chest computed tomography (CT) during a routine medical check-up. Physical and laboratory examinations showed no significant abnormalities. She had no history of medical illness and had never smoked. An initial chest radiograph showed a nodular opacity in the right middle lung field. Chest CT revealed a mass approximately 3.1 cm in diameter with a spiculated margin and heterogeneous enhancement in the right lower lobe of the lung, extending into the right major fissure. Additionally, there were adjacent ground-glass opacities located posterior to the mass.
test_results: Microscopic examination showed that tumor cells were arranged in diffuse pattern and reveal round nuclei without prominent nucleoli and moderate amount of cytoplasm. The tumor cells were diffusely stained with p53, thyroid transcription factor-1, and Ki-67 on immunohistochemical analysis. On histological examination, the tumor was grossly 1.8×1.5 cm-sized and ashen gray-colored mass with ill-defined margin. The mass was firm to palpation without pleural, vascular, and lymphatic invasion. It was composed of large epithelioid malignant cells with undifferentiated appearance, syncytial growth, and adjacent reactive lymphoplasmacytic cells influx. Moreover, some of the malignant cells were positive for in situ hybridization with EBV-coded small RNA (EBER). Any glandular and squamous cell differentiation was not detected.

case_report: An 18-year-old male with a history of four years of bipolar affective disorder presented with symptoms including decreased need for sleep, overactivity, excessive cheerfulness, overplanning, and overspending. Over the initial two years, he experienced multiple episodes of mania, each lasting approximately three weeks, followed by spontaneous recovery. Intermittently, he had depressive episodes characterized by poor sleep, reduced appetite, lethargy, sad mood, and lack of interest in activities. In the past year, he sought treatment from various medical facilities but did not adhere to long-term management. During his most recent manic episode, he was prescribed olanzapine 10 mg/day, aripiprazole 15 mg twice daily, and sertraline 100 mg/day by a psychiatrist. After one week, he reported tremors, leading to the discontinuation of aripiprazole and an increase in olanzapine to 20 mg/day, while continuing sertraline 100 mg/day. Two days later, the tremors worsened, and within the following week, he developed rigidity in all four limbs and mutism. He then discontinued all medications and presented with altered consciousness, unresponsiveness to questions or commands, high-grade fever, sweating, and fluctuating blood pressure.
test_results: Non-contrast CT of the brain showed early atrophic changes. His serum CPK at 1622 IU/L.

Dermoscopy revealed homogeneous glomerular vessels throughout the lesion, with an erythematous background and a keratotic border.

case_report: A 24-year-old male from India arrived at the emergency room with a sudden decrease in vision in the left eye that began one day prior. He reported pain and redness in the left eye for the past three weeks, along with a frontal headache. He did not experience nausea, vomiting, cough, fever, night sweats, changes in appetite or weight, joint swelling, or skin rash. There was no history of contact with tuberculosis patients or sick individuals, nor any recent travel to his hometown. He had no known history of ocular or systemic diseases such as diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, or systemic vasculitis. His surgical and drug history were unremarkable. On examination, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and counting fingers in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye was normal. The left eye showed moderate conjunctival injections, micro-cystic corneal edema, a clear lens, trace cells in the anterior chamber, 360-degree iris neovascularization, and a sluggish, slightly dilated pupil. Intraocular pressure measured 11 mmHg in the right eye and 45 mmHg in the left eye. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed vascular sheathing and peripheral ischemic retina with neovascularization. The left eye fundus showed vitreous hemorrhage, intraretinal hemorrhage, extensive retinal ischemia reaching the macula, and vascular sheathing. Systemic examination was normal.
test_results: The wide field angiography of the right eye showed mid-peripheral areas of vascular leakage and vascular staining representing retinal neovascularization and vasculitis, respectively. The left eye illustrated an extensive area of persistent hypo-fluorescence involving the macula along with vascular staining.

case_report: A 38-year-old Caucasian female with no significant prior medical history presented to the gynecological clinic with polymenorrhea. She reported experiencing abdominal discomfort in the right hypochondrium for the past 4 months, which had been gradually increasing. The discomfort was described as a feeling of fullness that worsened after eating. Her obstetric history included a cesarean section 6 years ago. She is a current smoker and has a family history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Physical examination revealed a soft, non-distended, and non-tender abdomen with a palpable mass in the right hypochondrium. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory tests indicated anemia with a decreased RBC count (3.2 × 10^6/μl), hemoglobin (10.9 g/dl), and hematocrit (32.2%). Abdominal ultrasound showed a 9.1 × 7.3 cm heterogeneous mass in the right hypochondrium and an approximately 5 cm cystic lesion on the left ovary. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed an 11.5 × 8.5 × 9 cm well-defined mass adjacent to the inferior margin of the liver with calcified areas, and no enlargement of para-aortic lymph nodes. During laparotomy, a large mass was found occupying the mesentery and was completely excised after releasing adhesions with the ascending colon.
test_results: Pathology specimens revealed prominent, hyalinized penetrating capillaries, rearranged lymphocytes and regression in lymph follicles.

case_report: A 10-week-old girl, born full-term with maternal hypertension during pregnancy, had no significant past medical or family history. She presented with a one-day history of multiple episodes of nonbilious vomiting, blood in stool, lethargy, and fussiness. Physical examination revealed a diffusely tender abdomen with mild distension and audible bowel sounds. No skin vascular lesions were observed. Abdominal ultrasound indicated colocolic intussusception without significant interloop fluid collection, and color Doppler flow was noted within the walls of the intussuscipiens and intussusceptum. An air contrast enema was used to attempt reduction of the intussusception, initially located at the rectosigmoid junction. With pressure maintained below 120 mm·Hg, the intussusception was reduced to the proximal descending colon, but free intraperitoneal air was detected via fluoroscopy. Laparoscopic exploration identified an intussusception at the distal descending colon with fibrinous exudate along the descending colon, indicating a perforation site. A segmental colonic resection with anastomosis was performed. The resected large intestine segment showed a telescoped section with the intestinal wall measuring 0.2 to 0.5 cm. A small perforation was identified, but no gross vascular malformation was evident. Microscopic examination revealed mucosal ischemic changes with vascular congestion and a vasoformative anomaly in the submucosa, involving the overlying mucosa where the lamina propria contained a dense network of capillary-sized vascular spaces.
test_results: Immunohistochemistry revealed that the endothelium was positive for vimentin, CD31, CD34, GLUT-1, and nonreactive for D2-40.

case_report: A 7-year-old male patient presented to Children’s Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine following a canine-induced injury. The patient received five intramuscular injections of a purified and concentrated Vero cell rabies vaccine (PVRV) over 25 days as a preventive measure. Prior to the rabies vaccination regimen, the patient had a haircut, and both scalp and hair appeared normal. Approximately one week after the final PVRV dose, the patient developed a solitary patch of hair loss on the scalp, which progressed to seven distinct areas of hair loss within the following month. Physical examination revealed multiple non-erythematous, non-scaly patches of hair loss. Anamnesis with the parents indicated no recent medication intake or significant medical history temporally associated with the onset of the hair loss, from the period of rabies vaccination to the development of the condition.
test_results: Dermoscopic analysis revealed yellow dots and the characteristic “exclamation mark” hair pattern. Laboratory evaluations reported all trace element levels within normal limits.

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with a recurrent lump in the right lumbar region. There were no associated urinary or bowel complaints. She had undergone surgery twice for similar lumps in a rural hospital 10 and 3 years prior. Her discharge card from the previous surgery indicated a diagnosis of lymphangioma. Case papers from the first surgery 10 years ago were not available. On physical examination, a lump in the right lumbar region just lateral to a previous paramedian incision was palpated. The rest of the abdomen was unremarkable. Ultrasonography revealed a multicystic complex mass in the right lumbar region measuring 25×8×7 cm. A computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a 25×10×6.5 cm well-defined, non-enhancing, lobulated, multiloculated cystic lesion in the right paracolic gutter on the lateral aspect of the ascending colon. Inferiorly, it was abutting the lateral wall of the urinary bladder. Similar morphology lesions were observed in the pouch of Douglas and mesentery. The patient underwent surgery with a retroperitoneal approach as the majority of the mass was retrocolic in position. An incision was made below and parallel to the 12th rib, extending from the posterior axillary line and going anteriorly towards the umbilicus, with the patient in the left lateral position. Initially, the retroperitoneal component of the lesion was dissected out from the kidney and ureter, and lastly from the retroperitoneal surface of the colon. During this process, the peritoneum was opened and the intraperitoneal component, including the pelvic component, was completely removed. Intraoperative findings showed a cystic multiloculated mass loosely attached to the serosal surfaces of the ascending colon, extending into the pelvis with intraperitoneal extension into the pouch of Douglas. The rest of the appendix, cecum, large and small bowel appeared grossly normal. Both ovaries and the uterus were visualized and found to be normal. The lesion was friable, so care was taken to avoid rupture and contamination of the pelvis with the cyst fluid. Complete resection of the lesion was performed.
test_results: Histopathology showed cystic spaces lined by flattened cuboidal to hobnail epithelium separated by thin fibrous septa. The lining epithelium showed strong immunopositivity for calretinin and immunonegativity for CD31.

case_report: A 26-year-old woman was admitted to the West China Hospital, Sichuan University, China, with a complaint of spontaneous nipple discharge from her left breast for one month. Her medical history included a previous lumpectomy on her left breast due to a palpable mass. The postoperative pathological report indicated a complex fibroadenoma with stromal cell proliferation and local lobulated structures. She reported no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Physical examination revealed a firm mass with a clear margin in the lower inner quadrant near the nipple of the left breast, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter. A single duct non-bloody discharge from the left nipple was observed upon squeezing. There was no evidence of nipple retraction or skin dimpling. Ultrasonography identified mammary duct ectasia and a solid-cystic mass measuring 28 × 20 × 20 mm near the nipple-areola complex (NAC) of the left breast. Galactography of the left breast showed mammary duct ectasia and multiple irregular filling defects in the dilated duct. The mass and the associated mammary duct were removed through a circumareolar incision. Two intraductal neoplastic lesions measuring 20 × 20 × 20 mm and 28 × 20 × 20 mm respectively were found in the dilated duct system. Cytology of the nipple discharge showed no tumor cells.
test_results: The histological examination showed a biphasic tumor, with mesenchymal and epithelial components. The mesenchymal cells highlighted moderate stromal hypercellularity, marked nuclear atypia and occasional mitoses. Ki67 immunohistochemistry to assess the index of proliferation showed 20% to 30% positive.

9. Ki67 immunohistochemistry to assess the index of proliferation showed 20% to 30% positive.

case_report: A 29-year-old female, gravida two, para two (G2P2), experienced a second pregnancy following the loss of her first child due to respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) shortly after birth. Throughout her second pregnancy, regular prenatal ultrasonography was conducted, and there were no complications such as polyhydramnios or hydrops fetalis. At 30 weeks of gestation, ultrasound imaging identified a solid mass in the left lung. The baby was delivered via cesarean section at 34 weeks of gestation, weighing 2.4 kg and measuring 48 cm in length. The Apgar scores were 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. The newborn exhibited no respiratory issues at birth and was discharged home with stable vital signs. At 20 days old, the infant experienced sudden cyanosis and was admitted to West China Hospital, Sichuan University.
test_results: Chest computed tomography (CT) showed a large mass lesion in the left lower lobe. On gross examination, the lung showed a solid mass measuring 3.3 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.7 cm in size. Microscopically, the tumor surrounded the airway with peribronchial growth and connected to the pleura. No capsule was visualized. The tumor was composed of immature cartilage, highly cellular spindle cells and oval cells interlacing fascicles. The cytoplasm of the spindle cells was eosinophilic. Nucleoli were inconspicuous. There was no central necrosis, anaplasia or pleomorphism. Mitotic figures were rare, and one per ten high-power fields was present in the case. Strong vimentin positivity was observed in the spindle cells and oval cells. Smooth muscle actin (SMA) was strongly positive in the spindle cells, but oval cells showed faint to negative reactivity. S100 was positive for cartilage and negative for spindle and oval cells. CD34 was negative for tumor cells. The Ki67 index was approximately 8%. Pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antibody (EMA), anaplastic lymphoma kinase 1 (ALK-1), desmin and OCT3/4 were negative. No ETV6-NTRK3 fusion or ALK rearrangement was detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Fifty-six next-generation sequencing (NGS) analyses were performed, and JAK2 detected deletion mutations at sites ranging from 780 to 879 (c.780-879del), leading to a frameshift mutation in exon 7. SMO found a point mutation at the acceptor splicing site of exon 5 (c.1140 + 1G > A).

case_report: A 71-year-old male was referred to our department due to a computed tomography (CT) scan performed for choledocholithiasis, which incidentally showed a large cystic lesion approximately 90 mm in size near the cecum. The patient had a laparoscopic appendectomy at our hospital 12 years ago. Shortly after the appendectomy, the patient was examined for sleep apnea syndrome (SAS). Additionally, he had a total gastrectomy for early gastric cancer 6 years after the appendectomy. Review of the initial surgical report indicated that the appendiceal root was ligated and detached, but the appendectomy was incomplete due to severe inflammation. A retrospective review of a CT scan performed one month post-appendectomy for SAS examination suggested a remnant appendiceal tip. Six years post-appendectomy, a preoperative CT scan for gastric cancer showed a reduced remnant appendix, and during the gastric cancer surgery, no specific findings were noted except for adhesions between the cecum and the abdominal wall. Follow-up CT scans revealed that the appendiceal remnant gradually increased in size seven years post-appendectomy, eventually forming a 92*45 mm cystic lesion.
test_results: The cyst wall contained columnar epithelial and muscular tissues.

case_report: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a congenital hemangioma located on the tip of the nose. He was the sixth child born to parents who are related by blood. His weight was recorded at 4.9 kg, placing him in the 25th–50th percentile, his height was 57 cm, also in the 25th–50th percentile, and his occipitofrontal circumference measured 39 cm, falling within the 50th–75th percentile. Upon initial physical examination, a depression was noted in the left anterior chest wall, the left nipple was positioned higher than usual, the right areola was underdeveloped, and there was hemifacial microsomia on the left side. A chest X-ray revealed dextrocardia and deformities in the left side of the chest wall. Transthoracic echocardiography confirmed dextrocardia and indicated an unusual connection of the right pulmonary veins.
test_results: An axial chest CT confirmed dextrocardia and demonstrated that right heart chambers were positioned posteriorly, left heart chambers anteriorly, and descending aorta was located on the left with normally connected vascular structures. There was asymmetry of the right-sided pectoralis muscles. Hypoplasia of left-sided anterior ribs was demonstrated with a 3D-volume rendered CT scan. Hypoplasia of the left pectoralis muscle was confirmed by ultrasonography.

case_report: A 32-year-old female presented with increasing facial pain localized to the left posterior jaw, extending halfway down the mandible, accompanied by recurrent episodes of shock-like pain rated as grade 4 on the Barrow Neurological Institute (BNI) pain scale. The patient reported a progressive increase in facial pain severity, predominantly on the left side, with occasional right-sided pain and temporal pain. Her medical history includes muscle pain and cramps in the jaw and masseteric region, for which she received multiple Botox injections to the masseters, temporalis, and lateral pterygoids. These treatments provided temporary relief for headaches and pain, but symptoms persisted. Other treatments, including dry needling, physical therapy, medication, and chiropractic adjustments, did not yield long-term relief. The patient also has a history of fibromyalgia and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome. Physical examination revealed left facial numbness. Various pain medications, including Tegretol, were administered for pain management, but results were unsatisfactory. After exploring other treatment options, the patient eventually chose to undergo surgical intervention.
test_results: Head computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed osteomatous growths along the left petrous bone that compressed the trigeminal nerve.

case_report: A 31-year-old Filipino female presented to the emergency department with a high-grade fever lasting 2 weeks. She experienced tender swellings in both groin areas, making walking difficult. She was prescribed a 1-week course of oral augmentin and a subsequent 5-day course of oral moxifloxacin by her family practitioner, but her condition worsened. Ten days after the fever began, she developed a rash on her hands and legs, along with circumoral numbness, but no swallowing or breathing difficulties. Over the next 4 days, the rash spread to her face and ears, accompanied by tender swellings in her armpits. She has no significant medical history and has been working in Singapore as a domestic helper for the past 8 years. She is single, with no sexual activity or gynecologic issues, and has not returned to her native country in the past 3 years. She reported no weight loss, night sweats, joint swellings, arthralgia, alopecia, or dry eyes or mouth. There is no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, her temperature was 39.2°C, pulse rate 120 beats per minute, and blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg. Significant findings included an erythematous papulonodular eruption on the extensor surfaces of both upper and lower limbs, multiple indurated plaques on the face (nasal bridge, brow, outer maxillary area, earlobes, and pinna), ankle edema, and tender, enlarged, and matted cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. Routine investigations showed leukocytosis of 36.18 × 10^9/L, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 80 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein level of 159 mg/L. HIV testing, antinuclear antibody, C3, C4, and double-stranded DNA levels were normal. Serum alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 316 IU/L, with otherwise normal liver transaminases. Her albumin level was 34 g/L. A computed tomography scan of the neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed no intra-abdominal or hepatobiliary source of infection or abscesses but revealed multiple enlarged and necrotic lymph nodes in the axilla and inguinal regions. Closer examination revealed bilaterally thickened greater auricular nerves and lateral peroneal nerves. Complete examination of the central nervous system did not reveal any sensorimotor loss.
test_results: Histological examination showed a diffuse inflammatory infiltrate within the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, sparing the epidermis. The inflammatory infiltrate was composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, foamy macrophages, and neutrophils. Some of the inflammation involved the nerves and adnexal structures. Large numbers of acid-fast bacilli were identified on Fite and Ziehl-Neelsen stains.

case_report: A 28-year-old male with a history of hypertension and aortic stenosis presented with paresthesia of the left foot, stiffness in the lower back and neck, and weight loss of 15 pounds over the past few months. His vitals were stable at presentation. On physical examination, the cranial nerves were intact, and strength and sensation in extremities were normal, except for bilateral foot drop and decreased lower extremity tone. X-rays of the lumbar spine revealed sclerosis of the L4-L5 vertebral bodies and small sclerotic densities in the left iliac bone. An MRI showed a large sclerotic lesion at L5 and small sclerotic lesions in the bilateral iliac. A CT scan of the torso demonstrated prominent bilateral axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, retroperitoneal and iliac lymph node enlargement, and widespread sclerotic foci in the bones.
test_results: A subsequent ultrasound-guided left inguinal biopsy showed atypical lymphoid proliferation. A CT-guided retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy showed mild kappa‑predominant plasmacytosis, with faint monoclonal lambda chains on protein electrophoresis. A lymph node biopsy showed an abundance of plasma cells that were polytypic for kappa and lambda. High kappa (56.3 mg/L) and lambda (31.5 mg/L) hematological test values, with a ratio of 1:79. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) levels were elevated at 1,156 pg/mL. Electromyography studies were consistent with severe axonal loss and demyelination.
