case_report: A 2-year-old Japanese girl presented with erythema and papules on her fingers and knees. After one month, she developed facial erythema following sun exposure. She was treated with a topical corticosteroid, but the skin condition persisted. Four months later, she was referred for further evaluation due to the worsening skin rash. Physical examination showed a characteristic rash on the face, hands, fingers, and knees. There was no clinical evidence of muscle pain. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 8,570/µl, elevated serum creatinine kinase levels at 467 U/l (normal range: 43–290), and aldolase levels at 13.5 U/l (normal range: 2.7–7.5). Indirect fluorescent antinuclear antibody testing revealed circulating autoantibodies against the nucleus at a titre of 1:320 with a speckled pattern. No signs of active lung involvement were found on auscultation or chest X-ray imaging.
test_results: Inflammation of the bilateral quadriceps muscles was detected by magnetic resonance imaging. A biopsy specimen from an erythema on the knee showed dermal perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates and marked oedema of the superficial dermis with mucin deposits. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) for MSAs were positive for Tif1γ and Mi-2 at titres of 60 (cut-off < 32) and 54 (cut-off < 53), respectively. The patient’s sera reacted with Tif1γ and Mi-2 in immunoprecipitation-Western blotting analysis.

case_report: A 66-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department experiencing central crushing chest pain that extended to her left arm and was accompanied by breathlessness. She had a history of chest pain three years prior, during which a coronary angiogram showed unobstructed coronary arteries with only mild atheroma in the left anterior descending artery (LAD). Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, essential hypertension, osteoarthritis, and microcytic anemia. She reported no recent flu-like symptoms, was a non-smoker, and did not use recreational drugs. Her medications were aspirin 75 mg daily, bisoprolol 1.25 mg daily, diltiazem 120 mg three times daily, nicorandil 10 mg twice daily, rosuvastatin 10 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, isosorbide mononitrate MR 120 mg daily, glyceryl trinitrate sublingual spray as needed, metformin 1 g twice daily, gliclazide 40 mg daily, and ferrous fumarate 200 mg twice daily. Physical examination revealed normal findings with a blood pressure of 130/74 mm Hg, sinus rhythm at 69 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Initial and subsequent 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) were normal. Troponin levels measured three hours after the onset of pain were < 3 ng/L (reference range 0 - 14 ng/L). Chest X-ray and baseline blood tests were normal, with a hemoglobin level of 121 g/L and an admitting blood sugar level of 10.7 mmol/L. The GRACE score at presentation was 95, indicating a moderate risk for major adverse cardiac events. She was admitted to the acute cardiac unit for monitoring. Initial treatment included a loading dose of aspirin, clopidogrel, fondaparinux, morphine analgesia, and glyceryl trinitrate spray. Despite initial relief, the pain recurred more severely, prompting a decision for further urgent evaluation.
test_results: Coronary angiography revealed a linear filing defect with an overlying thrombus in the first obtuse marginal branch of the circumflex coronary artery, with otherwise unobstructed coronaries.

case_report: A 28-year-old woman from Syria presented with nephrotic syndrome starting during the 29th week of her first pregnancy. Clinically, she exhibited anasarca with pleural effusions, ascites, and peripheral edema. Upon admission to the hospital, her blood pressure was normal without the use of antihypertensive medication. Initial laboratory results showed spot urine proteinuria of 17.2 g/g creatinine, hypoproteinemia of 3.8 g/dl [6.6–8.3 g/dl], serum albumin of 1.83 g/dl [3.9–5.0 g/dl], and serum creatinine of 1.4 mg/dl [<0.9 mg/dl] with an eGFR of 51 ml/min/1.73 m2 (CKD-EPI formula). There were no preexisting conditions in her medical history. Data on renal function prior to her pregnancy are unavailable. Her medical history revealed that her older sister, who resides in Syria, was also diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome, which progressed to ESRD and was treated with a kidney transplant. The cause of ESRD in the sister remains unidentified, but her kidney disease also began during pregnancy. Both parents, who also live in Syria, reportedly do not have any known renal disease, although they have not been tested for asymptomatic microhematuria or microalbuminuria. Extensive diagnostic workup was performed, revealing negative results for phospholipase A2- (PLA2-) receptor- and thrombospondin type 1 domain-containing 7A (THSD7A) antibodies, as well as ANA, ANCA, and anti-GBM antibodies. Preeclampsia was excluded by a negative soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1/placental growth factor (sFlt/PlGF) ratio. Given the clinical presentation, steroid therapy with prednisolone 1 mg/kg body weight was initiated. At 37 + 0 weeks of gestation, the patient was admitted to the obstetrics department for pharmacological induction of labor. Due to fetal distress and significant vaginal bleeding caused by premature placental detachment during labor, an emergency C-section was performed. case_report: A 4-year-old child, previously in good health, presented with 12 hours of generalized swelling and reduced urine output. The child had experienced a viral upper respiratory infection 7 days prior, without fever, skin lesions, or other symptoms. Physical examination revealed widespread swelling, a weight of 19 kg, height of 115 cm, blood pressure of 140/75 mmHg, respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, and no fever. Laboratory results showed severe anemia with hemoglobin at 6.6 g/dL, low platelet count (60,200/mm3), protein in the urine (55 mg/m2/hour), and impaired kidney function (creatinine 1.7 mg/dL). Additional findings included low albumin levels (1.8 mg/dL), high lipid levels, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (2,082 U/L), increased reticulocytes, and fragmented red blood cells in peripheral blood. The direct Coombs test was negative, and haptoglobin levels were decreased. Serological tests for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis were negative. Complement levels were C3 at 115 mg/dL and C4 at 38 mg/dL. Tests for antinuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic autoantibodies, and anti-cardiolipin antibodies were all negative.

case_report: A 15-year-old male was brought to the emergency department from a local hospital because of sudden gastrointestinal bleeding. He experienced severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood, and passing black, tarry stools. Upon admission, the patient reported no prior symptoms before this bleeding episode. case_report: A 60-year-old male resident of Rosheim, Alsace (northeast France) presented with a nodule on the left orbital floor on 8 July 2008. He had recently traveled to Casamance, southern Senegal, in April 2008. Physical examination revealed a palpable nodular lesion on the left orbital floor. Magnetic resonance imaging identified an inflammatory nodular lesion. The patient underwent antibiotic and steroid therapy, which did not alleviate his symptoms. The nodule was surgically excised in September 2008, measuring 5 cm at its longest dimension.
test_results: Microscopically, it consisted of polymorphic inflammatory granuloma tissue containing plasmocytes and eosinophilic polymorphonuclear cells, with an epitheliogigantocellular granuloma surrounding a nematode cross-section. The nematode cross-section was composed of a thick laminated cuticle with external longitudinal ridges. A polymyarian muscle fiber was visible, surrounded by a pseudocoelomic cavity. Lateral chords and male gonads were visible in some other sections.
diagnosis: Ocular Dirofilariosis due to Dirofilaria repens

case_report: A 46-year-old man with no prior health issues presented with sudden onset of limb ischemia, characterized by pain, paleness, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, and paresthesia, mainly affecting the right limb. An emergency contrast-enhanced CT scan from the aorta to the thighs was performed. The scan ruled out aortic dissection but revealed a complete occlusion of the distal right common, right external, and internal iliac arteries, as well as the common femoral artery. Additionally, there was an occlusion of the left profound femoral artery and mild arteriosclerosis, with the occluded segments showing hypodense thrombotic material. The CT scan also indicated an asymptomatic subacute left-sided kidney infarction and a small right-sided posterior cerebral infarction. The patient had a history of moderate nicotine use and denied symptoms such as dyspnea, fatigue, cough, fever, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, stroke-related symptoms, chest pain, or lower extremity edema. He was not on any long-term medication. Upon admission, his vital signs included a respiratory rate of 20/min, blood pressure of 161/105 mmHg, heart rate of 74/min, and oxygen saturation of 97%. An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed moderate biventricular enlargement and severe systolic left ventricular dysfunction with an estimated ejection fraction of 35%, without wall thickening, valvulopathy, or pericardial effusion. Due to a poor transthoracic acoustic window, transesophageal echocardiography was performed and showed a significant amount of spontaneous echo-contrast in the left ventricular cavity, without signs of wall thickening, valvulopathy, or pericardial effusion. Initial laboratory tests showed a slightly elevated lactate level of 3.2 mmol/l, which increased to 6.3 mmol/l before normalizing post-intervention, and leukocytosis of 11/nl, peaking at 24/nl two days post-admission before normalizing. The patient underwent an emergency open thrombectomy via femoral access on the right limb, along with a full fasciotomy on the right calf. The next day, he developed compartment syndrome in the right thigh and worsening arterial perfusion in the left limb, necessitating fasciotomy of the right thigh and revascularization of the left limb. The left popliteal artery was completely occluded, indicating impaired perfusion, which required urgent revascularization. The revascularization was complex due to a mix of fresh and older thrombus, scarring, vessel shrinking, and perivascular inflammation. It was achieved through hybrid surgery, including open thrombectomy of the femoral and popliteal arteries and all crural vessels, endarterectomy, patching of the popliteal and tibiofibular arteries, stent-angioplasty of the popliteal artery, angioplasty of the anterior and posterior tibial arteries, and fasciotomy of the left calf. Post-surgical lab results indicated rhabdomyolysis with a creatinine kinase level up to 206000U/l and acute renal failure with a creatinine level of 4.7 mg/dl. Further lab tests showed no peripheral eosinophilia, and both p-ANCA and c-ANCA were negative. Tests for antiphospholipid syndrome and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia were negative, and protein C and S levels were normal. Coronary angiography on day 6 showed no coronary heart disease.

case_report: A 5-year-old Moroccan child, raised as a boy, presented to the pediatric emergency department with respiratory distress. He is the only child of a healthy consanguineous couple and was born at home. At the age of two, he underwent posterior hypospadias repair surgery. The parents noted early development of pubic hair. There is a family history of a newborn death for an unknown reason ten years ago. The patient exhibited fever, tachypnea, chest pain with cough, bilateral lung crackles, 90% oxygen saturation, and arterial hypertension of 180/100 mmHg (>99th percentile for age and height). Thoracic radiography showed signs of acute pulmonary edema, prompting immediate treatment. The patient weighed 27 kg (>97th centile for age, SD score: +3) and measured 128 cm in height (SD score: +4). Physical examination revealed pubarche classified as Tanner stage 4, abnormal external genitalia with a 5.5-centimeter phallus-like organ in stretched length, complete fusion of the labioscrotal folds, a single perineal orifice, hyperpigmented scrotum-like structure, non-palpable gonads, Prader Score IV, and no mammary development.
test_results: The patient’s karyotype was 46 XX. Biological tests revealed hypokalemia at 3 mmol/l, normal natremia, and glycemia, low cortisol at 200 ng/dl at 8 a.m., low plasma rennin activity at 40 ng/dl/h, low aldosterone at 3.31 ng/dl. Levels of testosterone, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone were high, respectively, at 100 ng/dl, 850 ng/dl, and 1018 ng/dl. 17OH progesterone was moderately high at 845 ng/dl, with a very elevated deoxycorticosterone DOC dosage at 5619 ng/dl, 11-desoxycortisone at 13 340 ng/dl, and adrenocorticotropic hormone ACTH at 54,3 ng/dl. There was a considerable bone age increase to 13 years for a chronological age of 5 using the Greulich and Pyle method. An abdominopelvic ultrasound (US) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) disclosed a uterine vestige with ovaries and follicles, without testicles.

case_report: A 31-year-old woman, who was pregnant unintentionally, had a routine obstetric ultrasound at 13 weeks of gestation that revealed a mixed mass in the bilateral pelvic cavity. She had regular menstrual cycles and used condoms for contraception. Her pregnancy history included one full-term delivery via cesarean section due to the baby's size. Physical examination showed a soft abdomen with a palpable mass in the left adnexal area, without tenderness. Ultrasonography indicated a normal-sized uterus with a well-defined edge and heterogeneous myometrium. Cystic masses with solid lesions were found in the left adnexa, left and right iliac fossa, and right-posterior uterus, measuring 46*44*39 mm, 30*72*73 mm, 41*59*60 mm, and 43*87*93 mm, respectively. Color Doppler flow imaging (CDFI) showed rich blood flow signals in these areas. The left and right omentum were thickened by 17 mm and 11 mm, respectively. Chest CT revealed diffuse thin-walled cystic changes in both lungs. Laboratory analyses showed an elevated Alpha-fetoprotein level (17.19 ng/mL) and an elevated serum level of cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) at 50.70 U/mL. Serum levels of cancer antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) and cancer antigen 153 (CA-153) were within normal values at 12.95 and 23.70 U/mL, respectively. Serum levels of premenopausal and postmenopausal ROMA were normal at 7.61% and 23.67%, respectively. After admission, the patient requested termination of pregnancy and underwent curettage under B-ultrasound monitoring, which was completed without complications, leading to her discharge. On the 12th day postoperatively, positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET-CT) showed a cystic-solid shadow of soft tissue in the left adnexal area and multiple low-density cystic shadows in the retroperitoneum and both sides of the pelvic cavity. Enlarged left inguinal lymph nodes with increased fluorodeoxyglucose activity were noted, while the right inguinal lymph nodes, intestines, and stomach showed normal activity. 24 days after the curettage, the patient was readmitted. Ultrasonography revealed an increased mixed echo in the left adnexa, measuring 81*84*78 mm, and in the right-posterior uterus, measuring 43*109*106 mm. The mixed echo in the left iliac fossa measured 20*60*64 mm, smaller than before, while the echo in the right iliac fossa remained unchanged. Rich intralesional vascularization was observed. Additional imaging evaluations, including pelvic enhanced CT, enhanced pelvic MRI, computed tomography urography (CTU), and three-dimensional reconstruction, showed heterogeneous enhancement of bilateral ovaries and a widespread cystic-solid mass in the pelvic and retroperitoneum. The upper edge of the cystic part reached the level of the renal artery, encasing the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, iliac artery, and vein, and embedding the middle and lower part of the ureter. The shape and density of both kidneys were normal.
test_results: Immunohistochemical staining results demonstrated the positivity of neoplastic cells for Vimentin, Smooth-Muscle-Actin, Desmin, and Caldesmon, indicating a likely origin from mesenchymal tissue. Subsequent analysis revealed HMB-45 (partially positive) and Melan-A (negative), effectively excluding the possibility of malignant melanoma. Furthermore, negative results for S100, CK pan, and EMA suggested non-neural and non-epithelial tissue origin. Notably, positive staining for D2-40 (vessel +), CD34 (+), and CD31 (+) indicated lymphatic infiltration and the potential for differentiation into vascular endothelium. Ki-67 exhibited a positive value of 5%, suggesting a higher likelihood of benign tumors with a lower proliferation rate and a more favorable prognosis. The results for estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) were positive.

case_report: A 77-year-old Japanese woman, para 7, who went through menopause at age 48, experienced sudden left lower abdominal pain and visited a primary care doctor. Imaging revealed torsion of a left ovarian cyst, and she was transferred to our hospital for surgery. She had a history of left-side breast cancer and underwent total left mastectomy at the age of 67, with no recurrence. She was a carrier of hepatitis C, but her liver function and coagulation were normal, and she was being followed-up without medication. She was taking nifedipine and candesartan cilexetil for hypertension. Her family and psychosocial history were unremarkable, and she had no history of trauma. Imaging showed a 7.5-cm long elliptical mass in the left adnexal region that was continuous with the uterus. The ovary was atrophic due to age and difficult to identify; the appearance of blood and continuity with the surrounding pelvic peritoneum suggested a retroperitoneal hematoma. Physical findings at admission were: height, 144.5 cm; weight, 57.2 kg; body mass index (BMI), 27.4 kg/m2; blood pressure, 112/50 mm Hg; pulse, 72 bpm; and body temperature, 37.1 °C. Physical examination detected no significant findings. On external and internal examinations, no palpable masses or tenderness were noted in the left pelvic area. Transvaginal ultrasound revealed an atrophied uterus; however, the bilateral adnexa could not be identified due to atrophy. The hematoma in the left pelvis was identified, consistent with imaging findings. Blood test results showed a hemoglobin value of 9.5 g/dL, a hematocrit value of 28.4%, a white blood cell count of 7970/μL, and a C-reactive protein level of 0.05 mg/dL. Urinalysis revealed mild occult blood. After admission, the hematoma did not enlarge, and hemoglobin and hematocrit levels remained stable. After 11 days of bed rest, with no exacerbation of the inflammatory response, lower abdominal pain was relieved, and she was discharged. After discharge, further investigation of the cause of her bleeding was planned on an outpatient basis, but 6 days later, she was readmitted due to relapse of symptoms caused by retroperitoneal bleeding from the same site. The hematoma had grown to 11.7 cm, and imaging showed an abnormal vascular network extending from the left side of the uterus to the left adnexal area.
test_results: Angiography of the left renal artery confirmed that the contrast medium discharged from the left kidney did not flow into the inferior vena cava (IVC) but flowed back into the LOV. Subsequent venography also confirmed that the blood from the LRV did not flow into the IVC but regurgitated into the LOV and the lumbar vein. Left ovarian venography showed retrograde blood flow into a dilated and tortuous aneurysm in the pelvis and into the right internal iliac vein via a vein around the uterus. Postembolization LRV imaging showed blood flow to the upper left lumbar vein and vertebral plexus. CT on the second day after the procedure confirmed good embolization of LOV and reduction of the retroperitoneal hematoma to a size of 6.4 cm.

case_report: A 64-year-old man, previously in good health, underwent phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation in the left eye. Prior to surgery, the fundus examination showed no abnormalities, and his best-corrected visual acuity in the left eye was 6/24 due to nuclear sclerosis. A single peribulbar injection of 5 ml lidocaine 2% with epinephrine 1:200,000 was administered using a 25-gauge 25 mm needle through the temporal portion of the inferior lid, without any external compression applied to the eye. On the first day after surgery, the patient reported no issues, and his visual acuity had improved to 6/6. However, examination revealed a left afferent pupillary defect. Dilated ophthalmoscopy of the left eye showed several large confluent peripapillary patches of retinal whitening resembling soft exudates.
test_results: Fundus fluorescein angiography revealed multiple hypofluroscent areas in the peripapillary region corresponding to the areas of the soft exudates. Swept-source optical coherence tomography of the left eye revealed edema of the inner retinal layers with hyperreflectivity of the nerve fiber layers corresponding to the areas of retinal whitening.

case_report: A 57-year-old man with no history of smoking has experienced a persistent nonproductive cough for an extended period. His medical history, as well as family and exposure histories, are unremarkable. After a mild airway infection one month ago, his cough worsened, and he developed exertional dyspnea. He did not report any fever, night sweats, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He was transferred to our hospital for intervention related to 'endotracheal polypoid tumors'. Physical examinations, including auscultation of the neck and chest, did not reveal any abnormalities.
test_results: The thoracic CT showed multiple nodular ingrowths in his trachea, many of which exhibited mineral radiodensities. During white-light bronchoscopy, numerous submucosal nodules arising from the antero-lateral wall of the trachea were observed, starting from the subglottic zone to the carina. The posterior tracheal wall and the bronchial mucosa beyond the carina appeared normal. Histological examination of the biopsied nodules revealed submucosal cartilaginous tissues with foci of ossification and overlying pseudostratified columnar epithelium. There was no evidence of microbes, granuloma, amyloid deposition, or neoplasm.

case_report: A 39-year-old Caucasian female presented to the ophthalmology clinic from the emergency department with sudden onset bitemporal hemianopia. Her medical history included typical migraines. There was no previous ocular history. Family medical history included Factor V Leiden and Protein C deficiency. General and neurological examination showed no abnormalities. CT brain imaging revealed a thin rim of pituitary tissue along the floor of the sella turcica, suggesting a partial empty sella and possible idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). In the ophthalmology clinic, intraocular pressure was within normal limits and best corrected visual acuity was 6/6 bilaterally. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) showed normal retinal anatomy in both eyes. Humphrey 24–2 visual field testing demonstrated enlarged blind spots bilaterally, indicating temporal field defects. Anterior segment and posterior segment examination was normal, with no evidence of tilted or swollen discs in either eye. Magnetic resonance (MR) brain with venogram showed no abnormality or thrombosis. A referral to neurology was made for further assessment. Six months later, neurology review revealed that the patient’s headaches had evolved from sporadic and migrainous to continuous daily headaches over the course of 3 years. The scotoma persisted in the absence of these headaches. The enlarged blind spot despite the absence of papilloedema raised concerns about IIH. A lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 22.5 cm H2O. Cellular analysis of cerebral spinal fluid showed elevated protein and albumin levels of 1300 and 1100 mg/L respectively. White cells were elevated at 11 × 10^9 cells per litre, with normal glucose levels. Oligoclonal bands IgG were present, but these were not paired with a serum sample. Coagulation and vasculitic studies were normal. Subsequent neurology review revealed progressive worsening of headaches and visual disturbances. The patient reported gradual deterioration in hearing, intermittent tinnitus preceding her visual symptoms, episodic vertigo, intermittent word finding difficulties, and subjective short-term memory impairment.
test_results: Fluorescein fundus angiography demonstrated multiple BRAOs and arterial wall hyperfluorescence (AWH) in the infratemporal region of the right eye, while the examination of the left eye remained normal. Repeat MRI at this time demonstrated several small T2 hyperintense foci within the deep white matter tracts of both cerebral hemispheres, the corpus callosum, and the thalamic and basal ganglion in addition to the typical linear ‘spoke’ lesions within the roof of the corpus callosum.

case_report: A 29-year-old African-American active-duty male, previously in good health, visited his primary care physician due to concerns about elevated blood pressure readings. He reported no headaches, visual changes, shortness of breath, chest pain, or lower extremity swelling. He maintained a well-balanced diet and exercised regularly. He intentionally lost five pounds over the past six months and did not experience fatigue or decreased endurance. His medical history included sickle cell trait and right wrist pain from a right scaphoid wrist nonunion fracture six months prior, which showed significant intramedullary cystic changes, a large radiocarpal joint effusion, and loss of bony architecture on radiographs and MRI. He underwent anterior and posterior interosseous neurectomy with distal pole excision and was in occupational therapy. His family history included hypertension in his mother and maternal grandmother. He did not consume alcohol but used e-cigarettes/vaping with nicotine daily. On physical examination, his vitals were normal except for a blood pressure of 153/101 mmHg. He was in no acute distress, had a regular heart rate and rhythm, and clear lungs on auscultation. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory evaluations revealed pancytopenia with mild neutropenia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, renal injury of undetermined chronicity, hypercalcemia, a protein gap, elevated liver-associated enzymes, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis without contrast showed multiple lung nodules with more confluent opacities in the right middle and lower lobes and splenomegaly. The patient was admitted for further evaluation. He received fluid resuscitation and allopurinol and was transferred to an outside hospital due to limited resources at the initial institution. At the outside hospital, he required two packed red blood cell transfusions for anemia, and his hypercalcemia was treated with fluids, calcitonin, and diuretics. A bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy showed unremarkable flow cytometry and immunophenotyping, hypocellular marrow with maturing trilineage hematopoiesis, no increase in blasts, and polytypic plasma. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT) revealed widespread FDG avid non-enlarged lymph nodes with splenomegaly and significant splenic hypermetabolic activity, as well as numerous bilateral punctate pulmonary nodules with areas of consolidation showing hypermetabolic activity. Laboratory results on hospital day two included elevated ACE level, hypercalcemia, and renal injury with nephrotic-range proteinuria.
test_results: Pathology revealing non-caseating granulomatous inflammation with numerous multinucleated giant cells in a background of fibrosis. Stains were negative for atypical mycobacteria and fungal infections.

case_report: A 71-year-old man presented with progressive tremor and rigidity of the head, which had worsened over time. The head tremor appeared approximately six months prior and caused his head to move to the right unintentionally, requiring him to stop it by placing his left hand on his chin. This occurred more frequently during the day while reading or eating. Over the past year, he developed daytime sleepiness, overnight awakenings, forgetfulness, difficulty concentrating, occasional shoulder pain, and loss of smell. Initial examination showed a mini-mental exam (MMSE) score of 30/30. Cranial nerves were intact except for a subjectively reduced sense of smell. Superficial sensation was normal, and reflexes were 2+. A head tremor was observed while sitting and looking straight, with limitations in cervical range of motion, including flexion, rotation, and extension. Gait was normal without balance issues. Muscle tone was normal except for increased tone in the neck. Motor strength was 5/5 in all four extremities. Neck palpation revealed tenderness in the sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles without signs of inflammation. The patient received botulinum toxin A injections every six months. Family history was unremarkable, with no history of movement or neurological disorders. Personal medical history included hypotension, mild bilateral neurosensorial hearing loss, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). He had a cholecystectomy 20 years ago due to gallstones. Routine visits continued every six months. Three years later, the patient experienced balance problems and difficulty getting out of bed in the morning due to a sensation of body 'freezing.' He had trouble negotiating curbs and multitasking while walking. He played golf four times a week but had issues walking on grass and stabilizing after exiting the golf cart. No major falls were reported, though he did fall when rising suddenly from a sitting position. Intermittent hypotension readings and orthostatic hypotension episodes were noted. Examination showed increased rigidity and tenderness in the neck, with improving neck tremor. Muscle tone was increased, more on the right side. Sensation remained normal. While walking, he exhibited decreased arm swing, difficulty turning back, decreased amplitude in upper extremity movements (bradykinesia), and increased rigidity in both upper and lower extremities. He denied hallucinations or memory problems.

case_report: A 41-year-old Japanese woman presented to the cardiology department with chest pain and ST depression in lead II, III, aVf, and V4-6 on electrocardiography. Emergency coronary angiography identified triple-vessel disease with aneurysms in the left anterior descending artery and sinuses of Valsalva. Her medical history included hypereosinophilia and elevated serum immunoglobulin E (IgE), without asthma symptoms. Twelve years prior, blood tests showed an eosinophil count of 11,000 cells/µL and an IgE level of 1,217 IU/mL. She had been treated with steroids and anti-allergic agents, specifically prednisolone and suplatast tosilate. During the current admission, her eosinophil count and serum IgE levels remained elevated. Preoperative examination revealed involvement of multiple systemic arteries, predominantly bilateral, including the internal thoracic, radial, subscapular, iliac, femoral, popliteal, and hepatic arteries, with no involvement of the renal or cervical arteries. Most affected arteries exhibited multiple stenoses or aneurysms. Skin biopsy showed no evidence of vasculitis. She underwent aortic root replacement with a composite mechanical valve graft and coronary bypass surgery using saphenous vein grafts (SVGs) to the left anterior descending artery (LAD), diagonal branch, posterolateral branch, and posterior descending artery (PD). case_report: A 63-year-old male retired US military service member arrived at the emergency department with pain and drainage in his left ankle for one week following an open reduction internal fixation (ORIF). The pain was described as 8/10, sharp, and localized to the medial and lateral aspects of his left ankle, accompanied by serous drainage. He also experienced nausea, chills, and headache, but no fever, vomiting, chest pain, or shortness of breath. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, managed with metformin 500 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg daily. In 2016, he had a methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus infection in his left elbow, treated with cefazolin 8 g IV for six weeks. Documented allergic reactions included flushing, urticaria, and maculopapular rashes to cephalexin, clindamycin, morphine, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (TMP-SMX), penicillin, meperidine, and oxycodone. In the emergency department, he received ketorolac 15 mg IV, vancomycin 2 g IV over two hours, and piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV and was admitted for cellulitis. His vitals were normal without signs of sepsis. Laboratory results showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 57 mm/hour and C-reactive protein of 1.00 mg/dL without leukocytosis. An X-ray of his left ankle indicated soft tissue swelling and evidence of his recent ORIF. Upon admission, vancomycin was continued, and piperacillin-tazobactam was replaced with cefepime 2 g IV. Due to concerns over prior reactions to penicillin, cefepime was recommended. Within hours, he developed mild periorbital edema and a pruritic, erythematous, morbilliform rash on his neck, back, and upper chest. He confirmed allergies to several medications, but this reaction was different from previous ones. The next morning, his periorbital edema increased, and the rash, though improving, remained erythematous. He started cetirizine 10 mg twice daily and diphenhydramine 25 mg every six hours as needed. Vancomycin was adjusted to 1000 mg over 90 minutes. He began tolerating weight-bearing on his left foot and received acetaminophen 650 mg every four hours. The rash persisted the following day, and he developed annular violaceous patches with an erythematous rim on his cheeks and forehead, along with a solitary patch on his left upper back.
test_results: His skin biopsy showed dyskeratotic cells within the epidermis with eosinophils in the epidermis and superficial dermis. Also present was superficial dermal perivascular lymphohistiocytic inflammatory infiltrate with occasional neutrophils.
diagnosis: Generalized Fixed Drug Eruption  induced by Cefepime

case_report: A 53-year-old male presented to the emergency room with left-side chest and flank pain, accompanied by shortness of breath for the past two weeks. The pain was described as a constant, dull ache of moderate intensity in the left flank area, occasionally radiating to the left chest and groin, with no specific factors worsening or relieving it. Additional symptoms included new-onset exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and generalized muscle aches, but no fever. His medical history included end-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to biopsy-confirmed membranous nephropathy, renal vein thrombosis, and hypertension. He had been on hemodialysis for four years and adhered well to outpatient treatments. His medications included aspirin, amlodipine, carvedilol, hydralazine, lisinopril, and sevelamer. During hemodialysis, he received intravenous iron sucrose and doxercalciferol. Physical examination showed a body temperature of 36.9°C, heart rate of 67/min, blood pressure of 175/95 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Decreased breath sounds were noted bilaterally, while heart sounds were normal without murmurs or gallops. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness at the left costophrenic angle. There was no peripheral edema or skin changes. Laboratory findings included leukopenia, normocytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia with a WBC count of 3.3×10^3/μL, hemoglobin of 9.5 mg/dL, MCV of 92 fL, and platelet count of 118×10^3/μL. The comprehensive metabolic panel indicated stable ESRD with a BUN of 24 mg/dL, creatinine of 7.9 mg/dL, normal electrolytes, normal liver function with total bilirubin at 0.3 mg/dL, and normal albumin and total protein at 4.6 g/dL and 7.8 g/dL, respectively. Troponin levels were negative, and INR was normal. Serum iron was 40 μg/dL, and ferritin was 487 ng/mL. Elevated ESR at 57 mm/h and CRP at 10.1 mg/L were noted. Complement C3 was low at 64 mg/dL, while C4 was normal at 15 mg/dL. ANA and anti-DNA antibody tests were negative.
test_results: Transthoracic echocardiography (ECHO) confirmed a large (3.7×2.6 cm) pericardial effusion with indentation of the right ventricle. Anti-histone antibody was positive.

case_report: A 20-year-old woman presented with a slight fever and right lower abdominal pain. Blood tests showed no notable abnormalities, and abdominal computed tomography revealed swollen lymph nodes around the ileocolic region. She was prescribed acetaminophen. Although her symptoms temporarily improved, the right lower abdominal pain worsened a month later. She was hospitalized due to severe abdominal pain and referred to the Department of Gastroenterology. Her body mass index was 19 kg/m2. She had a history of constitutional jaundice but did not drink or smoke. There was no family history of abdominal pain-related disease or resistance to lidocaine. Physical examination at admission revealed localized tenderness in the epigastric region and lower right abdomen. Blood tests showed no notable abnormalities, and abdominal and gynecological ultrasonography did not show any abnormalities, including those related to the mesenteric lymph node. Gastrocolonoscopy also showed no abnormal findings. The patient experienced brief but sharp abdominal pain on movement but not at rest. She could not consume sufficient food at meals due to abdominal pain while sitting. On the seventh day of hospitalization, a medical examination request was made to investigate the cause of abdominal pain. Two localized tender points were identified, one at a right lower abdominal point and the other 3 cm above the navel, both with an area < 2 cm2.
test_results: The Carnett's sign was positive. Hypoesthesia was observed at the same site. We confirmed that there was no obvious lesion caused by the abdominal wall ultrasound in the painful area. We injected 5 ml of 1% lidocaine subcutaneously into the painful lesion and the pain improved soon after.

case_report: A 2-year and 10-month-old girl with no significant medical history was admitted due to a febrile rash persisting for seven days. Laboratory findings on admission included leukocytosis at 21,770/mm3 (neutrophils at 17,220/mm3, lymphocytes at 3,890/mm3, and monocytes at 990/mm3), hypochromic microcytic inflammatory anemia (hemoglobin at 10.4 g/dl, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) at 78.60 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) at 27.50 g/dl, and ferritin level at 443 mg/l), thrombocytopenia at 91,000/mm3, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) at 403 mg/l, accelerated sedimentation rate at 99 mm, and significantly elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) at 2641 IU. Electrocardiogram (ECG) and troponin levels were normal. Serological tests for cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex, and HIV) were negative. Prothrombin time was prolonged, and the peripheral blood smear showed schistocytes, helmet cells, and platelet clumps.
test_results: The cardiac ultrasound revealed coronary dilation.

case_report: A 47-year-old male with a one-year history of exertional shortness of breath and palpitations was admitted due to sudden onset syncopal episodes. He reported no headaches, chest pain, palpitations, leg edema, persistent fever, weight loss, or loss of appetite. Four years ago, he was seen at a trauma center following a bike accident. An X-ray at that time revealed a lytic lesion in the distal end of the right femur, with destruction of the lateral cortex, breaks in the anterior and posterior cortex of the lateral condyle, extension to the distal femoral articular surface, a pathological fracture, and periosteal reaction along the lateral aspect of the distal femur. A CT scan of the right lower femur showed an expansile lytic lesion in the lateral condyle of the femur, with an associated soft tissue mass extending outside the cortical margins, containing calcific densities and bony fragments. A biopsy was taken from the lytic lesion of the fractured lower end of the femur. The patient underwent curettage followed by cement application with cancellous leg screw. Fifteen days later, bone cement removal, bone grafting, and internal fixation with a condylar blade plate were performed. Postoperatively, the patient had minimal restriction of right knee flexion. Clinical and radiological follow-up showed healing of the lesion. The cut section of the curettage material consisted of multiple hemorrhagic and tiny grey-white focal areas. Microscopy revealed bony trabeculae and a tumor composed of sheets of mononuclear stromal cells and many scattered multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells. Histologic diagnosis was a giant cell tumor of the bone. The patient had multiple spotty pigmentations (lentigines) on his trunk for several years. He also had recurrent swelling of the submandibular region, requiring three surgical excisions. Pathological examination of the excised masses showed a poorly circumscribed lesion composed of myxoid nodules containing thin-walled capillaries along with spindle-shaped or stellate fibroblasts, consistent with superficial angiomyxoma. Cardiac examination revealed a normal sinus rhythm at 84 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg. The mitral first heart sound was slightly accentuated, but the pulmonic sound was normal. A Grade-I diastolic murmur was heard over the mitral area, and an opening snap was absent. The lungs were clear, and a chest radiograph showed slight cardiomegaly.
test_results: Trans-thoracic Echo cardiography revealed an intra-cardiac tumour attached to inter atrial septum, which was almost filling the left atrium & obstructing the mitral inflow. Moderate amount of mitral regurgitation was present. Coronary angiogram showed normal epicardial coronary arteries.
